dmlog.text: (the session opens — deliver the opening scene)

Dawn does not come to the Shimmering Maw so much as leak into it. You wake facing east — everyone does here, all of you laid out on the swaying boardwalk-inn like spoons in a drawer, and you don't yet know why, only that the innkeep watched to see that you did — and below the slatted floor the crater burns awake: acres of fused glass, poured in every color a wound can be, catching the low sun and throwing it back up through the boards until the whole hanging village glows from beneath like a lantern with people living inside it. The chains that hold it all groan. Somewhere children are already laughing, and the air is thick with a smell you can't place until you can: burnt sugar and iron, sweet and bloody at once. Against your ribs, under your coat, the thing you carried all this way sits heavy as a confession — the parcel the Ironwood Circle is expecting, the debt that bought your passage to a place no one here knows your old name. A boy of about nine has stopped at the foot of your bedroll. He is looking at the shape under your coat, not at your face. "You came in on the night-chains," he says, matter-of-fact. "They been asking after that. The tree folk. Since before you got here."
dmlog.dmNotes: Opening delivered.

dmlog.text: I keep my face easy and my voice easier, tucking my coat a little closer over the parcel. "The tree folk, is it? Good — a boy who knows who's asking saves everyone time. Tell me straight and there's a coin in it: what do the Ironwood Circle look like when they come asking, and how would I know one to sit down across from before one finds me first?"

The boy's hand is already open at his side, discreet, a professional's palm. He doesn't look at your face — he looks at the crowd, the way a cutpurse does, keeping tally of everyone's business but his own. "Two things give 'em away," he says quietly, watching a woman haul a milk-yoke past. "They don't hurry. Ever. You'll see a body who's got all the time in the world when everyone else is running late — that's one of theirs. And the wood. They carry a piece of it, always, whittled or raw, and they touch it when they think. Like it's telling them things." He finally glances up, quick. "They don't come as a mob. One comes. Sits down friendly. Asks after your health." A pause, and something honest slips through the practiced calm: "The one who's been asking after you — he's patient, mister. Patient's the frightening kind. He'll let a thing ripen 'fore he picks it." His open palm twitches, waiting on the promised coin. Above and around you the morning market of the hanging village is stirring to full noise now, and more than one face in it is turned, just slightly, your way.

payload.name: Batgal Sukhukh
payload.role: boy, street-eyes, cutpurse's palm — Sella's first informant in the Maw

dmlog.dmNotes: Batgal named via play; sold real tells on Ironwood Circle.

dmlog.text: I flick the promised coin into his open palm without looking at it, my eyes already drifting over the turned faces in the market. "Worth every bit. One last thing, and then you were never here." I lower my voice. "A patient man's a man who wants something specific. If I wanted to find a fence, or someone who trades in old debts and older secrets — where in this hanging place would a woman with all the time in the world go looking?"

Batgal makes the coin vanish the way water vanishes into sand — no flourish, just gone. He's already half-turned to leave, and he answers over his shoulder, low enough that it's meant to be the last thing between you. "You won't find a shop for that. Nothing that trades in old debts hangs out a sign." His eyes flick — once, deliberately — toward the far side of the crater, where the boardwalks knot together into something older and heavier, and a great tree grows impossibly straight up out of the glass itself, its roots fused into the colored ruin, black-barked and leafless in the dawn. "But every road in the Maw bends toward the Traitor's Tree eventually. Folk go there to make bargains they don't want witnessed. The tree's been keeping secrets since before the village hung — that's the story, anyway." And then, so quiet you almost lose it under the market noise: "If a patient man wanted to catch someone, that's where he'd wait. It's polite, see. Lets you come to him." Then the boy is simply not there anymore, folded into the crowd, and you're left with a coin lighter, a direction, and the cold little arithmetic of a man who's happy to let you walk to him.

payload.name: coin
payload.note: paid Batgal for information

payload.name: The Traitor's Tree
payload.note: black-barked tree fused into the glass crater; where unwitnessed bargains are struck; rumored the patient Ironwood man would wait here

dmlog.dmNotes: Named the Traitor's Tree myth; telegraphed the trap.

dmlog.text: I settle back onto my bedroll, in no apparent hurry — let the watching faces see a woman who's tired from the road and nothing more. The Traitor's Tree can wait; a patient man's own game is patience, and I'll not walk into his parlor blind and hungry. First I want to know what I'm actually carrying, so I turn my shoulder to the crowd, ease the parcel out under the cover of my coat, and check whether it's sealed — and whether I can learn what's inside without leaving a mark that says I looked.

You turn your shoulder to the crowd, all road-weary slump, and let the parcel slide into your lap under the coat's shadow. It's a flat thing, wrapped in oilcloth the color of old tea and bound crossways with waxed cord — and where the cord knots there's a seal, a disc of dark ironwood pressed into red wax, grain and all, the kind of mark you can't forge because the tree that made it grows in exactly one place. The wax is your enemy. Lift the seal wrong and it crazes, spiderwebs, and any patient man who's handled a hundred of these will read a broken seal the way you read a marked card. But you have thieves' tools warm in your palm, a slim horn probe among them, and the dawn is cold enough to keep the wax stubborn. This is a matter of hands — of easing the cord out from under the disc without stressing the wax, peeling the oilcloth back along its own folds, and reading what's inside before the whole thing has to go back looking untouched.
dmlog.dmNotes: Plot object authored: Ironwood Slab = map of anchor-chains + hit-list. DC15 SoH.

dmlog.text: The cord is tighter than it looked, the wax more brittle, and the instant you feel it start to go you know you've lost — the seal parts from the oilcloth with a dry tick and a wedge of it flakes away, the ironwood disc split clean across its grain. There's no reading this as anything but opened. Whatever's inside, you'll learn it now with the door already closed behind you: a slab of black ironwood, a carved map of the crater's chains, a scored list of a dozen names with two struck out. You have the knowledge. You also have a broken seal in your lap and a debt-holder in this village who values nothing so much as knowing exactly who touched his things.

payload.name: The Ironwood Slab
payload.note: carved map of the crater's anchor-chains; a list of ~12 names, two crossed out. Sella has read it. SEAL BROKEN — unmistakably opened; cannot be delivered as untampered.

dmlog.text: A broken seal and a debt-holder who prizes nothing more than knowing who touched his things. Fine. I press the wax back into place as best I can and slip the disc away — but I take my time first with those dozen names, mouthing each one and burning the two that are struck through into my memory, because a patient man wants his ripe fruit whole, and now I know something about what he's really counting. If he means to catch me, I'll not walk in empty; I'll walk in knowing which two names already got picked.

The two struck-through names sit at the top of the list, and you give them the attention a con artist gives to the mark's own signature. The first is scored out with a single clean line, almost respectful: Haldrek Sunn. The second is crossed twice, hard, the cut so deep it split the grain: Wemric Sunn. Same name, father and son by the look of the spacing — a house, then, not two strangers, and the twice-struck one done with something past business. The ten below them are alive, if a list like this can be said to leave anyone alive. You press the ruined wax back over the disc, and it sits there crooked and pale-veined, a lie any child could see through, and you pocket it anyway because there's nowhere in the Maw to put a thing like this down. And that is precisely when you feel it — not a hand, not yet, but the particular quiet of being looked at with intent. Across the swaying market a man has stopped. He is not hurrying. He turns a pale sliver of whittled wood over and over between two fingers, and he is watching you with the mild, unbothered patience of someone who has already decided how this ends and is only waiting for you to catch up. He inclines his head, the smallest courtesy, and does not come closer. He lets you come to him, or run. Either way he has all morning.

payload.name: Haldrek Sunn
payload.note: top name on the slab, struck once (clean). Head of a house; picked.

payload.name: Wemric Sunn
payload.note: second name, struck twice deep (grain split) — personal. Same house as Haldrek; father/son. Picked.

payload.name: The Patient Man
payload.note: Ironwood Circle agent; whittles a pale sliver, never hurries; clocked Sella + parcel at dawn; approaches solo, lets targets come to him. Name not yet given.

dmlog.dmNotes: Crossed names = the Sunn house being dismantled; antagonist onstage, telegraphed.

dmlog.text: I let a slow smile find my face — the one I use when I've decided to like someone — and I walk toward him at his own unhurried pace, hands loose and visible, the ruined disc a comfortable weight I make no move to hide. "You've been waiting on me since before I got here," I say as I close the distance, taking the seat across from him uninvited, "so let's not waste your morning pretending either of us is surprised. I opened it. I know what house you buried, and I know ten more names are still breathing. Tell me your price for a clean start in the Maw — and I'll tell you why I'm worth more to you carrying that list than crossed off it."

He lets your whole speech land before he moves, and when he does it's only to set the sliver of pale wood on the table between you, pointing at your heart like a compass finding north. "Voss," he says — so he had your name too, before you got here — "I'm Corran Vale. No relation to your borrowed one, I'd guess." The smile he gives back is genuine, which is worse than if it weren't. "The Ironwood Circle doesn't buy clean starts. We grow them, slow, and we prune what won't take." He taps the ruined seal without touching it. "You've done me a small courtesy, opening that. Now I know you're the kind who looks. The question you've handed me is whether a woman who looks is a tool or a liability — and those two things get very different mornings in the Maw." He folds his hands. He is in no hurry at all. "So. Sell it. Tell me why the list is safer in your pocket than in the crater. And Voss — I've listened to frightened people lie for twenty years. Make it worth the breath."
dmlog.dmNotes: Named Corran Vale; revealed Ironwood Circle; DC18 long-shot gambit.

dmlog.text: He hears you out, and the smile stays, but something behind it goes still and appraising — he's caught the seam where your pitch stops being true and starts being sold. "Mm," he says. "Half of that I believe." He doesn't tell you which half. "Here's what your breath's bought: you live, and you're useful to me by dusk, or you're a loose end by dark — those are the terms, and they're not generous, they're arithmetic." He slides a splinter of ironwood across the table; you understand you're meant to keep it, and that it is a leash, not a gift. "Bring me the man who told you which house I buried — because someone did, Voss, you didn't guess the Sunns — and we'll talk about your three days. Come back empty and I'll assume the mouth was your own."

payload.name: Corran Vale
payload.note: Half-bought Sella's pitch. Conditional reprieve: by dusk deliver whoever told her about the Sunns, or she's a loose end. Gave her an ironwood splinter = a leash.

dmlog.text: A splinter of ironwood that's a leash, not a gift — and a task with teeth in it. I close my hand around it and pocket it beside the ruined disc, giving him the small satisfied nod of a woman taking a deal she means to keep. "Dusk, then. You'll have your mouth," I say, rising unhurried the way he'd respect — and I don't correct him that no one told me the Sunns, because a man who thinks he knows where my leak is will watch the wrong hole. Then I fold myself back into the market to go find a boy named Batgal before anyone else does.

Corran's nod back is unhurried and complete, a man filing you exactly where he wants you, and you turn before he can watch your face too long. Nearly two hours of the deal was spent in the sitting; the sun has climbed off the crater's rim now and the glass below has gone from blood to a hard white shine that hurts to look at, the market thickening to full clamor around you. Batgal will not be near where you last saw him — a boy who says you were never here is a boy who moves — but you know his kind. They work the choke-points: the swaying rope-bridges where crowds bottleneck and pockets press together, the low decks where the coin is smaller and the watching is thinner. You start down toward the underside of the hanging village, where the boardwalks sag closest to the glass and the light comes up from below through the slats, and you go the way you learned to move in a city that wanted you dead: unhurried, unremarkable, one more tired traveler with nowhere to be. Behind and above you, you can't say for certain whether one of Corran's quiet people has peeled off to follow. That's rather the point of them.

payload.note: descending the hanging village to find Batgal

dmlog.dmNotes: walk_advance + discovery Lower Decks = leave-and-return begins; DC14 Investigation for Batgal.

dmlog.text: The lower decks swallow him. You quarter the bridges and the sagging under-market for the better part of an hour and turn up nothing but the wrong faces — and every minute you spend hunting is a minute you spend visibly hunting, head turning, pace breaking, all the tells you'd mock in a mark. By the time you give it up the sun's high and you've taught anyone watching exactly what you're afraid of losing: a small boy who knows something. You've not found Batgal. But you've painted a target on him for anyone who thinks to ask why Sella Voss spent her morning turning over the underside of the Maw.

payload.note: fruitless search burns another hour

dmlog.text: Every minute of hunting taught the crowd exactly what I'd pay to protect. Fine — I stop hunting like a fool and start thinking like the fence. I stop dead in a shaded nook, buy a skewer of whatever's smoking on the nearest brazier to look like any other idle body, and I quietly turn my read on the Lower Decks: who down here trades in children — runners, cutpurses, lookouts — and which grown mouth Batgal answers to, because a boy that sharp belongs to someone, and it's faster to buy his handler than to chase the boy.

You buy the skewer — something grey and sweet and probably not what the vendor called it — and you eat it slow with your back to a tar-black post, and you stop looking for a boy and start looking at a system. It resolves the way these things always do once you stop chasing. The children move in a current, and all currents have a drain. Every runner on this deck, sooner or later, drifts past one particular stall: a mender of nets and rope down where the boardwalk sags lowest, hung with coils and hooks, run by a broad woman with forearms like a docker's and a way of never quite watching the children who leave things on her counter and take things away. Iron straps bind every crate and coil in her stall — the good ironwork, guild-marked. Twice you watch a small hand pass her something and get a nod, and the nod is the whole transaction. She is who Batgal answers to. And when a runner leans in to murmur to her, she leans down to listen with the patience of someone who has learned that children see everything and are asked nothing.

payload.name: Maddan Strole, the Netmender
payload.note: Iron-Strap Guild clearing-house in the Lower Decks; runs the deck's child-runners as eyes; rope-mending is cover, information is her trade. Batgal answers to her.

dmlog.dmNotes: Maddan Strole the Netmender = Iron-Strap Guild clearing-house (Sella's own secret guild — reveal held, primed). DC13 Insight, Sella WIS -1.

dmlog.text: You read the stall and read it wrong — you take the net-mender for the drain when she's only an eddy, and you're still congratulating yourself when a hand closes light and certain around your wrist from behind. Not a child's hand. "You've been counting my runners," says a voice at your shoulder, low and unbothered, and you turn into a lean man with iron-strapped knuckles and a lazy, dangerous patience of his own. "Down here we like to know why a fresh face wants to know who the little ones answer to. So." His grip doesn't tighten; it doesn't need to. "Let's you and me go somewhere quiet and you can tell me."

His grip is certain but his face is bored — this is a man who does this ten times a week, and bored men love a story that makes them feel clever. I let my shoulders drop and my voice go low and confidential, leaning into the pull rather than against it, walking with him like we're already partners. "Quiet's good, I've got no wish to make it public either — because the truth is I'm counting your runners to buy one, not steal one. The tree folk are hunting a boy who talked out of turn, and I'd rather your people hand him to me for coin than let the Ironwood Circle come down here asking the hard way. You'd be doing your little ones a kindness, and getting paid for it."

The enforcer lets you walk him, which is its own answer — bored, like you read him, a man collecting a fresh face because that's the job and not because his heart's in it. He steers you not to some quiet killing-nook but back toward the net-mender's stall, and you understand you're being brought to Maddan Strole the way a cat brings a mouse to the doorstep: for inspection, not yet for eating. She's already watching you come. And your pitch is good — it's the right play, Iron-Strap against Ironwood, coin and kindness in the same breath — right up until it isn't. Because you've said the words "the tree folk" a shade too loud on an open deck, and you've named a boy who talked, and from three stalls down a man who was in no hurry at all goes very slightly more still. You feel it the way you felt it at dawn. Corran's people were already down here. They followed you to Batgal's own handler, and you've just told them, out loud, that the boy is worth taking. The enforcer's grip loosens — he's felt the shift in the deck too, the way a dog feels weather. Maddan's eyes cut past you to the still man and back, doing sums. And the still man steps off his post and starts toward the stall, unhurried, and he is not alone: two more peel from the crowd behind him, hands loose, ironwood cudgels riding easy at their hips. Talk brought you here. Talk is done.

payload.name: Maddan Strole
payload.note: the Netmender — Iron-Strap Guild clearing-house on the Lower Decks; runs the children as eyes. Now caught between Sella's offer and three arriving Ironwood men. Not yet committed.

dmlog.dmNotes: Talk failed forward into the fight. 1x CR1/2 leader + 2x CR1/8 muscle vs L1 Rogue 9HP. Capture-intent possible. Iron-Strap tie primed as mid-fight lever.

dmlog.text: I let the enforcer feel my weight shift like I'm cornered — then I tear my wrist free, rip open the pack, and dump all thousand ball bearings across the sagging deck between me and the three of them, right at the choke where the rope-bridge narrows. "Careful footing, boys!" I call, and I bolt for the bridge while they're finding the glass crater with their heels, cutting the far tie-rope behind me with a dagger as I cross.

The bearings go out in a bright hissing sheet, a thousand little suns skating across the boards and pinging down through the slats into the glare below, and you're already moving — "Careful footing, boys!" — onto the rope-bridge as it bucks under your weight. Behind you the first Prune-Man hits the bearings at a run and his boots go out from under him in a windmill of arms. The bridge sways sickeningly over the drop, the fused glass a hard bright nothing a long way down, and the far tie-rope is three strides ahead, then two, your dagger already reversed in your hand. The Enforcer doesn't slip. He's the patient kind; he tests the boards with one foot and comes on anyway, cudgel loose, close behind you and closing. It's all in the crossing now — your feet on a heaving bridge, the drop under the gaps, and one clean cut to drop the whole thing behind you before he's across too.
dmlog.dmNotes: DC14 Acro escape; Enforcer kept alive for the dusk climax.

dmlog.text: The bridge wins. Your foot comes down where a plank isn't and the whole world tilts — you go to one knee, the dagger-stroke goes wide of the rope and bites wood instead, and the Enforcer is on you before you can draw back for a second cut. The cudgel takes you low in the ribs, a deep sick thud that folds you over the swaying boards with the crater grinning up through the gaps beneath your face. He plants a boot, unhurried, and reaches down to take a fistful of your collar. "You'll want to stop running now," he says, not even winded. The rope you failed to cut still holds. You are on the wrong side of it, on your knees, and his two friends are picking their way across the bearings to join him.

I lift my open hand off the boards — no weapon in it — and I let my voice pitch low and fast, just for the Enforcer and the woman still watching from her stall. "Maddan Strole watched me run instead of talk, and that should tell her something," I say, and I dig out the pale ironwood splinter, holding it up where the light catches it. "This is Corran's leash. I'm his by dusk — you break me here and you're not roughing up a fresh face, you're spilling the tree folk's errand-girl on Iron-Strap boards, and he is not a patient man about his property. Take me to Maddan. Let her decide if my throat's worth that."

The splinter of pale wood sits in your open palm, and it does more talking than you do — the Enforcer's eyes drop to it and something recalculates behind them, because he knows that grain, he carries its cousin at his own hip. Your voice is for Maddan, though, pitched to carry the length of the sagging deck: Corran's leash, the tree folk's errand-girl, spilled on Iron-Strap boards. You watch the net-mender go still at her counter. She has spent a lifetime learning the exact weight of other people's quarrels, and you've just set a heavy one on her scale — bleed you here and she owns whatever Corran does about it; stay her hand and she owns a favor from a woman who chose to run rather than talk, which is its own kind of recommendation down here. The Enforcer doesn't loosen his grip. He waits, like his master taught him, for someone else to decide. Every eye on the deck slides to Maddan Strole, and the moment stretches thin as bridge-rope over the shining drop.
dmlog.dmNotes: Persuasion DC15 on real leverage; no branch kills (capture-crew). All pivot to climax.

dmlog.text: Maddan's face doesn't change, and that's how you know you've misjudged the room one last time. "Errand-girls don't bargain," she says, bored, to the deck at large. "They run errands." The Enforcer takes that as the leave he was waiting for — the cudgel comes around, not to kill, his master wants you whole, but hard enough that the deck and the crater trade places and the bright glass rushes up to meet the side of your head. The last thing you hold, going down, is the splinter still in your fist, and the small cold thought that Corran was always going to get his property back — the only question was in how many pieces.

payload.note: Bluff failed; Enforcer clubbed Sella down non-lethally (3->0, unconscious/captured, NOT dead). Wakes in custody; dusk climax = captive-before-Corran.

dmlog.text: (Sella is clubbed unconscious and held; hours pass. It is dusk now. She comes to in Iron-Strap custody, badly hurt, the dusk deadline arrived — deliver the climax opening.)

You come back to the world one sense at a time: the sweet-iron reek of the crater, the creak of chains taking the village's weight, and under your cheek the tacky grain of Iron-Strap boards. Dusk has bled the glass below from white to a low smoldering amber, and it throws the whole underdeck in the color of a banked fire. Your hands are bound in front of you with waxed cord — Maddan's own knot-work, you'd bet — and the ironwood splinter and the ruined disc are gone from your coat. Maddan Strole sits on an upturned crate a few feet off, mending a net she does not need to mend, and she does not look up when your breathing changes. "He's coming up the low stair," she says. "Been very patient about it." And then he's there, Corran Vale, stepping out of the amber gloom in no more hurry at dusk than he was at dawn, and he crouches to your eye level with that genuine, terrible warmth. "Voss. Early, and in the wrong district, and opened." He turns the broken seal over in his fingers — so he has it now — and clicks his tongue, almost fond. "I'd made my peace with pruning you. But Maddan and I have been talking while you slept, and she raised a question I can't put down." His pale eyes hold yours. "She says the cord on your wrists is a guild knot, and that you didn't so much as flinch when she tied it — the way a body doesn't flinch at a thing it grew up with." Behind him, Maddan finally looks up from her net, and her flat gaze is a scale with your whole life on it. "So before I decide what you are," Corran says softly, "tell me true, and tell me now, with both of them listening: whose girl were you, Sella Voss, before you were mine?"

payload.name: The Broken Seal (recovered)
payload.note: Corran now holds the ruined ironwood disc + slab — proof Sella opened the parcel; the map/hit-list back in his hands.

dmlog.dmNotes: Climax opened; secret detonated via the guild knot; both faction heads over her; question put.

dmlog.text: I let the silence hang a beat, then meet Corran's eyes, not Maddan's. "Iron-Strap," I say, quiet and even. "Not this house — a chapter three cities gone, the one whose debts I ran from and whose knots my hands will never forget, which is exactly why the tree folk could buy my passage: a woman with a guild in her spine and nowhere left to spend it. So here's the truth under the truth, with both of you listening — I'm worth more standing between you than bled out on Maddan's boards. Corran wants a leash; Maddan wants a hand that ties her knots and knows how her people move. I can be the seam where Ironwood and Iron-Strap talk without either of you losing face — or you can prune me tonight and go back to watching each other across the crater. Cut the cord, and by dawn I'll show you which."

You claim it to Corran's face, not Maddan's — because the truth told to the harder man is the truth that carries — and you watch the word Iron-Strap change the temperature of the deck. A chapter three cities gone. Debts run from. Knots the hands never forget. It has the ring truth has, because most of it is, and you let the rest ride in on its back: that a woman with a guild in her spine and nowhere left to spend it is not a liability to be pruned but a seam to be used — the place where Ironwood and Iron-Strap could press a message through without either of them being seen to bend. Corran does not move for a long moment. The amber light dies another shade in the crater below. Then he looks — deliberately, the first time all day he's deferred to anyone — at Maddan Strole, and hands her the decision he's been holding, and the whole session comes down to a woman with a net in her lap deciding whether your throat is worth more open or shut.
dmlog.dmNotes: Final beat — Deception/cha DC16 (she IS proficient in Deception). Every branch lands a satisfying close; fail is a cliffhanger capture, not death. Shared Sleep taboo as closing image.

dmlog.text: Maddan draws a knife you never saw her reach for and cuts the cord off your wrists in one bored motion, the way she'd trim a frayed line. "Ironwood and Iron-Strap don't talk," she says, standing, "because neither of us will send a body the other can hang. A body that's already both — and already opened, and already owes — that's not a body either of us minds losing." She lets that sit; it's the truth of what you are and she wants you to hold it. "So. You're the seam." She looks at Corran; Corran, unhurried, inclines his head the fraction that means yes. "Three days," he says. "You still carry my list to the ten. But now you carry Maddan's word back the other way. Fail either of us and you'll find we're both very patient about the same grave." You get your feet under you, one HP and a whole future of borrowed rope, standing on fused glass gone the color of a dying fire — alive because you convinced two people who wanted you dead that you were more useful as a thread between them than as an example. It is, you think, the cleanest con you've ever run, and you ran it with the truth. Somewhere above, the village is lying down to sleep, all of them turning to face the same way in the dark, and no one has yet told you why.

payload.note: Sella talked her way from bound-and-bleeding into being the sanctioned go-between of two rival powers.
Spared Sella at dusk; terms widened — 3 days to carry the hit-list to the ten AND carry Maddan's word back. Her sanctioned go-between now.

payload.text: By full dark the Lower Decks know a new name walks between the tree folk and the guild — and two of the ten still-breathing names on Corran's list hear it first.

dmlog.text: "Three days." I hold Corran's eye a beat, then Maddan's, letting the tremor in my hands read as cold rather than the near-corpse fear it is — a charlatan's rule: name the thing that scares them before they name it for you. "Then let's not waste the first hour of it pretending we trust each other, because we don't, and that's exactly why this works. A man you trust can lie to you. I can't afford to — I die at both ends of the same rope." I roll my shoulder where the cord bit, buying a breath, reading Maddan's face for the tell of who actually holds my leash down here on the Lower Decks. "Two things before I start walking your list, Corran, or I'm carrying it blind and blind gets me killed by day two. First — the ten. I need names and where they lay their heads, not just faces, or I'm knocking on the wrong doors advertising your business to the whole Maw. Second—" I turn it soft, almost idle, the way you slide the real question in under the small ones "—my splinter and my disc. The disc's ruined, worthless to you, but a man walking your errand carrying nothing of his own looks like a man you've already buried. Give me back the splinter. Let them see I've still got something to lose. It sells the part." And I wait — not for permission, but to watch which of them flinches at the word *splinter*.

Corran Vale does not answer at once. That is his way, you suspect — the silence is the answer, and the silence is patient, and the silence has all the time in the world that you do not. When he finally speaks the words come slow, laid down one at a time like a man setting stones he means to stand on. "Ten names. Yes." A pause you could drive a barge through. "You'll have them. Where they sleep, who they sleep beside, which of them owes the wharf-tally and which of them is owed. That is your day-two protection, Seam, and I do not hand it across a table in a cell." He does not say when. He does not say how much at a time. He leaves that hanging where you can see it, the way a man leaves a coin on a stump to watch which way a stranger's eyes go.

Maddan Strole has not moved through any of this. He sits the way tired men sit — like the chair is doing him a favor — and the boredom on his face is real, which is the frightening part, because you have met bored men who were bored right up until the knife, and this is that kind of bored. But when the word leaves your mouth — splinter — something crosses him. Not a flinch. Slower than a flinch. His eyes go to Corran, just once, just for the length of a heartbeat, and then back to the middle distance, and the boredom settles over it again like silt over a dropped thing. He did not want to look. He looked anyway. And in a cell that runs on who-holds-whose-leash, a man who checks the druid's face before he lets himself react to a scrap of ironwood has just told you something he would very much rather you had not seen.

Corran's gaze comes back to you, level and terrible and unhurried. "The disc is slag. Keep your slag." His hand does not move toward the splinter. "The other thing." A beat. "Convince me a man walking my errand needs it, and not just that it comforts him to hold. I've buried men who confused the two."

He waits. So does Maddan — and Maddan is listening now in a way he was not a moment ago.

dmlog.text: (I roll Deception: 19)

Corran Vale does not answer quickly. He never does. The druid turns the ironwood splinter between two fingers — slow, considering, the way a man tests the give of a rope before he trusts his weight to it — and the crater below the Lower Decks throws up its dusk light through the plank-gaps, glass-glow the color of a bruise healing. Somewhere down in that fused ground the last sun is trapped and cooling.

"A man walking my errand," he says at last, tasting the words. "Not comforted. Staked." He looks at you a long moment, and there is nothing warm in it — only the patience of something that grows toward what it wants over years and is never once in a hurry. "Yes. A man carrying a thing he can lose walks straighter than a man carrying only himself. He steps careful. He comes back." A dry thing that is not quite a smile. "You've made me an argument for keeping you honest by giving you something to be dishonest with. That is either very stupid of me or exactly the sort of leash I favor."

He presses the splinter into your palm. Cold, denser than wood has any right to be, warm at the very core as though something in it is still alive and only sleeping. Your fingers close. It is yours again.

"Walk it, then, Seam."

And off past his shoulder, at the netmender's low stool where the confiscated tackle hangs, Maddan Strole stops mending. Just stops. The bone needle rests against the mesh, unmoving, and his flat bored eyes track the splinter from Corran's hand into yours — the same glance he threw when the word first crossed the deck, that little tug of attention a man gives the one thing in a room he has quietly decided is his. He says nothing. He does not need to. Then the needle moves again, in and out of the net, as if it never paused.

Corran has already turned back to his work. The low stair falls away below you toward the dusk-lit crater and the long walk in, and no one is holding you here anymore.

The splinter is a small cold weight against your fingers, and Maddan Strole has not looked away.

Netmender. Twice his attention snagged on the ironwood splinter — a proprietary glance he buries back into his mending. He wants that splinter, or knows something about it. Unresolved.

dmlog.dmNotes: Deception 19 vs DC 15 clean success; splinter returned; Maddan-glance kept as live thread.

dmlog.text: I close my fist around the splinter and let Corran have my back without a fuss. But before the stair takes me down, I turn just enough to put Maddan in my eye-line, casual, like I'm getting my footing on the drop. "Strole." I say it low, just for him, the netmender's needle the only witness. "You've been staring at my splinter like it owes you money. When I've walked Corran's list and I'm carrying your word back the other way — you and me are going to have a conversation about what this is, and what it's worth to a man who already knows." Not a threat, not a plea — an appointment. I don't wait for an answer. I take the stair down into the dusk-lit crater, splinter tucked away, and as I walk I turn my mind to the only free intelligence I've got before the names come tomorrow: where a vanished boy like Batgal would go to ground in a village where everyone sleeps facing east — and whether the Traitor's Tree, where patient men wait, is a place I can reach before full dark without a name to knock on.

You put Maddan Strole in your eye-line and give him the appointment. He doesn't rise to it. His hands go on working. Only his eyes lift, flat as slack water, to rest a moment on the closed fist where the splinter's gone. Not on you. On the fist. "A conversation," he says. "Walk your list, Seam. Bring me the word back. And keep that hand closed. You'd be surprised how many people down here lose a thumb walking careless." It isn't a threat. It's a man telling you the weather. But he doesn't say why. Then Corran has your back, and the stair takes you down. The crater opens under you — the Shimmering Maw strung on its chains over a bowl of fused glass that dusk has turned the color of a bruise healing badly. The chains creak. Woodsmoke and lye-stink drift up the Tanner's way. And you notice: every doorway you pass faces east, away from the crater's throat. Which means a boy who wanted to not be found wouldn't hide behind an east-facing door where a hundred neighbors sleep looking his way. He'd go where the town doesn't look. West. Down. Toward the throat, or toward the quiet ground beyond the chains where the Traitor's Tree stands — a black snarl of branches out past the last deck, close enough to reach on foot but far enough that the light will be gone before you get there. The splinter is a small hard weight in your closed hand. The stair ends. The crater is yours to cross, and the dusk is spending itself fast.

payload.note: Proprietary about Sella's ironwood splinter — watches the fist that holds it, not her face. Wants it badly, feigns boredom, won't say why. Issued a flat 'careless people lose a thumb' warning-as-weather.

payload.name: The Traitor's Tree
payload.desc: A black snarl of an ancient tree out past the last deck of the Maw, beyond the chains on quiet ground — reachable on foot but not before dark. 'Patient men wait' there.

payload.text: Every dwelling in the Shimmering Maw faces east, away from the crater's throat — a total unremarked custom. A person hiding from the town would go west/down.

dmlog.dmNotes: Hooks planted, no roll; Tree flagged as danger after dark, 1 HP telegraph banked.

dmlog.text: The Tree is called patient, so it can wait one more night — I'd rather meet it in grey morning with a name in my pocket and blood back in my body than as a gift the dusk hands it. So I don't cross toward the throat. Batgal went where the town doesn't look — west and down — but a frightened boy leaves a debt, a favor, a last person who saw him. I turn toward the Tanner's way, following the lye and woodsmoke: a tannery runs on cheap hands and asks no names — the kind of place that'd take a runaway for a night's shelter, and the kind of low-status door where a charlatan working a little pity and a little coin buys the first true thing I've heard since I woke on the block. As I walk I keep my chin down, the splinter-fist tucked at my hip out of sight, reading the crater for who's watching me walk — because Maddan's needle wasn't the last set of eyes on me tonight, and I'd bet my thumb on it.

The lye finds you before the Reach does — a wet, ammoniac slap that crawls up the back of the throat and stays there. Then the shapes: hides strung on frames like men left to weather, grey and stiff and swaying a little in the river-breath off the bend. Vats sunk into the mud, their skins of scum catching the last dirty orange of the dusk. This is a place that eats smells and gives back worse, and nobody works here who has anywhere else to be.

A woman is scraping a hide with a curved blade, long even strokes, the flesh-side curling off in grey ribbons. She doesn't look up when your shadow crosses her light. Ospra, someone calls her from the dark of the tan-house, and she grunts an answer without breaking rhythm. There's a lean-to behind her, sacking hung for a door, straw showing at the base. The kind of dark corner a place like this pretends not to have.

At the edge of the vat-yard, half a beat too still, a man in a good coat is watching a hide dry as though it fascinates him. It does not fascinate him. When your eyes pass over him he does not look away fast — he looks away slow, the way only someone who wants you to know he's there does it. Maddan's needle wasn't the last set of eyes. This one brought a better coat and worse patience.

Ospra scrapes. Waits, the way tired people wait — hoping you'll cost her nothing. The lean-to breathes straw behind her, and you can smell that a body slept there recently. She hasn't asked you what you want yet. She will, or she'll decide you're trouble and stop answering — that window is open now, and narrow.

dmlog.text: You reach for the seam and there isn't one — or she's stitched it shut against exactly your kind. The coin, when it shows, is the mistake. Her hand comes up flat before it lands. "No," she says, and the scraping stops, and stopped is worse than any answer. "I don't know your boy. I don't know any boys. Folk come, folk go, and folk who ask — " she nods, slow, past your shoulder, toward the vat-yard where the good coat stands too still — "folk who ask get watched. You've got a shadow, girl, and I'll not have it standing in my light. Go and take it with you." She turns her back. Somewhere the good coat shifts its weight, unhurried, and you feel the exact moment his attention settles all the way onto you and stops pretending to be anywhere else.

dm.closed: refused Sella entirely and pointed out the tail to her face; this door is shut for the night

dm.escalated: dropped the pretense of idleness after Sella spooked the tannery-hand; now openly attentive

dmlog.text: A good coat that wants to be seen isn't here to knife me — a knife-man doesn't advertise. He's here to herd me, or to be introduced. Running from him in the dark at one hit point is how I trip on the fused glass and save him the trouble. Ospra's true tell: she said "boys" and "my light" and nodded past me — she's not scared of me, she's scared of him. So I turn the tail into the play. I walk out of Ospra's light like she asked, slow, letting the good coat see I've clocked him, and I close toward a spot with a wall at my back and people in earshot, then stop and let him come the last steps. "You've been very patient," I say, easy, the way you greet a man you were expecting. "Patient men are Corran's, or they're the Tree's, or they're their own. Which are you — and whose word do I put it to when I tell them the Seam kept her hands closed and her appointment?" I keep the splinter-fist at my hip, out of sight, my empty ruined-disc hand open and visible between us — reading his coat, his boots, his stance for who paid for them, and reading his face for the flicker when I say Seam, because if that word means something to him I've just learned who already knows my new name.

He comes when you stop, unhurried, the way water finds a level. The good coat is wool, dark, the kind of cut that costs a season's wages and hides its seams — a townsman's coat, or a coat bought to pass for one. He halts at a courteous distance, hands loose and empty, and lets your question sit in the air between you a beat too long, the way a man does when he's been trained to make the other person fill silence.

"Patient," he agrees, mild, as if tasting the word. "That's a fair accounting of me." He does not answer which. He does not tell you a name. The lye-stink rolls off the vats behind him and he doesn't so much as blink at it — a man used to worse rooms. Off the drying-racks a hide-scraper's rhythm has gone quiet; the witnesses you gathered are listening too.

"You've got your appointment to keep," he says. "Nobody's stopping you keeping it. I'd only counsel you keep it soon." A courtesy laid over a clock. His eyes rest on your open hand a moment — noting the one you're showing him — then lift, patient, back to your face.

You said Seam. You watched for the flicker when you said it. Read him now — the coat, the boots under it, the set of his shoulders, and whatever moved behind his eyes on that word.
dmlog.dmNotes: Good coat = Ironwood Circle (Corran Vale's). Slow-drip on allegiance; branch degrees cost her the name on nearMiss/fail. Held at threshold. Social, not a strike; 1 HP safe this turn.

dmlog.text: It's the boots that tell you first. Not a townsman's boots at all — good leather but hard-used, oiled the way men oil gear they trust their lives to, and the soles cut for grip, not cobbles. The coat is a costume. Underneath it he stands square and unhurried, weight already settled, a man who has done violence patiently and expects to again — but he keeps his hands empty and his distance courteous, and that is the whole message: not tonight, and not with witnesses. Herder, not knife. And when you say Seam — there. A hairline stillness, a breath held a half-count too long before the patient mask smooths back over. The word is not new to him. Someone has already spoken your new name to this man, briefed him with it, sent him after the Seam by that name. His method reads coercion, the made example, the slow squeeze — Corran's Circle wears its patience like a virtue, and this is the Circle's patience walking in a good coat. He is here to make sure Corran's errand walks straight, and to let you feel the leash.

dmlog.text: Corran's, then. A leash I can see is a leash I can lean into — and a man told to keep me walking has to stay near the thing he herds, which means tonight I don't need to arrange a safe place to sleep; I've got one following me. "Soon. I hear it," I tell him — you don't waste breath fighting a man who agrees on the destination. Then I give him a truth wrapped around my need: "Here's the shape of it, friend, so you can tell whoever briefed you the Seam's not stalling. I'm at the end of a bad rope tonight — I walked off a block this morning and I've barely got the blood to prove it. I keep my appointment better rested than dead. So I'm going to find a wall and a roof till first light, and you're going to stand where you can watch me do it, and in the morning I keep walking Corran's list where Corran's man can see every step. That's the errand walking straight." And I mean it — I let him pick my cage. I ask him plainly, reading his answer for the tell: "Where does a woman on Corran's leash sleep in the Maw without waking up short a thumb? Because your own people gave me that particular warning—" no, Maddan's people did "—and I'd hate to embarrass the Circle by dying on the wrong deck the night before I'm useful."

He listens the way a good tailor listens — without interrupting, letting you spend all your thread. Then, quietly: "A rope's only bad if you don't know it's holding you. You've got that part right, at least." He takes in the pallor of you. A man doing arithmetic he's done before, on other people, in worse light. "Rested asset walks straighter. I'm not going to argue with true." A tilt of the head, up the slope. "The Miller's Leat — follow the channel to the wheelhouse. There's a dry loft over the grind-room, warm from the stones, and the wheel's noise means no one hears a floorboard, which cuts both ways. Old Dessa keeps it. Tell her Fenn sent you and she'll not ask a second question." Then the thumb. You watch it land — a small stillness, the first you've drawn out of him he didn't choose. "Iron-Strap told you that. Maddan's people mind their own knuckles. If the Strap's talking to you about what the Circle does to hands, the Strap's talking to you about the Circle. I'll let that be my worry, not yours. You just get to the loft." He steps back into the dark between two racks of hides, unhurried. Not gone. Positioned. You climb toward the Miller's Leat with a wall's worth of blood in you and a stranger's name in your mouth. Dessa's loft is dry. The stones hold the day's heat. Below, the wheel turns, and turns. You lie down. First light is a long way off, and you are only safe for as long as you are worth keeping. You close your eyes.

dmlog.text: First thing I do is nothing the coat can see. Ospra's slip pointed a frightened boy upriver, toward the wheel, toward here — I'd be a fool to walk out the front and start Corran's errand before I've searched my own roof. So before I present myself to Fenn, I work Dessa — quiet, early, host-to-guest, the hour when people are soft and truthful — while I gather my things. No coin this time (coin was the tell that sank me at the tannery): I thank her for the loft, ask her name proper, ask how a grind-room keeps warm all night and who tends the wheel in the dark — and only once she's talking do I let it drift. "You'll have had others come off the crater cold, wanting a wall. A boy, maybe, day or two back — half-grown, scared, upriver ahead of something. He'd not have given a real name." I read her hands and her eyes for the flinch, the pause, the glance toward any corner of this mill she doesn't want me looking at.

Dessa moves like the room is hers and always has been — pours from the small kettle without asking, sets the cup where your hand already is. She listens the way she pours: no wasted motion, eyes half-down. When you drift to the boy, she doesn't stiffen. That would be amateur. She keeps threading a bit of twine through a cracked bucket-handle, patient as the wheel outside. "Cold comes off that crater into everybody," she says. "Half the folk I keep came off it wanting a wall. Names are cheap up here. I don't buy them." And there — you're watching for it, so you catch it. Not a flinch. The opposite. A held stillness, the twine going quiet in her fingers for exactly one beat too long before it moves again, and her weight settling, unbidden, a half-inch toward the low door at the loft's north end — the one behind the meal-sacks, where the wheelhouse timbers step down toward the water. She doesn't glance at it. She makes very sure not to. The wheel turns. Somewhere under it, a board takes a weight and lets it go.
dmlog.dmNotes: Batgal IS here, hidden by Dessa; her discretion is the obstacle, gated behind Insight DC 13. Success cracks her toward helping + surfaces she isn't Circle-loyal. Facts persisted inside branches only.

dmlog.text: You catch the tell — the beat too long, the door she won't look at — enough to know she's holding someone close. But when you reach past the hands to the person, she closes the gap. She's done this longer than you've run cons; she feels your attention settle and stands, unhurried, putting her body between you and the north end of the loft as if only to reach the kettle. "You're a good guest," she says, and it isn't warmth — it's a door shutting soft. "Good guests don't go looking in a house that fed them." She's told you nothing and everything: there's a where, and she'll spend the morning making sure you don't find it. The cost is time you may not have, and a host who now watches your hands the way you watched hers.

dm.harbors: almost certainly sheltering runaway Batgal in the wheelhouse (north end) — Sella clocked the tell but not the hiding place
dm.loyalty: guards her frightened guests; won't give the boy to a stranger and is now steering Sella away
dm.guardUp: Sella's probe was caught; Dessa watches her closely, spends effort keeping her from the north end — costs Sella time and host-trust

dmlog.text: I back off the north door the instant she stands — hands open, a step given. She's not the Circle's and she doesn't give people up, and that's the most valuable thing I've found in this town: a locked door I don't have to break because I can make her open it herself, in time. "You're right, and I'm sorry — that was ill-mannered in a house that fed me." Then I give her the truth as a gift, not a lever: "I'll say one thing and then I'll go keep my own bad appointment. The boy you're not telling me about — if he's who I think, his name's a thing I already carry, not a thing I'm selling. I'm not the Circle and I'm not the good coat waiting outside your door right now. When he's ready — not before — you tell him the Seam kept her hands closed and asked after him like family, not like a debt. That's all. He'll know if it's true." I leave the north end untouched, gather my things, and go down to meet Fenn on my own feet — because the errand's the leash that keeps me alive to come back, and Dessa guarding Batgal all morning means he's safe exactly where I can find him tonight, when I've earned the right to be let in.

You leave the north end untouched — a small, deliberate mercy. The message you speak into the dry loft air, Dessa standing between you and the grind-room dark: The Seam kept her hands closed and asked after him like family, not like a debt. She doesn't soften. Dessa is not a woman who softens; she's a woman who weighs. But something behind her eyes shifts the way a held breath shifts before it's let go. "He'll hear it. Word for word. I don't promise you what he does with it." A beat. "But I'll tell him a stranger stood at that door and chose. That's more than most." She turns back to the grind-room and does not invite you to follow. You've bought nothing you can spend today — but you've bought a door, for tonight. You go down.

He's waiting where the leat-channel meets the descending stair, out of the wind, one shoulder to the stone, and does not pretend he wasn't watching the loft the whole while. Fenn looks rested in a way you resent. "You slept. Good. Corran's a man who pays by the day, and today's the first day. So." He gives you a name, spoken low, once: "Oskin Rell. Chandler by trade — tallow, wick, and lamp-oil, works out of a shed off Coalstack Row, east and down, where the smoke gets in your teeth." A pause. "Corran doesn't want him hurt. Corran wants him reminded — that the Circle knows where his light comes from, and where it could stop coming. You carry that reminder. How you dress it is your business — that's what you're for." He straightens off the wall. "I'll walk you as far as the Row-mouth. Not in. A chandler who sees me at his door learns the wrong lesson. One name today, Seam. Do it clean and there's a second tomorrow." He waits for you to move first.

dmlog.text: I take the name once and don't repeat it back. On the walk to the Row-mouth I work Fenn for the one thing he undervalues — not the threat, the reason. "Corran wants him reminded where his light comes from," I say, idle, watching my footing on the down-grade. "A chandler doesn't make the list for buying bad wax. What's Rell's light really cost the Circle — is he selling to someone he shouldn't, or not selling to someone he should?" Whatever Fenn gives or doesn't, I file it. Then Fenn hangs back and Coalstack Row is mine. I don't come in as the Circle's blade — I come in as a customer, coughing on the smoke, buying a measure of lamp-oil like a woman who needs to see in the dark, letting Rell get comfortable selling before I mention who sent me. When the deal's warm and his hands are busy, I set it down soft and terrible, no muscle, just weather: "Corran Vale knows where your light comes from, Oskin. He wanted you to hear that from someone who isn't holding a knife — this time. That's the whole message, and I'd rather deliver it than the next one." And then I stop talking — because the frightened silence after is where he'll tell me, unbidden, what he thinks I came about, and that's how I learn what Rell's really guilty of and what the Circle wants, both for free, while I read his face for whether this reminder just bought me a debt I can spend later.

On the walk down, the smoke of the Row rising to meet you, you put the question to him plain. Fenn keeps his eyes on the descending stair, not on you. Then, mild: "He's a chandler. He doesn't decide who he sells to. He decides where the oil comes from." A step, two. "Corran doesn't much mind who burns the light. He minds who owns the well." And that's the crumb — no more. Somewhere behind a shed full of tallow is a source, and the Circle wants it, and Rell is the door standing in front of it. At the Row-mouth he folds into a doorway's shadow and becomes a man who was never there.

Coalstack Row is a throat of smoke and rendered fat. Oskin Rell's shed is the third down — tar-black board, the door propped, inside a low warm dark hung with drying wicks like a hundred small nooses, the yellow reek of tallow thick enough to chew. Rell is a soft, careful man past fifty, forearms shining with old grease, ladling amber from a warm vat when your cough announces you. He brightens the way a lonely tradesman brightens at a paying face. "Cold morning for it. Come in out of the smoke — though I'll warn you, it's no better in here. Oil, is it? Or wick? I do a fine slow-burn wick, if it's reading you're after. Lady looks like a reader." He's already reaching for a measure, already talking price, hands busy at the tap — exactly warm, exactly comfortable, exactly the moment. He's waiting for you to name your measure.

dmlog.text: You set the words down soft — the light, where it comes from, the message that isn't a knife. And it lands: the ladle stops, the color goes, Rell believes every word. The reminder is delivered, clean and cold, exactly as Corran wanted. But the silence you leave — he fills it wrong, because you leaned a half-inch too far, let a shade too much knowing into your face, and a frightened man who thinks you already know everything stops confessing and starts managing. "Tell Corran," he says, steadying his hands by watching them, "tell him I hear him. It's handled. It was always going to be handled." Handled. He's guilty of something ongoing, something he thinks the Circle already half-knows — but he gives you the shape and not the meat. No name. No ledger. Just a man promising to fix a thing he won't name, and one glance, quickly killed, toward the floor by the vat. Reminder delivered, a thread to pull — but you overreached, and he's closed the door on the confession.

fields.secretKnown: message landed hard; promised Corran it's 'handled' — clearly guilty of something ongoing but gave no specifics

payload.what: Under Sella's reminder Oskin Rell promised the Circle it's 'handled' — betraying an ongoing guilty affair he won't name, and a hidden thing under a floorboard by his tallow vat. Sella overreached and he clammed before confessing details.

dmlog.text: "Handled" is a word a man uses when he's already got a plan I'm not in. But I'm not prying a board up in front of a terrified man with the Circle's leash waiting at the Row-mouth — that turns a delivered errand into a robbery. So I let him keep his dignity and plant a hook: I ease off, pocket my measure of oil, and give him the thing that'll keep him up all night working for me. "I'll tell him it's handled. But Oskin — I'm the one who came without the knife, and I'm the one who'll be sent with it if 'handled' turns out to be a word and not a deed. Whatever's under your worry, get it right before someone less kind than me comes to check the work." I let my eyes NOT go to the floorboard — deliberately, so he sees me not-look and knows I chose not to — then leave clean. At the Row-mouth I give Fenn the true report, no more: "Delivered. He folded. Says it's handled, and he's scared enough to mean it — but he's scared of the source, not of you, which means there's a well under that shed Corran's right to want." I keep the ledger under the floorboard to myself — that's mine now, a card for later. Then I ask Fenn the working question: is Corran's satisfaction measured by the message landing, or by the well actually changing hands? Because I want to know if I've bought a full day's grace, and whether my second name comes tomorrow or whether Rell's "handled" is a thread I'm expected to keep pulling.

You don't rob him. You let the silence stretch one beat past comfortable, and then you do the crueler, kinder thing: you look at Oskin Rell, and you very deliberately do not look at the floor by the vat. You let him watch your eyes decide not to travel there. "Get it right," you tell him, gentle as a tradesman quoting a fair price, "before someone less kind than me comes to check the work." You leave the amber measure of oil on his counter, paid for, and you leave the shed the way you came — a customer, nothing more, and a soft careful man standing very still in the tallow-dark, understanding for the first time exactly how much you chose not to take.

Fenn is where the smoke thins at the Row-mouth, and he unfolds when he sees your face. You give it to him straight and short: delivered, he folded, says it's handled — and he's scared enough to mean it. But scared of the source, you tell him. Not of Corran. Of the well itself. Which means Corran's right — there's something under that shed worth wanting.

Fenn listens without moving, and when you finish there's a small change in how he's looking at you — not warmth, but the stillness of a man revising an estimate upward. "Scared of the source, not of us," he repeats, tasting it. "That's a good read. Corran will like that read. He'll like it more than he likes you, which for you is the useful direction."

Then you put the working question to him plain. Fenn's mouth does something that isn't a smile. "Corran pays by the day because Corran collects by the day. Today you carried a name and the name heard you — that's today's coin, and it's paid. Tomorrow there's another name; there's always another name; that's what the list is." He lets that sit. "But you should understand what you're hearing when I say reminder. A reminder isn't the end of a thing. It's the first of a thing. Corran doesn't send a woman to frighten a chandler because he wants the chandler frightened." His eyes come back to you, flat and honest. "He wants the well. The message is how the taking starts. Whether you're the one who finishes it — that's above my reading. I carry you to doors. What Corran means to do once they're open is Corran's to say, and he says it slow."

The wheel-hum of the distant mill carries up the Row. The oil-measure is spent, the name is walked, and the day is young and getting older. Fenn waits, patient as his master, to see where you point yourself next.

Defined stakes: today PAID, second name tomorrow, reminder = opening move of taking the well. Ironwood 2→3/6.

dmlog.text: "He'll like the read more than he likes me — good. I don't need him to like me, I need him to keep needing me." The day's paid and the second name's a night away, and a Seam standing at the Row-mouth waiting on tomorrow is wasting her only free hours. But I've learned my lesson twice — coin at the tannery, overreach at the vat — so I don't go pull that floorboard and I don't chase the Tree at noon on a hunch. I use the leash's slack to learn. Both my guilds want the same well, which means the ledger under Rell's vat isn't just a card, it's the map of the war I'm standing in the middle of, and I need to understand the war before I pick which side I sell. So I make my own honesty the cover for my own errand: "Then here's how I earn tomorrow's name today. You said Corran collects by the day — let me collect intelligence he'll want. Rell's scared of a source. A well has an owner, and an owner in a town this small has a name and a place. I'd like to walk the Row and the ways down toward the throat while the light's good — no doors, no reminders, just a woman learning where the oil comes from, so when Corran decides to finish the taking he already knows I did the looking. You walk with me. You watch every step. Nothing about that breaks the errand." I'm asking permission to scout the well's source with the Circle's own leash as my alibi — reading Fenn for how far the slack runs, because the second thing I'm doing on that walk is mapping every way out of the Maw and every deck between me and Dessa's door tonight, and the man tailing me will teach me the town's bones without ever knowing he taught me.

Fenn hears the pitch out and the herder's sums come out in your favor. "Corran will take intelligence. So: we walk. But you walk where I walk. Not down onto the low decks past the resin-gate — that's the Circle's own ground. Not near the chain-anchors on the east face. And you don't touch anything down by the throat. Look all you like. Keep your hands to yourself. Learn me the well's owner and you'll have earned the walk."

So you go down. Coalstack Row feeds into a stepped way of soot-dark board and iron rung, decks strung one below the next on their great chains, and the smell changes — smoke giving over to something older, mineral, the cold breath of the crater itself. The Throat opens below: the crater's deep center, the fused glass not the calm rainbow sheet you saw from above but a pour, a frozen cataract of black-and-amber glass plunging into a dark the morning light won't enter. The oil comes up from there — seep-works, catch-troughs and pipe cut into the glass lip where something dark and slow wells out of the rock, and men in oiled leathers dip and carry.

And you notice: not one of them faces the throat while they work. They stand sideways to it. They set their backs to it to rest. Not one could tell you they're doing it. The east — the chain-anchors, the way up — that's where faces point. Away. You file it, cold.

Fenn is at your shoulder, watching your eyes as much as the works. Down here the light is bad and getting worse toward the dark below, and every deck has a way off it — ladders, a swaying rope-stair, a plank bridge to the next chain. You can feel the shape of the town's bones assembling in your head. But Fenn is right there, and reading exits is not the same as reading oil-troughs, and he is a man who reads people for a living. The throat breathes its cold breath. Fenn waits to see where you'll look next — and how long.

dmlog.text: You let your eyes do honest work on the oil so the other work rides invisibly beneath it. You watch who the leather-men answer to — an older woman on the lowest worked deck with a tally-slate and counting-beads, whom the dippers defer to and do not interrupt. She keeps the count. She keeps the troughs. If anyone owns what wells up from the throat, it is the tallywoman with the slate — and now you have her face and her deck. And underneath, while your gaze is plainly on the troughs, you map the bones: the rope-stair that shortcuts three decks, the plank bridge that lands you two levels under the mill-leat, the one iron ladder up the east face that nobody watches because everybody faces it. By the time Fenn touches your elbow to say you've seen enough, you have the well's keeper AND a clean dark line from the throat back to Dessa's loft for tonight — and Fenn, reading your face, sees only a woman who found Corran his intelligence.

Fenn's satisfied, and a satisfied herder's tongue loosens on the walk back up. I keep selling — because the more intelligence I'm worth, the longer the leash, and because I've a mouth to deliver by dusk and no mouth yet to give. So as we climb off the low decks I stay on the thread that pleased him: "Corran wants the well. Good. Then the man I ought to fear isn't Rell — it's whoever else is reaching for it, because that's the hand that'll cut mine off in the dark. Who fights the Circle for the throat, Fenn? You've a rival with saboteur's habits, I'd wager — the kind that doesn't buy a chandler's oil honest but from underneath, through a floorboard." I say the last light, almost idle, and watch his face for whether "Iron-Strap" or "Maddan" lands as a name he already carries — because if the Circle already fears an Iron-Strap ear in their business, then the mouth I hand Corran at dusk isn't a lie I invented, it's a leak I sniffed out, and that's a far safer thing to be caught holding.

Fenn climbs the way he does everything — at the pace of a man who has never once been late for anything that mattered — and lets your question hang a full three rungs of the iron ladder before he answers it. "Everyone in the Maw is reaching for something," he says, mild. "That's what a town hung over a hole is. A lot of hands, and one long way down." A crumb, and he knows it's a crumb; he's a man who pays exact change. But you didn't ask him for the answer. You threw three small stones into the water to see which one made a ring — Iron-Strap, Maddan, a chandler who buys his oil from underneath, through a floorboard — and you were watching his face the whole while, not his mouth. Something moved on one of them. A flat professional's face is a still pond, and a still pond shows a thrown stone better than a running one does. But it was fast, and a fast thing seen out the side of the eye is half wish and half witness, and reading a man whose whole trade is being unreadable is the hardest coin you can try to lift. You'd want to be certain which stone rang before you build your dusk on it.
dmlog.dmNotes: Sella is fishing for a scapegoat 'mouth' to hand Corran by dusk. Fenn's codex dm.ironStrapNote already establishes the Circle clocked the Iron-Strap friction, so a real read here is grounded, not invented. Reading a professional watcher = DC 15; her Insight is weak (WIS 9, +1) so this is genuinely hard. Fail has teeth per hard-and-dangerous.

dmlog.text: Nothing. Or — not nothing; the absence of a tell where you'd fished for one, which against a man like Fenn is its own answer and the wrong one. His face gives you the flat, courteous blank a card-sharp gives a marked deck, and you understand you've shown him the shape of your hand for free. "Rivals," he says, pleasantly, as if you'd asked after the weather. "The Maw's full of them. You worry about Corran's list; let Corran worry about Corran's rivals." He starts climbing again, and you climb behind him a little poorer than you started — no name confirmed, and a watcher who now knows the Seam goes digging at the Circle's seams the moment she thinks the leash has slack.

dm.clockedFishing: Insight fail (missed DC 15 by 3+): Sella learned nothing and tipped her hand — Fenn clocked plainly that the Seam fishes at the Circle's rivals/leaks when she thinks she's unwatched, and shut her down with the professional blank. Trust dinged; he watches her mouth now as well as her eyes.

dmlog.text: Fine — I showed Fenn a card, so I stop playing that hand and turn over a fresh one he can't read anything off of. A watched woman can still ask idle questions; it's only the answers I hide. So I let the leash be a leash and go up into the waking market of Coalstack Row, buying nothing, just a newcomer stretching her legs — and I go looking for the one thing that unlocks this whole crooked town: the story of the house that got crossed off. Not from Circle people. From the sort who remember: an old dipper off shift, a widow at a stall, anyone with grey in their hair and a slow morning. I don't say the name first. I let them. "I came in on the night-chains," I offer, rueful, "and already I've heard the Maw eats houses whole. Somebody told me there was a family — a proper one, a name that used to mean something — that just... stopped being. Is that a real thing that happened here, or a story they tell newcomers to keep us humble?" And when the name Sunn surfaces — because in a town this size a buried house is the best gossip going — I follow it soft: what did the Sunns own, what did they cross, and which one of them did the Maw hate enough to bury twice. Fenn can watch me learn my new home. He can't hear what I'm really counting.

Fenn can watch me learn my new home. He can't hear what I'm really counting.

The market of Coalstack Row wakes the way a poor market does — early, and without joy, and glad of any face that isn't asking for money. You buy nothing and cost no one anything, and that alone makes you rare enough that a body will talk to you.

It's an old dipper who gives it up, a man gone grey and stiff in the shoulders from forty years of hauling oil out of the cold, sat on an upturned crate with a heel of bread he's more interested in than in you — until you say the word house, and let the silence do the asking. He doesn't look at you. He looks at the bread. "Sunn," he says, like spitting a pip. "Aye. That's a real thing that happened here. Wasn't always the Circle kept the count down the Throat, girl. Was Sunns. Four generations of 'em, back when the well was the well and not the Circle's well. They knew the old ways of it — how you work down there without the crater taking a dislike to you." His jaw works. "Old Haldrek, he was the last that did it proper. Then—" and here his voice drops under the stall-noise, and his eyes flick, once, up past your shoulder to where a man in a good coat is very carefully looking at a rope-maker's wares and not at you. "Then his boy Wemric did a thing a Sunn doesn't do. Opened a door he was meant to keep shut. Let the wrong hand in." He crosses himself in a way you don't recognize — east, over the heart, a Maw thing. "They say that's why the tree's got the name it's got. But I've said more than my bread's worth already, and you've got a shadow that's better dressed than either of us." He turns his whole body away, done, a man who has just remembered he's afraid.

You have the shape of it now, if not the meat: the Sunns were the old keepers of the Throat before the Circle, and Wemric — the one struck twice, struck hard — betrayed something to let a new hand in. Whose hand, and what door, the old man won't say. And Fenn, forty feet off, has watched the whole exchange without hearing a word of it. He knows only the subject. In a town where the Circle buried the Sunns, that a Circle leash saw the Seam asking after them is not nothing. He does not come over. He simply files it, the way he files everything.
