dmlog.text: A story's only as good as the one hard thing you can prove, and I've got a hard thing waiting under a chandler's floor. I'm not going to pry it up like a thief — I spared Rell on purpose, and a spared man is a bought man if you collect gently. So I tell Fenn a true-enough thing at the Row-mouth: "Reminders go soft if you don't press the wax while it's warm. Corran wants him handled; I want to watch him start handling it. Give me the shed alone — a chandler who sees your coat learns the wrong lesson, you said so yourself." And I go back down into the tallow-dark to Oskin Rell, and this time I don't come as the knife or the customer. I come as the only friend he's got. "Oskin. I'm the kind one, remember? The next one Corran sends won't leave your dignity on the counter. So here's a door out that doesn't end with you under your own floor: whatever's down there that's got you saying 'handled' — you show me, right now, and you let me carry it. Not to Corran. Past him. I make your problem my problem, and in return you make me look like I sealed you tight, so the Circle stops sending anyone at all." I keep my hands open and my voice a chandler's own — soft, reasonable, selling him his own survival — and I read him for whether the fear I planted this morning has ripened into a man who'll lift the board himself just to have someone else hold what's under it.

Fenn hears your reasoning and does the small arithmetic that always comes out the same way: a pressed reminder serves Corran, and a chandler who never sees the coat sleeps worse, not better. "Warm wax," he agrees, and folds back into the Row-mouth's shadow to be a man who isn't there. The shed is yours.

Inside, the tallow-dark is the same low reek of a hundred small nooses, and Oskin Rell is exactly where a frightened man stands when he's been waiting all morning for the second knock — near the vat, one eye on the door, hands doing nothing and pretending to be busy. He goes stiller when he sees it's you again.

You don't reach for a knife or a coin. You reach for the thing under his own floor. You lay it out soft, a chandler quoting a fair price: you're the kind one, the next one won't be, and there's a door out of this that doesn't end with him under his own boards — he shows you what's down there, you carry it past Corran, and in return you dress him up as sealed so the Circle stops sending anyone at all. You make his problem yours.

And you watch the fear you planted this morning do its slow work in him. His eyes go to the floor by the vat — the glance he killed this morning, uncontrolled now — and back to your open hands, and to the door, and to your hands again. His mouth opens. He wets his lips. A soft, cornered man weighing the only two shapes his night can take: the stranger who spared him once, or the boards, and whatever's under them, and whoever comes next. He is one breath from a decision, and it could still go either way.
dmlog.dmNotes: The morning's mercy (deliberately not looking at the floorboard) is the load-bearing lever — advantage granted for it + planted fear. Deception (not Persuasion) because the 'friendship' is a cloak over Sella using his secret for her own dusk-mouth. Success reveals the Iron-Strap-skims-the-well secret = both her mouth material and the war-map keystone (ties Iron-Strap 'were here first / restore lost homeland' canon to the Sunn well). Fail has real teeth: a spooked double-dealer preparing to bolt.

dmlog.text: He wavers — you feel the yes rise in him — and then a lifetime of being the soft man who survives by giving nothing away pulls it back down. He does not go to the board. But something spills anyway, because a terrified man can't hold everything: "There's another," he breathes, so low the wheel-hum nearly eats it. "Another draw. Older than your Circle. I pay it off the top and I've always paid it and I can't stop paying it — that's the handled. That's all the handled I've got." He won't say who. He won't lift the board. But he's told you the shape: a second, older hand takes its cut of the well before the Circle ever counts. "Please," he says, and it's not a word, it's a man coming apart. "Please don't make me say it under this roof." You have the confession without the proof — and a chandler now so frightened he's a lit fuse, no telling which way he runs.

dm.partialConfession: T3: Sella's flip nearly landed (Deception near-miss vs DC15). Rell would NOT lift the board or name the party, but confessed the SHAPE: a second, older draw takes a cut of the Throat's oil off the top before the Circle counts, and he's paid it his whole life ('older than your Circle'). No proof handed over, no name. He is now a terrified lit fuse — unpredictable, may run or move the ledger.

dmlog.text: A frightened man who thinks he's out of doors does something stupid, and a Rell who bolts tonight dies and takes my proof with him. So before I leave I nail his feet to the floor with the one thing he wants more than air: permission to do nothing. I gentle right down, put myself between him and the panic. "Oskin. Listen to me. You don't lift the board. You don't say the name under this roof — I heard you, and I'll not make you. Here's what handled actually looks like: nothing. You keep selling the Circle its light. You keep paying the other its cut off the top, same as your father, same as always, and you change not one thing, because the second a man like you changes his habits, both sides smell it. You be the most boring chandler in the Maw. I carry the shape of this, not the name, and I keep the Circle off your floor. That's the whole deal, and it costs you a promise to stay exactly, precisely ordinary." And then — because I'll not walk to Corran holding half a card — I give Rell a way to hand me the name without ever speaking it. I don't ask him to talk. I just say it low, watching his hands and his eyes, not his mouth: "Don't answer. I'd never make you answer under your own roof. The strap you pay — it mends nets, doesn't it. Just don't correct me." And I read the flinch, the flicker, the not-correcting, for whether Maddan's the hand under this town's oil.

You watch the offer land, and it lands the way water lands on a man who's been on fire. Do nothing. Be ordinary. Keep both hands doing exactly what they've always done. It is the only mercy in the Maw that costs him nothing and saves everything, and Oskin Rell takes it with his whole body — the shoulders coming down an inch, the breath he's been holding since the second knock finally spent. "Ordinary," he repeats, like a prayer he can actually afford. "I can do ordinary. God, I've done ordinary my whole life." For the first time he isn't looking at the door. He's looking at you like a man looks at the one plank that held.

And then you give him the door that isn't a door — the name he can hand you without ever handing it over. You don't ask. You say it low, and you keep your eyes off his mouth and on his hands, where a frightened man keeps the truth he's guarding his tongue against: the strap you pay, it mends nets, doesn't it. Just don't correct me.

He doesn't correct you.

More than that — the twine-rough hands that have been fretting at each other all morning go still. Dead still, the stillness of a man refusing with his whole will to flinch, which is its own kind of flinch, the loudest one there is. He says nothing. He looks at the floor by the vat, and then very deliberately at the wall, at anything that isn't a yes. You have your answer in the shape of the silence he's keeping: a netmender collects the Maw's oldest debt off the top of the Circle's well. Maddan. You never made him say it, and that is precisely why you believe it.

payload.cause: defused his panic, gave him permission to stay ordinary, and refused to make him name the strap under his own roof — flipped him to a grateful, frightened ally

dmlog.text: Now I've got a card worth selling — and that's exactly when a smart woman stops and asks who she's selling it to. I've built Corran a mouth: an Iron-Strap hand, a netmender named Maddan, skimming his precious well older than the Circle itself. But I only ever heard the Circle's side of this war, and the last thing the Iron-Strap did was warn me — the thumb, what the Circle does to hands. You don't hand a man to the wolves before you've at least heard him howl. So I go to take the other side's measure while the light's still good, and I make Fenn my alibi for doing it. "Fenn — Corran wants the well, and the well's got a second hand on it that isn't ours. I mean to go put eyes on the Iron-Strap's piece of this before dusk, so I walk into Corran tonight knowing not just who skims him but how deep. They made an overture to me my first day; that's a door standing open. Let me be the one who walks through it and comes back with their shape. That's intelligence no one else on your leash can get you." And whatever slack he gives or doesn't, I point myself toward the Tanner's Reach, where the Strap first put a warning in my ear — going to find the netmender, or his people, and hear how Iron-Strap tells the story of the buried Sunns and the stolen well. Because before I sell Maddan to Corran, I want to know if Maddan's a thief or the last honest man in the Maw — and which answer sells for more.

Fenn lets the pitch finish, and for once he doesn't answer at the pace of a patient man. He answers a half-beat too fast, which from him is a shout. "No." Then, catching himself, slower: "Not no to the intelligence. Corran would take the Strap's shape gladly, and you're not wrong that you're the one who could fetch it." His eyes are flat on you now, and the thing he banked this morning — the Seam who goes digging at the Circle's seams the moment the leash feels slack — is right there behind them, doing sums. "No to me being the man who blessed it. You walk to the Iron-Strap, that's you walking, on your own two feet, and you'd best walk back Corran's, because there's a shape of woman who visits both wolves to see which one feeds better, and that woman doesn't get old in the Maw. Corran will hear you went. Corran hears everything. Make sure the story you bring him tonight is better than the story he'll already have." He does not stop you. He simply stops walking beside you — and you feel the difference in your spine, the way the leash has gone from a hand on your shoulder to a rifle sight between them.

You go anyway, up and across the swaying spans toward the Tanner's Reach, where the boardwalks give over to the river-bend stink of lye and wet hide and the water comes up brown and slow. It is Iron-Strap ground and it knows its own, and you are not three planks onto it before you learn that the Circle isn't the only power in the Maw that watches.

She's mending a net that doesn't need mending, which is how you know she was set there to wait — the tannery-hand from your first day, the one whose careless slip pointed you upriver, **Ospra**, and there was nothing careless about it. She doesn't look up from the twine. "You took your time," she says. "He said you'd come when you'd worked out there were two sides. Said you were the clever kind." Her needle doesn't pause. "Maddan'll see you. Now, while your Circle shadow's still deciding whether to report you. But you come to the netmender the way you'd come to a confessor, girl, because he already knows more of your day than you'd like — and he's the only man in this town who buried the same house you're carrying a list about." She bites the twine, and for the first time looks at you, and her eyes are not a tannery-hand's eyes at all. "Come on, then. Before your dusk gets here and picks for you."

dmlog.text: A confessor, she said. Fine — I know how to kneel without meaning it. I follow Ospra to the netmender and I go in soft and mostly honest, because a man who already knows my day catches a lie faster than a truth, and the truths I can afford to spend buy more here than silence would. I let him see a woman with tired hands and no love for the leash she's on. "Maddan. I'll save us both the dance — yes, I opened the seal; yes, I carry Corran's list; and no, I don't carry it gladly. I came in owing the Circle my passage, not my soul, and a woman who owes the wrong people learns fast to know the whole board before she plays a card." I set my honesty on the table like a coin I can spare and then I ask for his, watching his hands and his eyes the way I've watched everyone today: "Ospra says you buried the same house I'm carrying a list of. So tell me true, netmender, because I'll know if you dress it: what were the Sunns to you, and what's the cut you take off Rell's oil — a thief's skim, or an old debt somebody still owes the dead? And while you're being honest—" I keep it gentle, because this is the one that matters most "—why did your Ospra point a Circle-owed stranger upriver toward a frightened boy, my first hour in this town? What's the child to the Strap?" Then I shut up and let the old man fill the silence, and I read every line of him for the seam where the story he tells stops being the story he lives.

A confessor, she said. Fine — I know how to kneel without meaning it. I follow Ospra to the netmender and I go in soft and mostly honest, because a man who already knows my day catches a lie faster than a truth, and the truths I can afford to spend buy more here than silence would. I let him see a woman with tired hands and no love for the leash she's on. "Maddan. I'll save us both the dance — yes, I opened the seal; yes, I carry Corran's list; and no, I don't carry it gladly. I came in owing the Circle my passage, not my soul, and a woman who owes the wrong people learns fast to know the whole board before she plays a card." I set my honesty on the table like a coin I can spare and then I ask for his, watching his hands and his eyes the way I've watched everyone today: "Ospra says you buried the same house I'm carrying a list of. So tell me true, netmender, because I'll know if you dress it: what were the Sunns to you, and what's the cut you take off Rell's oil — a thief's skim, or an old debt somebody still owes the dead? And while you're being honest—" I keep it gentle, because this is the one that matters most "—why did your Ospra point a Circle-owed stranger upriver toward a frightened boy, my first hour in this town? What's the child to the Strap?" Then I shut up and let the old man fill the silence, and I read every line of him for the seam where the story he tells stops being the story he lives.

The netmender's place is a lean-to of drying nets and the low brown breath of the river, and Maddan is smaller than a man who buries houses ought to be — old, spare, hands like knotted cord from a lifetime of the same work, and eyes that have done a great deal of watching in a town that punishes it. He does not stand for you. He gestures at an upturned crate with a net-needle and lets your honesty sit in the air a while before he decides what to do with it.

"You spend truth like a woman who's counted it," he says at last. "Good. I'll not waste mine." He works the needle as he talks, and the story comes out in its rhythm — over, under, pull. "The Sunns kept the Throat before the word Circle meant anything but a shape. Four hundred years. They knew the well doesn't give — it's owed. You take the oil, you pay the count, you keep your face to the east so the crater never sees you take, and it lets you live. That was the whole religion of this place, girl, and the Sunns were its priests." Over, under. "Then a hard season came, and a hard man with it, and a door that was meant to stay shut got opened, and the Circle walked in where no one had ever been let. The Sunns went into the glass. All but the count itself — because a debt older than a family doesn't die with the family." He looks up. "That's your skim off Rell's oil. It isn't theft. It's the last tithe still being paid to the rightful dead, by the one man left who's owed the collecting. I don't take the Circle's cut. I take the Sunns' due, and I've taken it in the dark for thirty years, and I'll take it till the well is back in a right hand or I'm in the glass with the rest of them."

He sets the net down. "You asked why Ospra put you upriver toward the boy your first hour here." A long pause, the first thing all morning he's had to reach for. "Because some houses aren't all the way buried. Because there are things worth a stranger finding before the Circle does. That's all the answer you've earned, and it's more than's safe."

And there it is — the story, whole and clean and told in a workman's rhythm. Too clean, maybe. Because a man who's grieved a thing for thirty years should stumble somewhere in the telling, and Maddan stumbled only once, and not where you'd expect: not on the boy, not on the well, but on the door — on who opened it. The grief in that one word sat wrong, too near, too owned, the way a man grieves his own sin and not another's. If you're right about what you saw, you're looking at the traitor of the Sunns, dressed as their last loyal servant. If you're wrong, you're about to call a grieving old man a liar to his face, on his own ground, with your Circle shadow somewhere behind you counting the minutes. You'd need to be certain.

fields.role: the netmender at the Tanner's Reach; secret head/keeper of the Iron-Strap Guild — collects the 'Sunns' due,' the old tithe off the Throat's oil, as the last rightful claim of the buried keeper-house. Not a thief by his telling; the debt-keeper of the rightful dead.

dmlog.text: "Who I'd rather owe." I let that hang, and I don't answer it, because the moment I pick a wolf I stop being worth courting to both. Instead I put my cards down in an order I choose. I do NOT tell him what I read in him a moment ago — that ace stays up my sleeve, warm, mine. I give him the useful truth instead. "Here's my honest, netmender, since you spent yours: I won't be owned. Not by Corran, not by you. But owning and useful are different animals, and I can be very useful to a man who wants the same thing I've already decided I want." I lean on that last part, watching him. "Because I think we do want the same thing. Your Ospra didn't point me at that boy by accident, and I didn't keep my hands closed at Dessa's door by accident either. I already told them I'd treat the child like family, not like a debt — before I knew a thing about who he is to you. So maybe stop weighing me for a successor's chair and start telling me plainly: is the boy what's left of the house you buried? Because if he is, then you and I aren't negotiating — we're already on the same side of the one thing that matters, and everything else is just what I have to survive to keep him breathing." Then the hard ask, the one that pays my rent tonight: "Corran wants a name from me by dusk — the mouth that told me the Sunns. I mean to walk in and not get killed. What can the Strap actually put in my hand before then that keeps the Circle believing I'm theirs while I keep your boy off their list? Give me something real, Maddan, or the only card I've got to play at dusk is you." I say the threat mildly, a stated fact, not a knife — and I read him for whether it lands as leverage or as the moment he decides I'm too dangerous to let walk back out.

You lay the threat down mild, a fact and not a knife, and you watch it travel through him. It does not frighten him — you understand at once that very little does anymore; a man who's carried what Maddan carries has spent his fear down to the studs. But it lands, because it's true, and truth is the only currency he still respects. For a long moment the only sound is the river and the wet slap of a net he isn't mending.

"So you'd sell me to Corran," he says, without heat. "You could. It's the play, if all you want is to live to Wednesday." He sets the needle down for good. "But you didn't come to my ground and ask after the boy first if living to Wednesday was all you wanted. You'd have led with the knife."

He looks at you a long time, and then he gives you the thing you asked for, which is the truth. "Yes. The boy is what's left. Batgal Sukhukh is a name I bought him off a dead refugee's rent-book so the Circle would count him as nobody's. His right name is the one that got a house poured into glass. He is the last Sunn, and the well is his by four hundred years of a debt this crater still means to collect — and I have kept him alive by keeping him nothing, which is a thing you understand, Seam, better than most." He lets that bind you, gently, the way a good knot binds. "You already chose him at Dessa's door. I only watched you do it."

Then he gives you your dusk. "You want a mouth for Corran that isn't the boy and isn't me. Take **Dannad**. Coalstack Row, the cooper two doors up from your chandler — a Circle man who's been selling the Circle's business to my ear for a year, cheap, out of spite over a debt. He's real, Corran can prove him, and burning him costs the Strap a mouthful of stale bread and costs the Circle a hole in its own hull. Give Corran his leak. Let him find it inside his own house. It'll keep him hunting his own shadow for a month." His eyes harden, just slightly — the counter to your threat, delivered in the same flat kindness. "But understand the knot you're in now. Ospra will have your route from here. The boy is between us both — if you sell the Strap, he pays first, and you a breath after. I'm not threatening you, girl. I'm telling you we're tied to the same stone now, you and I and a nine-year-old king who mends nets thinking he's an orphan. Go keep your appointment. Come back when it's kept."

fields.role: the boy hiding at Dessa's loft — CONFIRMED the last Sunn; 'Batgal Sukhukh' is a bought cover-name (off a dead refugee's rent-book) so the Circle counts him as nobody. His true line is Sunn; the well is his by 400 yrs of the keeper-debt. Iron-Strap/Maddan protect him.

dm.heirConfirmed: T7: Maddan confirmed OUTRIGHT — Batgal is the last Sunn, the rightful heir to the well. 'Batgal Sukhukh' is a cover bought off a dead refugee's rent-book. Sella already chose to protect him (Dessa's door) before knowing. He is now the MUTUAL HOSTAGE binding Sella and Iron-Strap: if she sells the Strap, the boy pays first, then her. Ties tonight's Batgal-at-Dessa's thread to the throne of the whole well-war.

fields.role: a cooper on Coalstack Row (two doors up from Rell's chandlery); secretly a Circle man who's been selling Circle business to Iron-Strap for a year, out of spite over a debt

dm.sacrificialMouth: T7: the name Maddan handed Sella to feed Corran as her dusk 'mouth' — a REAL Circle-side leak (Dannad sells Circle business to the Strap). Verifiable by Corran, cheap for Iron-Strap to burn, and it turns Sella's forced delivery into a strike against the Circle (sets Corran hunting his own house for a month). Protects the boy and Maddan. Sella has NOT yet delivered it.

dm.nowShadows: T7: Maddan set Ospra to have Sella's route from the Tanner's Reach onward — Iron-Strap now shadows Sella as closely as the Circle (Fenn) does. She is openly double-leashed.

dmlog.dmNotes: No roll: her leverage is genuine (the threat is true; and per the crit-read Maddan needs a successor — though he doesn't know she saw that), so his cooperation is the honest NPC response — but the charter keeps agency with him: he GIVES with strings (the boy as mutual hostage; Ospra now shadows her; double-leashed). Paid off the Batgal-heir drip as an earned reveal (she'd already chosen the boy, demonstrating loyalty). Reused the existing roster stub npc:dannad as the sacrificial mouth (DM assigns meaning to an engine-rolled atom) rather than minting. Sella now has a concrete dusk play that protects the boy AND satisfies/damages Corran. Cost: fully enmeshed with BOTH factions now. Her crit-ace (Maddan = the Sunns' traitor) stays unspent.

dmlog.text: A card you can't prove is a bluff, and I don't walk into Corran Vale bluffing. So I make my way back down toward Coalstack Row — Ospra's eyes on me somewhere, Fenn's somewhere else, a woman walking between two watchers like it's the most natural thing in the world — and before I ever face the Circle I go quiet-confirm the mouth I mean to feed it. Dannad, the cooper, two doors up from Rell. I don't approach him. I buy nothing, I say nothing; I do what I do best, which is become a tired traveler resting in the right doorway with a good sightline, and I watch the cooper's shop the way I watched the oil-troughs: patient, sidelong, learning his rhythm — who comes to his door, what changes in his face when certain folk pass, whether there's a tell on a man who sells his own guild cheap. I want one provable thing I can set in front of Corran so my leak has teeth and not just a name. And while I watch, I take the town's temperature on ME — because Fenn swore Corran would already know I walked to the Strap, and a Circle that's decided I'm a traitor moves before dusk, not at it. So I read the Row for it: too many idle men, a face I saw at the Reach now here, the particular quiet that means a decision's been made about you. Then I find my wall and my sightline and I wait for the light to go long, rehearsing the only story that keeps me breathing: that I went to the wolf for Corran, and came back with his own house's leak in my teeth.

You find your doorway — a gap between a shuttered net-loft and a stack of empty oil-butts, smoke-shadowed, a clean line on the cooper's door forty feet down. And you do the patient work. It takes an hour to learn a man's rhythm and you have more than an hour to give.

Dannad is a big, sweating cooper with a grievance in his shoulders, the kind of man who slams a hoop home a little harder when certain faces pass. And they do pass — a Circle face, unhurried, wood turning in its fingers, and you watch Dannad's whole back change, the resentment coming off him like heat off the vat. That alone would tell you Maddan spoke true. But you get your provable thing near midday: a water-carrier stops at the cooper's for a drink he doesn't finish, and in the passing of the cup a folded chit goes the other way, cooper to carrier, quick as a card-palm — and the carrier doesn't drink upriver, he turns his yoke toward the Tanner's Reach. A courier line, running out of a Circle man's shop toward the Strap's ground. That you can prove. That has teeth.

What you can't read, watch as you might, is your own weather. You look for the too-many-idle-men, the decision made about you — and the Row gives you nothing, which against a patient enemy is not the same as safety. It's the stillness of a man who doesn't need to hurry.

You learn how patient near dusk, when the glass below has gone from white to a long low amber and your legs have gone stiff with waiting. A child you don't know — nine, ten, one of the Maw's countless errand-sparrows — stops at your doorway and does not look at your face, only sets a thing on the ledge by your hand and is gone into the crowd before you can close your fingers on more than the sight of it. A splinter of pale ironwood. The same wood Corran laid on the table between you this morning, the leash that wasn't a gift. Wrapped round it once, a thread, and under the thread a curl of bark scratched with three marks you understand without being taught: a tree, a setting sun, and a single tally-stroke. He knows where you've been. He is not angry — anger hurries, and Corran has never hurried in his life. He is only telling you, in the politest possible hand, that your appointment has a place now, and the place is the one every road in the Maw bends toward. The Traitor's Tree. Dusk. Come to him. He's had all day, and he has let you have it too, which is the most frightening courtesy of all.

fields.role: cooper on Coalstack Row (two doors up from Rell); a resentful Circle man secretly running a courier line to Iron-Strap — confirmed by observation

dm.provableTell: T8: Sella confirmed Dannad by patient watch — near midday he palmed a folded chit to a water-carrier who then turned his yoke toward the Tanner's Reach (the Strap's ground). A courier line running out of a Circle man's shop = the PROVABLE detail Sella can set before Corran so the 'mouth' has teeth, not just a name. Also read Dannad's open resentment (debt-spite) at passing Circle faces.

dm.knowsStrapVisit: T8: Corran KNOWS Sella went to the Iron-Strap (Fenn's 'Corran hears everything' held). He did NOT move against her early — characteristic patience. Near dusk he sent an errand-child with a token: a pale ironwood splinter (the same leash-wood), bark scratched with tree+setting-sun+one tally-stroke.
dm.summons: T8: Corran's summons — the dusk 'mouth' appointment now has a PLACE: the Traitor's Tree, at dusk. His ground, the myth-heart, where he told Sella (via Batgal, Day 2 open) a patient man waits and lets you come to him. Sella walks into the meeting with Corran ALREADY holding the story of her Strap visit — she must reframe it as intelligence-gathering FOR him (the double-agent cover she pitched Fenn) and deliver Dannad. Telegraphed, patient, lethal-adjacent.

dmlog.dmNotes: Prep beat: rewarded the recon with a provable Dannad detail (courier chit → the Reach) so the dusk delivery has teeth. Honored Fenn's T5 warning — Corran KNOWS about the Strap visit — telegraphed via a patient ironwood-splinter summons (danger telegraphed honestly: he knows, he's unhurried, that's the threat). Converged the unvisited Traitor's Tree thread into the climax location. Deliberately left Sella's own 'weather' unreadable (her weak Perception; a patient enemy's stillness ≠ safety) — genuine uncertainty into T9 without a roll. Montaged the wait; clock advanced to dusk. No dice — saving them for the confrontation.

dmlog.text: I go to the Tree. Of course I do — a summons from a patient man is the one appointment you keep early. The Traitor's Tree at dusk, black-barked and leafless out of the colored glass, Corran somewhere in its shadow turning a sliver of wood, and me walking up unhurried the way he taught me to, hands loose and visible, the ironwood splinter he sent me held plain between two fingers so he sees I read his hand and came anyway. And I do not wait to be accused. A guilty woman explains; a useful one reports. So I lead. "You know I went to the Iron-Strap today. Good — I hoped you would, because I went for you, and a man who wants a well ought to know I can walk onto his rival's ground and walk back off it. You asked me this morning for the mouth that named the Sunns. I'm going to give you something a mouth can't: the reason you were right that there was one." I let the splinter turn in my own fingers now, mirroring him. "There's a leak in your house, Corran. Not a stranger who guessed — a Circle man selling your business cheap. Dannad, the cooper on Coalstack Row, two doors up from the chandler you sent me to remind. He runs a chit out of his shop by a water-carrier's yoke, and the yoke turns for the Tanner's Reach, not the river. I watched it cross today with my own eyes; send anyone and they'll watch it cross tomorrow. That's your mouth — not the one that told me, the one that tells everyone. Burn him and you close the hole. Keep him and you feed him lies and watch where they surface." Then I give him the one true thing that sells all the rest, because a lie survives best carried on a truth's back: "And no — nobody named the Sunns to me. I read it off your own list, the two struck names, one crossed twice. I'm the kind who looks; you said so yourself, this morning, and you called it a question you hadn't answered — tool or liability. So here's my answer, laid at your feet: I looked, and what I found was your leak, not your secret. A liability hides that. A tool brings it to you at dusk." And then I shut up and let Corran Vale, who has listened to frightened people lie for twenty years, decide what he's looking at — and I hold my face the way you hold a good hand, easy and unbothered, giving him nothing to read but a woman telling the truth about a lie she means to keep.

The Traitor's Tree is worse up close, and quieter. Four hundred years of black bark grown straight up out of a wound of colored glass, leafless, its roots fused into the fracture like something that reached down to drink and was caught doing it. The dusk pours up through the crater below and lights the whole tree from beneath, so it stands in the amber like a thing on trial. This is where a Sunn opened a door. You feel the weight of that even not knowing the half of what you now know, and Corran Vale is exactly where a patient man stands in a place like this — not hidden, just still, one shoulder to the trunk, the sliver of wood going over and over between his fingers.

He lets your whole report land. He does not interrupt once. When you finish he is quiet a moment longer than is comfortable, and then he does the thing that tells you he was listening all the way down: he asks you only one question, and it's the one you didn't cover.

"The carrier," he says. "With the yoke. Describe his hands."

It's a small blade and a clever one — a man who ran the whole story in his head while you told it and found the one place a liar improvises. He watched you watch Dannad, or he didn't; either way he'll know from your hands, not your answer, whether you actually stood in that doorway or built it after the fact to dress a day spent turning your coat. He turns the wood. He has all the time in the world, and he is spending exactly none of it helping you. The amber light climbs the trunk between you. He waits.

dm.climaxSite: T9: revealed/entered at dusk as Corran's chosen meeting ground. The myth-heart — where a Sunn 'opened a door' (canon T2; DM-truth T6: the door was Maddan's own betrayal). Sella stands where the Sunns fell, choosing NOT to betray the boy — thematic mirror. Corran waits here, patient, testing her report.

dm.duskTest: T9: Sella LED with the report (no defense), reframed her Strap visit as scouting FOR Corran, and delivered Dannad (Circle-house leak) + the courier-chit proof, while giving the true 'no one named the Sunns, I read your list.' Corran let it all land, then probed the ONE improvisable detail — 'describe the carrier's hands' — reading her hands, not her words, for whether she really watched Dannad or built the story to cover a day of turning her coat. Deception check resolves whether he buys the loyal-tool framing over the double-agent truth.

dmlog.dmNotes: Climax. Corran's precision-trap ('describe the carrier's hands') is the honest test — a lie-expert probing the one improvisable detail, resolved by the Deception roll. Advantage because the pitch's spine is TRUE (real leak, really watched); DC16 because Corran is a 20-yr reader + set a trap. All three branches: she survives to reach T10, Dannad lands (he's real), and Maddan/the boy stay unnamed — the difference is her STANDING and danger. Fail is lethal-ADJACENT and telegraphed (patient countdown + he knows the loft), never an instant kill on an L1 at a dialogue — on-charter (danger telegraphed, honor-the-cool). Front clock ticks +1 in every branch (the Circle tightens its grip regardless — it got a leak to close). Thematic mirror: Sella stands where the Sunns were betrayed and chooses not to betray the boy.

dmlog.text: You give him the hands and they come out a shade too clean, the description of a woman who has decided what the carrier looked like rather than one who saw him — and the tree goes very quiet, and Corran stops turning the wood. That's the tell, and it's the worst one. A patient man only stops when he's arrived somewhere. "You know," he says, almost fondly, "the carrier's a woman." He lets that sit in the amber light until you feel the floor of it drop out. "Dannad's real — you got that much honest, and I'll close him, so thank you for the hull-hole. But you built the doorway, Voss. You spent your day turning your coat on the Strap's ground and dressed it in one true cooper. I told you this morning: useful by dusk, or a loose end by dark." He finally pushes off the tree, unhurried, and it's the unhurry that's the knife. "I'm not going to do anything about that tonight. You've a use in you yet, and I never waste a use. But you should know the arithmetic changed just now, at this tree, of all the trees in the world — and that a man who lets you walk away from here is a man who's already decided he can afford to lose you. Sleep well. You've a wall waiting, they tell me." He knows about the loft. Of course he knows about the loft.

dm.sawThrough: T9 DECEPTION FAIL (missed DC16 by 3+): Corran caught the built-story — sprung his trap ('the carrier's a woman' — she'd improvised a man's hands). Took Dannad (still useful) but concluded Sella turned her coat at the Strap and dressed it in one true cooper. Activated the 'loose end by dark' arithmetic: he won't strike TONIGHT (she has a use left, and it's telegraphed — patient, not merciful), but she is now a MARKED loose end on borrowed time, and he pointedly knows about Dessa's loft ('you've a wall waiting'). Danger clock now runs toward Sella. The boy/Maddan still unnamed, but Corran watching her every move makes tonight's trip to Batgal far more dangerous.
dm.knowsLoft: T9: Corran revealed he knows Sella's berth is Dessa's loft at the Miller's Leat — a pointed threat, and a hazard for tonight's return to the hidden boy.

dmlog.text: He knows about the loft. Of course he knows — and that single sentence rewrites my whole night, because the wall I earned to sleep behind is now the map I'd draw the Circle straight to the boy. So I do not go to Dessa's. Walking to Batgal tonight is the one move on this board that gets him killed, and I did not keep my hands closed at that door and stand where the Sunns were betrayed just to be the woman who finally leads the wolf home. I walk away from the Tree marked, unhurried, a tired asset going to her earned rest — and I let Corran's people believe that's exactly what I'm doing. But Iron-Strap has watched my every step since the Reach; Ospra has my route. So I use the one leash my failure didn't cut. Without ever breaking stride, without a glance that isn't idle, I spend the best thing I own — hands quick enough to lift a coin off a man mid-sentence — to leave the Strap a message where only a Strap watcher reads it: a chalk-mark on the third leat-post I know their runners check, a knot tied wrong in a hank of net-twine I trail my fingers through at Ospra's own corner, whatever dead-drop this town's second shadow keeps. The message is three things, small enough to carry in a knot: MOVE THE BOY. THE CIRCLE KNOWS THE LOFT. NOT FROM ME. I pass it under Corran's own watchers' noses, reading the street the way a card-sharp reads a table — timing the mark to the moment every eye is on something else — because if I'm caught signaling the Strap I've hanged the boy and myself both, and if I'm clean, then a nine-year-old king sleeps somewhere new tonight and never knows a stranger turned her whole bad day into his one good break.

You walk away from the Traitor's Tree the way a beaten thing walks, and you let every watcher in the dusk believe the beating took. It's the truest disguise you've got tonight, because it half did. But under the tired shoulders your mind is very clear and very cold, running the only route that ends with the boy alive, and it does not run through Dessa's door.

The Miller's Leat lies on your way to nowhere, and a woman going nowhere can trail her fingers along a rail. You've marked the Strap's dead-drops all day without meaning to — a con artist counts exits and drops the way other people breathe — and now you spend the counting. A hank of net-twine hangs at the corner Ospra worked this morning, and your hand passes through it idle, and leaves it knotted wrong in the particular way that a net-mender's eye snags on and a Circle man's slides past. Three things in one bad knot: move the boy, the Circle knows the loft, not from me.

The whole of it lasts less than a breath, and the danger is the same as any lift: it isn't the hand, it's the timing. You need every wrong pair of eyes pointed elsewhere in the exact instant your fingers do their work — and there are a great many wrong eyes on you tonight, the Circle's freshly sharpened, and you cannot know which of them is, right now, watching your hands the way you taught yourself to watch everyone's. The twine is in your fingers. The moment is now or it's gone. You reach.
dmlog.dmNotes: Set-closing beat. Sella spends her single best skill (SoH +5) at the crux to protect the boy she's spent the whole day protecting — refusing to lead the Circle to the loft. Success = a bittersweet clean close (loses standing/safety, keeps the boy — 'never felt cleaner'). Fail is a genuine cliffhanger (caught by the carrier Corran set on the drop — paying off HIS T9 win), never a flat death — the boy's fate held unresolved into Set 03. Maddan attitude +1 on any through-getting (she proved the alliance). Ties the arc's spine (the boy) to the mechanical crux with her actual class strength.

dmlog.text: It's the cleanest work you've done in the Maw, and no one will ever see it, which is the whole point of the best work. The knot goes wrong under a passing hand while three Circle men watch a bargeman drop a crate two decks down — you didn't cause that, you just waited for the Maw to hand you your instant, and it did, because a hanging town is always dropping something. Your fingers come away empty and idle and the twine hangs there holding its small terrible sentence for the one eye meant to read it. You don't look back. You don't slow. Somewhere behind you a net-mender's watcher will trail her own fingers through that corner within the hour, and snag, and read, and a boy who mends nets thinking he's an orphan will be gone from Dessa's loft before the Circle's patience runs its course — moved in the dark to another nowhere, never knowing that a stranger spent the worst day of her year buying him one more. You've lost your standing, your safe wall, and very likely the long odds on your own survival. You have kept the one thing you decided this morning was yours to keep. You walk into the dark of the Maw a marked woman, and you have never in your life felt cleaner.

dm.savedTonight: T10 SLEIGHT OF HAND SUCCESS (beat DC15): Sella passed Iron-Strap a clean dead-drop warning (knotted-wrong net-twine at Ospra's corner) — 'move the boy, the Circle knows the loft, not from me' — under the Circle's alerted watchers without being caught. Batgal will be moved from Dessa's loft in the dark before Corran acts. Sella protected the last Sunn at the cost of her own standing/safety, and he'll never know.

dm.sellaProvedTonight: T10: Sella warned the Strap to move the boy the instant she learned the Circle knew the loft — spending her best tradecraft and taking on all the risk. She proved, unasked, that her choice at Dessa's door was real. The successor Maddan was auditioning has paid her first true premium on the shared stone.

payload.cause: warned Iron-Strap to move the boy under the Circle's watchers, at cost to herself — proved the alliance real

dm.missedTheDrop: T10: Corran's freshly-alerted watchers did NOT catch Sella leaving the Strap dead-drop (her SoH beat DC15). He believes he's marked a useful loose end going to rest; he does not know she just moved his prize's heir out of his reach.

dmlog.text: The cleanest work of my life, and it buys me a night I have nowhere to spend. The loft is poison now — every road that ends at a warm bed ends at Batgal's throat — so I do the hard thing and end my night nowhere. But Corran let me walk, and a patient man who lets you walk keeps a string on you to see where you fray. So before I sleep I have to know: does his string still run to my ankle? I don't bolt — bolting tells a tail he's made. I walk tired, a beaten asset going to ground, and I let the Maw's own crookedness do my work: I take the route with the most turnings, the plank-bridges and the dropped decks and the press of the evening market where a hundred bodies smear one woman's trail, and twice I stop dead in a doorway like a woman whose legs have quit — not to rest, but to read the current behind me for the eddy a follower makes when the water he's swimming in suddenly stops. Who breaks stride when I break stride. Whose eyes were already on my back before I turned. And if there's a Circle shadow on me, I don't lose him clean — a lost tail is a reported tail — I let him keep a Sella-shaped shape to follow while the real me peels off into the Refugee Quarter's warren, where a coin buys an anonymous corner and no one's ever heard the name Voss, to sleep rough among people the Maw already decided don't count.
