The market of Coalstack Row at dusk is a good place to become no one. The dippers come off shift and the stall-women bank their coals and the whole crooked shelf of the town exhales at once, a hundred tired bodies going home over the same forty feet of swaying plank, and you pour yourself into the middle of it like water finding the low place. You walk the way you said you'd walk — beaten, slow, a used-up thing — and you take the route with the most teeth in it: the dropped deck where the boards go single-file, the resin-gate press where the crowd knots and stalls, the doorway of a shuttered oil-factor where a woman might simply run out of legs.

And twice you stop dead, and read the water behind you.

The first time you learn nothing but the shape of the crowd. The second time — the shuttered doorway, the amber light going long and bloody up the chains — you learn something, because the current behind you has an eddy in it. Somewhere back in the press a body did the thing a follower cannot help doing: when you stopped, it had nowhere to be. Not close. Not clumsy. A patient shape keeping the exact distance a professional keeps, and it is not looking at you now, it is looking with great interest at a rope-maker's wares it has no use for. Corran let you walk. Corran did not let you go. There is a string on your ankle and it runs back into the Circle's dusk, and the only question left tonight is whether you can read it well enough to cut it clean — shed it into the Refugee Quarter's warren so it keeps a Sella-shaped ghost and loses the woman — or whether it beds down knowing exactly which hole you crawled into.

You pick your instant. The crowd knots at the resin-gate. You reach for the turning.
dmlog.dmNotes: T1 set3. Opening the evening after the Tree. Sella marked. Real forward pressure = Corran's patient tail. Uncertain read -> rollRequest (Stealth, adv for clever approach), STOP at threshold. Fail ticks the internal front (Circle grip) since her hole is compromised.

dmlog.text: You cut it clean, and you cut it so well the cutting is invisible. At the resin-gate the crowd folds shut behind you like water over a dropped stone, and in the fold you become a stall-woman's daughter, a stooped shape under a borrowed shawl-corner, a nobody bound three ways from where Sella Voss was going. The string doesn't snap — snapping tells him — it just goes slack in his hand around a ghost that keeps walking sensibly home toward a wall that isn't yours. You watch him take it for one block, two, committed now to the wrong woman, and you read his coat in the last of the light: not Fenn, a younger runner, Circle-cut, careful. He'll report where the ghost bedded and it will be a lie, and Corran will spend a small piece of tomorrow being wrong about you, which is worth more than gold to a marked woman. You peel down into the Refugee Quarter as the amber dies — a warren of lean-tos and stacked lodging on the town's cheapest chains, where the Maw keeps the people it has already decided don't count, and where a copper buys a corner and no ears have ever heard the name Voss.

dm.tailSet: T1-set3: Corran put a soft tail on Sella after the Tree (patient, not moving against her yet) — a younger Circle runner, not Fenn. Sella READ it and SHED it clean in the dusk-market, feeding it a decoy ghost bound for a wall that isn't hers. Corran will get a FALSE report of where she bedded. She is NOT at the loft; she went to ground in the Refugee Quarter.

fields.role: A warren of lean-tos and stacked cheap lodging on the town's lowest chains — where the Maw keeps the uncounted. Sella's bolt-hole night 1 (Day 2). A copper buys an anonymous corner; the Sunn cover-name 'Batgal Sukhukh' came off a dead refugee's rent-book from here.

dmlog.text: A marked woman needs two things by morning, and the Refugee Quarter might hold both. So I don't just sleep — I work the only room in the Maw where being no one is the price of admission. I buy my way into a fire-circle the honest way, with the last warmth in my coppers and a shared heel of my own rations, and I become exactly what I look like: a night-chains newcomer who's crossed the wrong people uptown and needs a cheap corner where the landlord forgets your face and no work asks your name. From inside that skin I fish soft, the way the uncounted talk to the uncounted — never the real question first. I ask which lodging-houses are honest and which will rob a stranger, and I let the talk drift the way it wants to, toward the house with the bad luck, the one where a lodger checked in and never checked out and the room's still on the book — because that dead man's name is the one keeping a nine-year-old king alive, and I need to know how thin that paper is before the Circle ever thinks to pull it. And second, quieter, I take the quarter's own temperature: they've a council and their own grievances, I'm told, and every grievance in this town runs uphill to the same ironwood door. Who speaks for the uncounted here — and what do they hold against the Circle that a woman the Circle just marked might make common cause with? I trade what I can spare, I give more listening than talking, and I read the circle for the one face that goes still when the Sunn-shaped questions come too close.

The fire-circle takes your coppers and your ration-heel the way the poor take everything — without thanks and without forgetting, which is its own ledger. They make room. You are, tonight, exactly what you look like, and there is a terrible rest in that.

The voice of the circle is a broad, tired woman named **Susannah Holloway**, who has been in the Maw long enough to have opinions and short enough to still be angry about them. She answers your lodging-question sideways, the way careful people answer, and lets the talk drift where you steered it. "Honest houses," she snorts. "There's none. There's cheap and there's cruel. You want the sort that don't ask a name—" and here a younger man across the coals goes very still, a stillness you'd have missed if you weren't fishing for exactly it, "—you want off this quarter altogether. Saltwidow Row. There's a house there takes anyone, because the man that keeps the book stopped reading it years back. Room up top's been let to a dead man since before I came — checked in, never checked out, and the book still says he's home." She says it like a joke the town's been telling too long to laugh at. She does not know she's just told you where a boy's whole life is written in a dead stranger's hand.

You ask, softer, who speaks for the uncounted here, and what they carry against the ironwood door. And the fire goes quiet in the particular way a fire goes quiet when you've said the true thing. Susannah looks at you a long moment. "Speaks for us." She almost smiles. "You're new, so I'll say it once and you'll not repeat it. The Circle doesn't kill you, girl. That's the mistake up-town folk make, thinking it's blood they do. The Circle just stops counting you. Strikes the name, amends the book, and then whatever happens to the thing that used to have the name — well. Nothing happened to nobody, did it. We're all down here because somebody uphill decided we were a number they'd rather not carry." She pokes the fire. "And now the river's carrying us instead."

That lands last and it lands cold, because you've felt it under the boards all night without naming it: the water's high. Higher than the season. Someone says the gauge hit the ten-year mark yesterday and hasn't stopped climbing, and three houses up in the dry district already have the river in their cellars, and if the dry district's wet then the plan that keeps this quarter alive — the plan that says the low chains flood and the high ground holds — is a plan built on a lie the water hasn't finished exposing yet. The uncounted live on the lowest chains, in rooms built to flood, because the counted decided long ago whose cellar was worth keeping dry.

The young man across the coals has not looked at you since the word Saltwidow left Susannah's mouth. He is looking at the fire. He is listening to every word.

fields.role: Broad, tired, long-settled refugee — the de-facto voice of the Refugee Quarter fire-circle; speaks (guardedly) for the uncounted. Met Sella night 1 (Day 2), took her for a genuine night-chains newcomer.

dm.grievance: T2-set3: Susannah's read on the Circle, given freely to Sella as a fellow uncounted: 'The Circle doesn't kill you — it stops counting you. Strikes the name, amends the book.' The quarter's core grievance = administrative erasure by the Circle (grounds the Refugee Quarter dmOnly secret WITHOUT leaking it). She pointed Sella to Saltwidow Row for no-name lodging.

dm.coverTrace: T2-set3: The dead-man rent-book that gives Batgal his cover-name ('checked in, never checked out, book still says he's home') is at a lodging house on SALTWIDOW ROW — the keeper stopped reading his own book years ago, top room let to a dead man since before Susannah arrived. The boy's whole legal existence is written in a dead stranger's hand there. Cover-integrity thread: as long as that book stays unread, the boy stays nobody; if the Circle ever pulls it, the cover unravels.

dm.floodRising: T2-set3: TELEGRAPH of the external front (hard-season/flood). River gauge hit the ten-year mark yesterday and is STILL climbing; three upper-district (dry) houses already have water in their cellars — meaning the evacuation plan (low chains flood, high ground holds) is built on a failing assumption. The uncounted live in rooms built to flood; they drown first. Live, advancing danger to Sella's bolt-hole and the whole quarter.
dm.stillFace: T2-set3 HOOK: a young man across the fire-circle went STILL the instant Sella's questions turned Sunn/Saltwidow-shaped, and stopped looking at her, listening hard. Unidentified — could be a Circle ear, an Iron-Strap watcher, or someone who knows what the Saltwidow book really holds. Unresolved thread.

dmlog.dmNotes: T2 set3. Night in the Refugee Quarter. Willing-source gather-info among genuine peers -> no roll; reward the honest approach with real but partial drips. Grounded the quarter's dmOnly erasure-secret as a THEME (Susannah's 'stops counting you') without leaking the specific gaol-death noun. Seated the flood (external front 0->1) as live telegraphed danger. Planted two threads: Saltwidow Row (the boy's cover-book) + the still-faced young man. Susannah revealed+contacted.

dmlog.text: The young man who went still at the word Saltwidow is a loose thread with legs, and a thread like that walks straight uphill to Corran if I let it. So I do nothing in the circle — I laugh at Susannah's joke, I share the last of my ration like a woman with nowhere to be, I let the fire believe I've forgotten him. But I mark his shape, his shoes, the set of his shoulders, and when he finally peels off into the dark — and a man that quiet always leaves first — I give him a ten-count and I go after him through the warren, soft-footed, using the lean-tos and the wash-lines and the dark the way I used the market crowd, close enough to keep his back and far enough to be no one behind him. I want to know where he goes and who he answers to before I ever let him see my face. And when the lanes go empty enough that it's just the two of us and no witness — a dead-end, a wash-yard, wherever the warren gives me a wall at his back — I close the distance and I put myself between him and wherever he was hurrying, easy, hands open, a fellow night-owl who couldn't sleep. "You left the fire quick, friend. And you went stiff as a plank when the old woman said Saltwidow. So let's you and me have the little talk you were about to go have with someone else — because whoever you're carrying that word to, I can pay better, or I can be a much worse problem than the coin's worth. Which of those I am is entirely up to how the next minute goes." And I read him — Circle, Strap, or just a frightened man who knows something — before I decide whether to buy him, turn him, or scare him back into the dark with a false trail in his teeth.

You give the fire nothing — a laugh, the last of your ration, a woman with nowhere to be — and you let the quiet young man forget he ever went stiff. He leaves first, the way the quiet ones do, folding up off his heel and away into the dark between the lean-tos. You give him his ten-count. Then you go.

The warren at night is a rogue's country and you were born for it: wash-lines to break your outline, the slap of the river under the boards to eat your step, a hundred black doorways to be nobody in. You keep his back and never his notice, close where the lane's loud, far where it's still, and you learn the shape of a frightened man from behind — because that's what he is, you see it in the walk now, not a hunter's walk at all but the fast, tucked scurry of something that expects a hand on its collar. He is not going uphill toward the ironwood door. He is going deeper down, toward the low chains, toward the water. Toward home.

The lane dead-ends in a wash-yard hung with dripping nets, the river black and close through the slats underfoot, and there is no one but the two of you. You close the distance and put the wall at his back before he knows the wall was a trap, easy, hands open, and you say your piece — the fire, the word Saltwidow, the little talk he was about to go have with someone else, pay better or worse problem, up to how the next minute goes.

He goes white. Not the white of a caught spy — you've cornered spies, and they get still and careful and start counting your exits. This is the other white, the one that comes up from underneath: a boy's terror in a grown man's face, both hands come up open and empty and shaking, and a sound in his throat that is trying very hard to become words and failing. "You're — " he gets out, and stops, and you watch him decide you're the thing he's been dreading, the hand from up-town come at last. "You're one of them. You came for the book." His eyes flick — not to an escape, not to a weapon — to the black water under the slats, the way a man looks at the only door he thinks he has left. Whatever he is, he is about to do something, and it's the next half-second that tells you what. You look at him — really look, the way you look at a mark when the whole game rides on reading true.

dm.stillFace: T3-set3: Frederick Brackett IS the young man who went still at 'Saltwidow' in the fire-circle (T2). Sella tailed him from the circle — he went DOWN toward the low chains/water, not uphill to the Circle, walking like a frightened man expecting a hand on his collar. Cornered in a wash-yard. He read Sella as 'one of them, come for the book' and looked at the black river as his only exit — a man on the edge of a desperate act. NOT reading as a spy (spies count exits; he's terrified from underneath).

dmlog.dmNotes: T3 set3. Tail resolved as rogue competence (no roll). Uncertain gate = the Insight READ of the cornered man, DC 15. SUBVERTS the 'Circle spy' telegraph: Frederick is one of the erased, and the read opens the real machinery of the uncounted (corpse-rooms hide struck names — the boy's cover-infrastructure). FAIL carries real teeth (exposure/cover-blown + a loose man branding her Circle), not a free scene. Pre-roll events reveal+contact Frederick (she IS face to face regardless of the die). STOP at threshold.

dmlog.text: You read him clean and the read rewrites the whole scene. He is no one's ear. He is one of the erased — Frederick Brackett, a name that used to be in a book uptown and isn't anymore, struck and amended, the way Susannah said. Saltwidow Row didn't make him go still because he's guarding it; it made him go still because that dead-man's house is where the quarter files its own — the room let to a corpse is not a landlord's bad luck, it's a hiding place the uncounted use to keep a name breathing after the Circle strikes it, and he has a brother, or had one, in exactly such a room. He thinks you're Circle come to read the book and finish the striking. And the tell that saves you both: at his belt, a small drawstring bag, and when his shaking hand pressed it you heard the click of stones — a dozen river-pebbles, each scratched once, a tally a man keeps when the town won't count his dead for him. He's not a threat. He's the opposite. He is a door — into how the uncounted really survive down here, and straight to the machinery that keeps Batgal a living nobody — and he is one true word away from throwing himself in the river rather than let you have the book. You know exactly what he is now, and exactly what he needs to hear. The choice of what you spend on him is yours.

fields.role: A young 'erased' man of the Refugee Quarter — his name was struck from an uptown book by the Circle. Keeps a bag of a dozen scratched river-pebbles: a private tally of the quarter's dead the town won't count. Terrified of anyone 'come for the book.'

dm.trueRead: T3-set3 SUCCESS (Insight): Frederick is NOT a spy — he's one of the erased. KEY REVEAL: the Saltwidow dead-man lodging isn't just where Batgal's cover-name came from — it's the quarter's living machinery: rooms let to corpses are hiding places the uncounted use to keep a struck name breathing. He has/had a brother in such a room. He read Sella as Circle come to finish the striking, was one word from jumping in the river. He is a DOOR to how the uncounted survive AND to the boy's cover-infrastructure. The pebble-bag = his tally of the uncounted dead. Sella now knows exactly what lever holds him.

dmlog.text: He thinks I'm the hand from up-town, and the fastest way to prove I'm not is to stop reaching for him and put something of my own in his hands instead. So I step back, not forward — I give him the water, unblock his only door, and let my own hands fall open and empty. "No. Look at me — look. If I were the Circle you'd already be struck; the Circle doesn't corner you in a wash-yard, it just stops writing your name and lets the dark do the rest. I know that because they did it to me tonight." I say it plain, no play in it. "My name's mud uptown as of dusk. There's a man in a good coat who decided I'm a number he'd rather not carry, and I ran down here to the only chains in this town where being no one is safe. So you and me are the same animal, friend, however little you want a stranger for a cousin." And I nod at the bag on his belt, the one his hand keeps pressing. "You keep a count. Twelve stones, each one scratched — twelve the town wouldn't count, so you count them. I'll not touch it. I only want you to know I saw it, and that where I come from that's called keeping faith, not madness." Then, soft, the real ask — and I keep the boy out of it entirely, because his name is mine to protect, not to spend: "I don't want your book. I want what it does. A woman the Circle's struck needs to learn how a name keeps breathing after they cross it out — how you people do it, the dead-man rooms, the trick of it. Not to use your dead. To save my own skin, and maybe one other's I'll not name. Show me that much and you'll have done a marked woman a mercy she won't forget — and mercies, down here, are the only coin that ever comes back." And I let him choose, and I read whether the truth landed or whether I've a bolt to catch.

You do the one thing his terror can't argue with: you give him back his door. You step off, unblock the black water, let your hands fall open and empty, and you say the true thing plainly — no play in it — that the Circle doesn't corner a man in a wash-yard, it just stops writing his name, and you know because they did it to you tonight. That your name's mud uptown as of dusk, a man in a good coat who decided you're a number he'd rather not carry, and you ran down here to the same low chains he did, for the same reason.

You watch it work, because truth works on a frightened man the way nothing else does — it doesn't calm him, exactly, but it re-aims him. The wild thing in his eyes stops looking at the river and starts looking at you, at the possibility, terrible and new, that the shape in the dark is not the hand come to strike him but another struck thing hiding in the same shadow. His breath comes ragged and stays. He does not jump.

And when you nod at the bag on his belt — twelve stones, each scratched, twelve the town wouldn't count so he counts them, and you'll not touch it, you only saw it, and where you come from that's keeping faith not madness — something in his face breaks that isn't fear. His hand closes over the bag, and his eyes are wet, and he says, hoarse: "Nobody's — nobody up there's ever once called it faith."

So the ground is yours to ask from. And you make the ask small and honest and you keep the boy out of it entirely: not his book, but what the book does — the trick of how a struck name keeps breathing, the dead-man rooms, so a marked woman can save her own skin and maybe one other's she'll not name.

He goes quiet. And you understand the size of what you've asked, because it moves across his face like weather: this is not his to give. The dead-man rooms are the only thing standing between the uncounted and the dark, and a man does not hand a stranger the key to the whole quarter's survival because she said a good word over his pebbles — however much he wants to, and you can see that he wants to, wants a cousin in the shadow so badly it hurts him. He weighs you. A frightened man deciding whether the first person to call his grief faith is worth the only secret his people have. You hold still and let him find his answer.

dm.sellaDisclosed: T4-set3: To prove she's not Circle, Sella DISCLOSED to Frederick that the Circle struck HER tonight — 'a man in a good coat' marked her a number he'd rather not carry. He now holds that leverage over her (a marked woman's secret). She honored his pebble-tally as 'keeping faith,' which cracked him open. She asked — keeping the boy OUT of it — to be taught the dead-man-room trick (how a struck name keeps breathing) for herself 'and one other I'll not name.'

dmlog.dmNotes: T4 set3. Defuse resolved free (she gives him his door + names his fear + honors the tally). Uncertain gate = the ASK (learn the survival-machinery), Persuasion DC 15, ADVANTAGE for the give-first/self-leverage gambit. Pre-roll persist: she disclosed her Circle-mark regardless of outcome (durable leverage he now holds). Success = the dead-man-room system (grounds the boy's cover-infrastructure + gives Sella an escape hatch). Fail has teeth (spent a real secret for nothing; another man knows she's marked). Boy kept out of it per player's cautious framing. STOP at threshold.

dmlog.text: The truth kept him out of the river, but it isn't enough to buy the thing you asked for, and you feel the trade go wrong the moment his face closes. You gave him a real secret — that the Circle struck you — to earn one back, and he takes yours and keeps his, not from malice but from a terror older and heavier than tonight's: the certainty, bred into every uncounted soul in this quarter, that the day you trust the wrong stranger is the day the whole shadow-network drowns. "You're struck, maybe," he says, backing toward the lane, hands still open, apologetic and immovable. "Or maybe that's exactly what they'd send you down here saying. I'm sorry, cousin. I am. But I'll not be the man who let the hand in." And he's gone, quick and quiet, not shouting this time — he believes you enough not to raise the alarm, which is the one mercy in it — but he's gone with your secret in his pocket and none of his in yours, and you've spent a real card and a night's sleep to end exactly where you started, except that now one more frightened man in this town knows the Circle wants you gone.

dm.refusedButSilent: T4-set3 FAIL: Frederick believed Sella enough NOT to jump and NOT to raise an alarm, but would NOT trust her with the dead-man-room machinery — 'the day you trust the wrong stranger is the day the whole network drowns; maybe that's exactly what they'd send you down here saying.' He left quiet, holding her disclosed Circle-mark, giving nothing back. Net: Sella spent a real secret (she's Circle-struck) for nothing; one more man knows the Circle wants her gone. No alliance.

dmlog.text: Frederick left quiet, but a man who just refused me is a man who might talk himself into fear by morning, and he knows the corner I took. So I don't sleep where I started. I drift deeper into the warren and find a new nothing-place to fold myself into — a gap behind a stack of flood-boards, wall at my back, one eye on the lane — and I make myself smaller than the marked woman the whole town's looking for. And as I lie down to steal what sleep I can before my last day comes, I finally see the thing the Maw's been telling me sideways since I crossed the night-chains: everyone in the warren sleeps the same way. Every bedroll, every huddled shape, every child — all of them turned to face one direction, backs set square against the crater's colored glow, the way the oil-dippers never face the Throat, the way the whole town crosses itself east over the heart. A mother reaches out in her sleep and turns a boy who's rolled the wrong way, without waking, the way you'd right a thing that must not be left wrong. I don't know why it matters. But I've learned this town punishes the ones who don't know its rules, and Maddan told me the well is owed, not given, and you keep your face from it so the crater never sees you take. So I do as the uncounted do — I turn my back on the glass, put my face to the east with the rest of them, and let their custom be my camouflage and their god's blind spot my roof. And then, for the first time since dusk, I close my eyes and let go, and I see whatever a marked woman sees when she finally sleeps facing the way the drowned all face.

You fold yourself into the gap behind the flood-boards, and you do the wise thing and the humble thing at once: you turn your back on the glass. Face to the east, like the mother and her righted boy, like every drowned-looking shape in the warren, backs set square against the crater's slow colored breathing. It costs you nothing and it might be everything, and either way it is the best camouflage in the Maw — a woman lying the way the uncounted lie is just one more of the uncounted.

And because you lie the right way, the dream lets you in.

You understand, the moment it takes you, that it is not your dream. It is the warren's dream, the one they all face east to be allowed to have and not the other one — the shared water they lie down into together the way people in a flood climb onto the same roof. You are in the crater. Not above it on the swaying chains but down in the colored glass, and the glass is colored because it is full — full of faces, thousands, pressed into the fused glaze like flowers in ice, and every last one of them is turned east. Turned away. Because the ones who face the crater get called, and the ones who get called go down into the glaze and become the color, and you know this in the dream the way you know your own name: the well doesn't take oil. Oil is the tithe you pay so it doesn't take you. You keep your face to the east so the thing at the bottom of the Maw never catches your eye and decides it would like your face in its window. The Sunns knew the counting of it. Someone stopped paying it right. And far off in the shared dark you feel the others dreaming alongside you — a warren of turned backs, a boy somewhere dreaming the same drowned glass — and one cold place in the water where a face is not turned away, is looking up, is looking, patiently, for whoever's new.

You wake with the dawn in your teeth and your heart going hard, Day 3, your last day, and the taste of colored glass at the back of your throat. You are rested. You are also, for the first time, properly afraid of the hole this whole town hangs over — not the Circle's grip on it, the thing itself. Below you the river is louder than it was. The flood is still climbing. And a full day's debt to a patient man comes due before this one ends.

dm.sharedSleepWhy: T5-set3 DREAM-DRIP (Sella's shared-dream sense while sleeping east-faced in the Refugee Quarter — interpretive, not hard canon yet): the east-facing / Shared-Sleep taboo exists because the crater CALLS. Faces of the taken are fused into the colored glass, all turned east. The well 'doesn't take oil — oil is the tithe you pay so it doesn't take YOU.' You keep your face east so the thing at the bottom never catches your eye and adds your face to its window. The Sunns knew the correct counting of the tithe; 'someone stopped paying it right' (ties to Wemric/Maddan's failed penance + the well-war). In the shared dream: a boy dreaming the same glass (Batgal, a Sunn), and one un-turned face in the water 'looking, patiently, for whoever's new' — an omen aimed at Sella. Deep 'why' of the crater dripped one notch; still not fully canon.

dmlog.dmNotes: T5 set3. She conformed to the Shared Sleep taboo -> the dream goes RIGHT (no roll; no failure state). Long rest fired (rest event). Used the shared-dream to drip the crater's deep 'why' (the taboo set-01 flagged undripped) as honest supernatural imagery, grounded in Maddan's T6 'the well is owed, keep your face east' + the Sunn well-rite -- persisted as an interpretive dm note (NOT fact_canonized; it's a dream-sense, not proven). Route-around: advance to Day 3 dawn. Flood still climbing (external front) kept live in the wake. No dmOnly faction-noun leaked.

dmlog.text:
I wake the way a hunted thing wakes — all at once and without moving, eyes open before the rest of me is allowed to. Dawn, grey and wet, my last day already leaking in under the flood-boards. And something is wrong. I know it before I know what it is, the way you know a card's been switched: the warren's hush has the wrong texture. Not the hush of sleepers — the hush of people pretending very hard to still be asleep. Somewhere close, bodies have gone still that shouldn't be still yet, and the ordinary dawn-noise of a camp waking has a hole cut in it, a moving hole, the shape a predator makes in a herd that's decided its best odds are to be furniture. There's a wolf in the fold. It slipped the sentry in the dark and it's in here with us now.
So I do not sit up. I do not run — running at dawn in a strange warren is how the furniture gets noticed. I stay exactly the low nothing I went to sleep as, one more turned-away back among hundreds, and I use the only edge I've got: I'm awake and it doesn't know it. From flat on the boards, cheek to the wet wood, I read the warren through the forest of bedrolls and washing-lines and stacked flood-boards — where's the hole moving, how fast, with what patience. Is it one shape or more. Does it move like Circle — unhurried, entitled, a man who's never been made to leave anywhere — or like Strap, or like something with no coat at all. And above everything: is it quartering the warren at random, culling the rolls the way Susannah says they do — or is it cutting a straight line, and is that line bending toward the gap behind the flood-boards where a marked woman thought she'd hidden. I keep my breathing a sleeper's breathing and I gather every scrap the grey light gives me before I so much as twitch, because whatever I do next, I only get to do it once, and I'd best know what I'm doing it to.

You read the warren from flat on the boards, cheek to the wet wood, and the grey light gives it up to you a piece at a time. The moving hole has a shape, and the shape has a good coat. Circle. One man, unhurried, entitled, walking the sleeping rows the way a man walks his own orchard — and a half-step behind him a second, smaller shape with no coat worth robbing, carrying a board and a stub of chalk. Not a knife. A clerk. And that is somehow worse, because you understand in one cold rush what a Circle man does in the Refugee Quarter at dawn with a clerk and a chalk and a flood climbing the low chains: he is taking the count. Going roll by roll, row by row, deciding in a stub of chalk who is on the list for the high ground when the water comes and who is a number the town would rather the river carried off. Susannah's whole grief, made flesh and given a ledger. He strikes a name and moves on, and the struck don't wake, because the struck have learned that waking is how you get noticed being struck.

He is quartering the warren clean and slow, and he has not looked at your row yet. But he will. The line of his counting bends this way like water finding the low place, and when it reaches the gap behind the flood-boards it will find a face he has very good reason to know on sight — the Seam, marked at dusk, bedded down among exactly the uncounted a patient man would read a great deal into. Your decoy told his master you slept behind a wall that isn't yours. This man will tell him you slept in a grave. You cannot un-be here. You can only not-be-seen being here — stay the furniture you went to sleep as while a professional's eye rakes your row in the dawn — and read the rest of him while you do it, or twitch wrong and hand the Circle the one thing your whole bad day was spent denying it: your address.

The chalk scratches. He steps to the next row. He is four rows out.

dm.dawnCount: T6-set3 (engine rest-risk 'threat slipped past the sentry' honored): a Circle enforcer + a clerk with chalk are taking the DAWN FLOOD-COUNT through the warren — striking names off the high-ground/evacuation roll as the flood climbs, deciding who the river is allowed to carry off. Converges internal front (Circle grip) + external front (flood) + the quarter's erasure grievance. NOT hunting Sella specifically, but his counting-line bends toward her row; if he clocks the marked Seam bedded among the uncounted, her dusk-decoy (false bed-location fed to Corran's tail) UNRAVELS and Corran learns where she really hides.

dmlog.dmNotes: T6 set3. Honors the engine's WILD rest-risk (threat inside on waking) as a Circle dawn flood-count -> converges internal+external fronts + the erasure grievance. Gate = Stealth (stay furniture while a pro rakes her row), DC 15. Success = unseen + reads that Susannah is marked-to-drown (raises stakes/moral hook). Fail = exposed on her last day, decoy unraveled, internal front ticks. STOP at threshold (counter four rows out).

dmlog.text:
You become wood. Not a held breath — a held breath is a thing a watching eye can catch — but the true slack of the genuinely asleep, learned off a hundred marks, your face gone stupid and heavy, one hand curled open and empty the way no one poses it. His eye rakes your row and finds nothing worth a chalk-mark: another uncounted lump, no coat, no coin, no name he needs. The chalk does not scratch for you. He steps past, and past, and the danger drains out of the row behind him like a tide going out.

And because you never moved, you got to watch — and you read the whole grim engine of him. He isn't reading faces; he's reading the roll in the clerk's hand and striking anyone the roll can't vouch for, which means the count isn't about who you are, it's about whose name is written down safe and whose isn't. The uncounted are being struck because they were already unwritten. And you clock the two names his chalk lingered on longest before it fell: a lane down toward the water where the flood-boards are already dark with wet — and Susannah Holloway's row, because a woman who speaks for the uncounted is exactly the sort of name a patient Circle would like the river to solve. You have his purpose, his method, and the two people his dawn just quietly sentenced, and he never knew a marked woman lay four feet off his boot reading him like a hand of cards.

dm.countRead: T6-set3 SUCCESS (Stealth): Sella stayed unseen and READ the Circle counter fully. He strikes by the ROLL (whose name is written safe), not by face — the uncounted get struck because they were already unwritten; it's erasure-by-flood. His chalk lingered longest on (a) a low lane by the water already going wet, and (b) SUSANNAH HOLLOWAY's row — the Circle would like the river to solve the woman who speaks for the uncounted. Sella is UN-clocked; decoy intact. She now knows Susannah is marked to drown.

dm.markedToDrown: T6-set3: The Circle's dawn flood-count struck Susannah's name off the high-ground/evac roll — a patient way to let the rising river 'solve' the voice of the uncounted. She does not know. Sella does.

dmlog.text: The chalk struck Susannah's row. I lay four feet off that man's boot and watched him sentence the one woman down here who took my coppers and told me the truth, and I'll not spend my last morning pretending I didn't see it. Words failed me at the wash-yard — Frederick took my secret and gave me nothing — so I don't bring words this time. I bring what I witnessed, which is the one currency the uncounted can't refuse: a warning with a date on it. I wait out the counter, let the good coat and his clerk climb back up to the high chains, and I let the warren start to breathe again. Then I go find Frederick first — he's the network, and he's the man I owe a better second meeting — and I don't ask him for anything. I hand him a thing. "You were right not to trust me last night. So don't. Trust this instead, and check it yourself: a Circle man walked your rows at first light with a clerk and a chalk, and he struck names off the flood-roll — the list that says who gets the high ground when the river comes. He struck the wet lane by the water. And he struck Susannah Holloway, because a woman who speaks for you is a name the Circle would rather the river solved. I'm not asking you to believe me because I'm your cousin. I'm telling you to go count your own dead before they're dead, and move the ones the chalk crossed out — Susannah first — to high ground the Circle doesn't hold, tonight, before the water does the Circle's striking for it. That's not a secret I want from you. That's a secret I'm giving you. Do what you want with the woman who brought it." And then I go to Susannah myself if she'll hear me, and I tell her plain to her face that her name came off the list, and that the flood is the blade now, and I read them both — is the marked stranger finally worth believing when she comes bearing a warning instead of a want.

You wait out the good coat. He and his clerk climb back up toward the high chains with their chalk and their ledger of who the river's allowed to keep, and slowly, the way a held breath lets go, the warren remembers how to make morning-noise. Then you go to Frederick, and you do the thing you didn't do last night: you bring nothing to take and everything to give.

He goes stiff when he sees you — a man braced to refuse a stranger twice. And then you don't ask. You hand him the count instead, flat and dated and checkable: the Circle man, the chalk, the flood-roll, the wet lane, and Susannah's name struck off because a woman who speaks for the uncounted is a name the Circle would rather the river solved. You tell him to go count his own dead before they're dead. You tell him it's not a secret you want — it's one you're giving. And you watch a thing happen in Frederick Brackett's face that words could never have bought: the marked stranger who cornered him in the dark has come back at first light not for the network but to save it, and asked him for nothing at all.

"You lay in that row," he says slowly, working it out. "You lay right there and watched him do it." He doesn't finish. He doesn't have to. He goes — quick, quiet, the way he does everything — and comes back grey, because he checked, and it's true, every mark of it. And when he comes back he is not the same man. "Cousin," he says, and this time the word has weight in it, a debt acknowledged. "What I wouldn't open last night. Come to me after and I'll open it. You're in the rooms if you want them." The thing your secret couldn't buy, your deed just earned.

But Susannah is the harder door, and not the way you feared. She hears you out at her cold fire, this broad tired woman, and she does not disbelieve you for a heartbeat — she's known the shape of this her whole life, she only never had the date. And then she does the thing that makes her who she is and makes your morning worse: she will not run. "Off the list, am I." A grim little nod, like a bill come due. "Then I'm off it with the rest of the off-list, girl, and I'll not climb to dry ground over the heads of my own so the Circle can drown them quieter without me shouting about it." She pokes the dead coals. "You want to save Susannah Holloway, you'll have to save her row. All of it. The whole struck lot of us." She looks up at you, and there is something almost kind in it, and entirely merciless. "That's the price of the warning you brought. You went and made it yours."

payload.cause: came back at dawn to save the network instead of use it — a true warning given freely, asking nothing; the deed earned the trust the words couldn't
brought a dated, checkable warning that the Circle struck her name off the flood-roll

dm.wontRunAlone: T7-set3: Told her name was struck off the flood-roll, Susannah REFUSED to save only herself — 'I'll not climb to dry ground over the heads of my own.' DEED reverses the T4 Persuasion failure: Frederick flips (attitude->Friendly) and OPENS the network — the machinery she failed to buy, now earned by action-over-words. dmlog.text:
Save the row. I can't fight the Circle and I can't hold back a river, so I do the only thing a con artist can: I find the person who already wants what I want and I make it his idea. And there's exactly one power in this Maw whose whole reason to breathe is the drowned and the crossed-out — the man who's spent thirty years paying a dead house's tithe. Maddan. So I don't go to Corran with the second name he's owed, not yet. I spend my morning buying the row a chance instead.
I signal Iron-Strap the way I signaled them for the boy — I trail my fingers wrong through the twine at Ospra's corner, a knot that says PARLEY, URGENT, THE SEAM, and I let their own watchers walk me in, because a woman who arrives on Ospra's leash is a woman the Reach won't knife on sight. And when I'm across the nets from the old netmender I don't dress it. "Maddan. Your Circle is going to drown the uncounted and call it weather. I watched it this dawn — a good coat and a clerk striking names off the flood-roll, deciding who gets the high ground when the water comes. Susannah Holloway. A whole row of the crossed-out. They're not knifing them; they're just not counting them, and letting the river do the striking, same as they did your Sunns. Here's what I bring you: the Refugee Quarter's own dead-man network is open to me now, twenty-some rooms and the people who run them, and every one of those uncounted souls is a heart the Circle has already thrown away. You want to restore a drowned house? Start with the one that's drowning tonight. Move the struck row to high ground the Circle doesn't hold — your people and mine, the network's rooms and the Strap's muscle — and you don't just save them, you show every uncounted wretch in this town who counts them when the Circle won't. That's not charity, netmender. That's how a buried house digs itself back up: one saved row at a time, until the drowned are yours and the Circle's counting a town that's stopped believing in its ledger." And I let the man who needs a successor see exactly what kind of successor I could be — and I read whether he takes the cause, or tells me why a careful old traitor can't.

You leave the wrong knot at Ospra's corner — PARLEY, URGENT, THE SEAM — and the Reach answers the way it answered before, a tannery-hand's careless slip that is nothing careless at all, and you let Iron-Strap's own watchers walk you in, because a woman on Ospra's leash is a woman the lye-yards won't open in the dark. Maddan is where he always is, small and spare among the drying nets, needle going over and under, the river breathing brown behind him. He lets you cross the whole yard before he looks up.

You don't dress it. You lay the dawn on the nets in front of him — the good coat, the clerk, the chalk, the flood-roll, Susannah's struck name, a whole row of the crossed-out left for the river to strike so no Circle hand has to. Same as they did his Sunns, you say, and you watch the word land in the old man like a hook set in something that never stopped bleeding. And then you spend the thing you came to spend — not the secret you hold over him, that stays in your sleeve where it's warm — but the cause: the network's open to you now, twenty-some rooms and the hands that run them, every one an uncounted soul the Circle already threw away. You want to restore a drowned house, netmender? Start with the one drowning tonight. Move the struck row. Your muscle, the network's rooms. Save them and show every uncounted wretch in the Maw who counts them when the Circle won't — because that's how a buried house digs itself up, one saved row at a time, until the drowned are his and the Circle's counting a town that's stopped believing in its ledger.

And you let him see it — what kind of successor the woman across the nets could be.

The needle has stopped. That's the first thing. Maddan Strole sits very still, and you have never seen the careful old man's face do quite this, because you have handed him, whole and gift-wrapped, the exact shape of the thing thirty years of patient tithing has been a substitute for — not a debt paid in the dark, but the drowned pulled up into the light and made to belong to him. He wants it the way a starving man wants bread. And that is precisely why he is afraid of it, and you can see the fear working against the wanting: a man who has kept a boy-king alive for a decade by never once being seen to move does not openly move a hundred souls against the Circle in a single night without betting everything he has hidden — the boy included — on one roll of a flooding river. He looks at the nets. He looks at you. He is an old traitor deciding whether the successor who just walked in is the redemption he's prayed for or the recklessness that finally drowns his whole long penance. "You clever, dangerous girl," he says softly, and it is not yet a yes and not yet a no. "You've no idea what you're asking me to spend." He waits, and the river waits, and it is your word that tips him.

dm.rescuePitch: T8-set3: Sella signaled Iron-Strap (PARLEY/URGENT knot at Ospra's corner), reached Maddan at the Reach, and pitched the RESCUE-ALLIANCE: the Circle is drowning the uncounted by chalk (dawn flood-count, Susannah + a whole struck row off the high-ground roll) — 'same as they did his Sunns.' She offered the now-open dead-man-room network (~20 rooms) + framed saving the struck row as how a buried house digs itself up (win the uncounted's loyalty from the Circle). Played hard to his successor-hunger. She did NOT spend her traitor-secret ace (still unspent). Maddan is torn: wants it desperately, but openly moving Iron-Strap risks everything he's hidden (the boy included). On the knife-edge.

dmlog.dmNotes: T8 set3. Node moved to the Reach (route-around, travel). Pitch to Maddan (Friendly ally) = his life's cause but a huge risky ask of a careful man. Persuasion DC 15, ADV (aligned + successor-bait). Pre-roll persists the pitch + that she did NOT spend the traitor-ace. Branches SCALE commitment (full quiet-rescue / partial tools-only / three-rooms) rather than ally-refuses-flatly — hard-and-dangerous via degree, not betrayal. Success ticks the Iron-Strap power clock (faction advances 'restore the drowned' agenda) + escalates the well-war. STOP at threshold ('it is your word that tips him').

dmlog.text: "...God help me," he says, and sets the needle down for good, and the setting-down is a decision thirty years in the coming. "Alright. But we do it as I've kept a boy alive, girl — in the dark, where the Circle can't be seen to lose, or it isn't a rescue, it's a funeral with witnesses." And then, faster than you'd credit an old man, the plan is his and it is better than yours: not a march to high ground the Circle would simply meet, but the network's own trick turned to flood-work — the struck row moved room by room into the dead-man lodgings above the waterline, names the Circle already thinks it killed climbing into the graves it dug and pulling the lids shut while the river rises under the counted's feet instead. Boats from the Strap's quiet fleet. Ospra to run the routes. His own oldest hands on the muscle. "They'll strike a row and find it empty in the morning," he says, and there is something terrible and young in his old face, "and no name to blame it on, because they're all dead men already, aren't they. On the books." He looks at you a long moment. "You've done a thing today, Seam. You've shown an old man his war has a front he forgot he was allowed to fight. Whatever you are — successor, or the cleverest liar who ever walked onto my nets — you're mine now, and I'm yours, and the drowned are both of ours." The rescue is on. And so is the well-war, hotter than it has ever been, because the Circle is about to lose a hundred souls it counted as already dead.

dm.committedRescue: T8-set3 SUCCESS: Maddan COMMITTED Iron-Strap to the rescue — but reshaped it his way (quiet, not open defiance): the struck row moved room-by-room into the dead-man lodgings above the waterline (the network's own trick turned to flood-work), Strap boats + Ospra running routes + his oldest hands on muscle. 'They'll strike a row and find it empty, and no name to blame.' Named Sella his own ('successor, or the cleverest liar' — 'you're mine now, I'm yours, the drowned are both of ours'). Escalates the well-war: the Circle is about to lose ~100 souls it counted dead.

dmlog.text: The rescue's set for dusk, and now there's exactly one thing left that can drown it: Corran Vale, who owns my leash and my last day both. I learned my lesson at the Tree — I cannot out-lie a man who's spent twenty years reading liars, and I'll not try. So this time I bring him no lie at all. I bring him the truth, sharpened into a knife, and I make the meeting mine instead of his. I surface to Fenn — the good coat who's carried me since the night-chains — and I don't skulk; I ask, plainly, for an hour of Corran's morning on open ground of my choosing, a busy deck where a patient man can't do anything quiet. And when Corran comes, I don't kneel and I don't explain. I lead with the thing he doesn't know I have. "I'll not waste your morning, so here's the trade, clean: your good coat walked the Refugee Quarter at first light with a clerk and a chalk, and struck names off the flood-roll — deciding who the river's allowed to keep. I watched him do it. I can name the lane and the woman and the hour, and I'm the sort who's already written it down twice and left it with strangers who don't love the Circle. Now — you're a patient man, so be patient with the arithmetic. A guild that quietly lets a quarter drown is a guild. A guild that gets caught doing it, when the water's this high and the whole Maw's watching its own cellars fill, is a guild that just handed every rival and every outside eye the one story that ends with the Circle's grip pried off this town for good. That's not a threat, Corran. I don't make threats to men who can out-wait me. That's me showing you the same courtesy you showed me at the Tree — the arithmetic, laid plain, so you can do the sum yourself." Then the ask, small and survivable: "So pull the count back. Let the low chains keep their places on the roll tonight. And take your string off my ankle — call me struck, call me dead, forget the name Voss entirely, and I forget a chalk-mark at dawn and take my written pages to my grave. You lose one wet morning's cruelty and one loose end you were only ever going to have to kill. I lose a name I'm sick of anyway. Everybody keeps their town." And I hold his eyes, and I keep the netmender's secret buried deep in my chest where it belongs, and I read whether the coldest man in the Maw takes the clean exit I've built him — or decides a woman who can do that sum out loud is one he can't afford to let breathe.

You do not skulk. You surface to Fenn on the swaying spans like a woman with business, and you ask — plainly, in the open, where asking can't be mistaken for scheming — for an hour of Corran's morning on ground of your choosing. Fenn takes the request the way he takes everything, at exact change, and something moves behind his flat courteous eyes that might, in a warmer man, have been respect for a mouse that walks up and knocks. "He'll come," Fenn says. "He always comes when it's interesting. Pray it's interesting."

You pick the busiest deck in Coalstack Row, the market at full mid-morning boil, a hundred witnesses and no quiet corner, because a patient man does his worst work in quiet and you mean to allow him none. Corran Vale comes unhurried through the press, and the press parts for him without knowing why, and he stops an arm's length off with the sliver of ironwood already turning in his fingers. "Voss," he says, mild as milk. "You look rested, for a loose end."

And you do not kneel and you do not explain. You lay the knife on the table truth-first, the way you learned at the Tree not to lay a lie: the good coat, the clerk, the chalk, the flood-roll struck at dawn — you watched it, you can name the lane and the woman and the hour, and you're the sort who's already written it down twice and left it with strangers who don't love the Circle. And then you give him the arithmetic, not the threat — that a guild that quietly drowns a quarter is a guild, but a guild caught doing it, with the water this high and the whole Maw watching its own cellars fill, has handed every rival and every outside eye the one story that pries the Circle's grip off this town for good. You offer the clean exit: pull the count, leave the low chains their places tonight, take the string off your ankle — call Voss struck, dead, forgotten — and you take your written pages to your grave.

Corran listens the way he listened at the Tree — all the way down, not one interruption. When you finish, the wood stops turning. And you cannot yet tell, watching that still cold pond of a face, whether it has stopped because he's arrived at the clean exit you built him — or because a man who spent twenty years reading liars has just found, somewhere in your true and reasonable arithmetic, the one seam where the truth thins into a bluff, and is deciding that a woman who can hold the Circle's own throat and do the sum out loud in a crowded market is precisely the loose end a patient man cannot ever afford to let breathe. He looks at you for a long, long moment. "That's a great deal of sum," he says softly, "for a woman who left her pages with strangers." And he lets that hang, and he waits, and it is the next thing in your face that tips him.

dm.marketDeal: T9-set3: Sella surfaced via Fenn, requested an OPEN-GROUND meeting (busy Coalstack Row market, no quiet corner — denying Corran his patient quiet). She led with TRUTH not a lie (her Tree lesson): the dawn flood-count/erasure, a claimed dead-man's-switch ('written twice, left with strangers'), and the strategic arithmetic — a guild CAUGHT drowning a quarter, water this high, hands rivals/outside eyes the story that pries the Circle off the town. Ask: pull the count, free her (call Voss dead), and she buries it. Ace (Maddan=traitor) kept unspent. Corran probed the SEAM: 'a great deal of sum for a woman who left her pages with strangers' — testing whether the dead-man's-switch is real (it's a bluff; she has no pages).

dmlog.dmNotes: T9 set3 CLIMAX. Node moved to Coalstack Row (open ground she chose). Corran = hardest target. Persuasion DC 17, ADV (true-ground per her Tree lesson + sound logic + chosen crowd). The SEAM = the dead-man's-switch is a bluff (her one untruth in a true play); a 20-yr reader probes exactly there. Branches: success (deal taken, count pulled, leash cut, Voss becomes a dead name); nearMiss (bluff caught but sum survives -> count pulled, leash held); fail (bluff called -> count NOT pulled, leash held, she's now his top target, crowd is why she lives). Ace stays unspent. STOP at threshold ('it is the next thing in your face that tips him').

dmlog.text: He finds the seam, and this time the seam is the whole game, because a bluff laid in front of Corran Vale is a lie by another name and you swore you'd not bring him a lie. "No," he says, gently, almost sorrowful, the way he told you the carrier was a woman. "You didn't write it down twice. You didn't leave it with anyone. You're a woman alone with a true thing and no way to make it loud, standing in a crowd hoping the crowd is your knife." The wood turns, once. "And that's a shame, Voss, because the true thing was good — it really would have been a bad story for us, if it could ever have been told. But it can't, now, because the only mouth that can tell it is standing on a market deck having just informed the Ironwood Circle, to its face, that she is both able and willing." He does not raise a hand — not here, not in the boil of a hundred witnesses; that was your one true piece of armor and it's the only reason you walk off this deck. "Go home, dead woman," he says, and the dead woman is not the mercy it was a minute ago, it's a sentence with a date not yet written on it. "Enjoy your flood." The count is not pulled. Your leash is not cut. And a patient man now has one clean item left on his morning's list, and it is you.

dm.calledTheBluff: T9-set3 FAIL: Corran CAUGHT the dead-man's-switch bluff ('you didn't write it down, you're a woman alone with a true thing and no way to make it loud'). The true intel was real ('a bad story for us, if it could ever be told') but she has no way to make it loud — so he did NOT pull the count and did NOT release her; worse, she has told the Circle to its face she's able+willing to expose it, so she is now the one clean item on his list. Only the open-market crowd (her one true armor) let her walk off the deck alive. Danger SPIKED; rescue cover NOT protected by Corran.

dmlog.text:
So Corran keeps his leash and his loose end, and he's a patient man with one clean thing left on his list, and the thing is me. Fine. I gambled my freedom on a bluff a better man than me couldn't have sold, and I lost it clean. But losing taught me the last thing I needed: I can't talk my way off Corran's list. There's only one way off a patient man's list, and it's the one this whole quarter's been teaching me since the night-chains. You don't run from the striking. You let it land, and you climb into the grave it digs, and you pull the lid shut, and you live.
He wants Voss struck? I'll strike her myself, and do it cleaner than his chalk ever could. I go back down to the low chains, to Frederick, and I take the room he offered — not as an escape hatch to keep in my back pocket, but for real, tonight, before the water and the rescue turn the whole quarter to chaos I can disappear inside. "You said I was in the rooms if I wanted them. I want them. Put Sella Voss in a dead man's bed on the Saltwidow book and let her drown in the flood with everyone the Circle already killed. I'll pay her rent in coppers to a keeper who can't read, same as the rest of your dead, and I'll come up on the far side of tonight as whoever the room says I am." And then I don't hide from the rescue — I run it. This is my dusk now, not Corran's: the struck row moving room by room into the graves the Circle dug, the network's hands and the Strap's boats and Ospra on the routes, and me in the middle of it, no longer a marked woman with a name to lose but a dead one with nothing left to take — the safest thing in the Maw, exactly like Frederick said. I find Maddan's eye across the moving dark and I let him see his successor at her work, and I keep his oldest secret buried where it's kept me useful, and I spend the last hour of Sella Voss doing the one thing she turned out to be for: counting the uncounted, and carrying them up out of the water the Circle meant to drown them in. Let Corran find an empty leash and a name off the book by morning. Let him do the sum. I'll be a dead woman keeping faith in a drowned house, and I have never once in my life been anything I was less ashamed of.

You walk off the market deck a woman with one clean thing left on Corran Vale's list, and you carry that knowledge down the chains like a stone, all the long morning down to the low country, and somewhere on the way it stops being a stone and becomes a key. Because he told you what to do, at the Tree and again just now, and you were too busy fighting it to hear it: he wants Voss struck. So strike her. Do it cleaner than his chalk ever could.

Frederick doesn't ask why when you come to him and say you want the room for real. He's one of the erased; he knows the only door out of a book is a grave in it. "There's a bed on the Saltwidow register," he says, quiet, "belonged to a man named Corliss who's been dead nine years and paid up every month since. He won't mind the company." And that's it. That's the whole terrible mercy of the uncounted: a keeper who can't read, a corpse's coppers, and a name the town already believes is gone. Sella Voss checks into a dead man's room as the light goes long, and she does not check out, and the book still says she's home.

And then you do not hide. You run it.

The dusk turns the whole low quarter to moving water and moving dark, and into that cover the struck row goes — not up to high ground where the Circle could meet them, but sideways, into the graves the Circle dug, name by name climbing into rooms let to the dead while the river rises under the counted's feet. Frederick's hands. The Strap's quiet boats sliding the black leats. Ospra a shape at every turning, running the routes. And you in the middle of it, no longer a marked woman with a name to lose but a dead one with nothing left to take, which is, exactly as he promised, the safest thing in the Maw. You count them as they go. You are, it turns out, very good at counting the uncounted — a con artist's whole trade is knowing precisely who's really in a room — and you carry Susannah's whole struck row up out of the water one dead name at a time, and somewhere in the moving dark a nine-year-old who mends nets thinking he's an orphan sleeps dry in a grave of his own, one more Sunn the crater didn't get.

You find Maddan's eye once, across the black. The old traitor looks at his successor at her work — counting his drowned up into the light, keeping his oldest secret buried in her chest where it has kept her useful — and he doesn't smile, because men like Maddan don't, but something in him settles the way a debt settles. You're his now, and he's yours, and the drowned are both of yours.

By morning the Circle will strike a row and find it empty. They will pull the Saltwidow book to make their count and read a column of the long-dead, and among the dead, in a fresh clean hand, one Sella Voss, drowned in the flood, name off the ledger, nobody the town need carry. Corran will do the sum. He is a patient man, and the Maw is small, and a dead woman who keeps turning up alive is a sum he will one day sit down and work again. But not tonight. Tonight the water is loud and the graves are full of the living and you have never, in the whole grasping length of your life, been anything you were less ashamed of. Sella Voss is struck from the book of the Shimmering Maw. Something quieter and harder and cleaner than Sella Voss walks up out of the flood on the far side of the dark, keeping faith in a drowned house, and goes on.

payload.what: Sella Voss is struck from the town book of the Shimmering Maw — recorded 'drowned in the flood,' Day 3 — a self-engineered legal death: she took a dead man's room on the Saltwidow register (Corliss, dead nine years, rent paid in coppers to a keeper who can't read) and became one of the uncounted. On the books she is dead; she lives, uncounted and un-strikeable, as Maddan's successor within the Iron-Strap/Refugee-Quarter cause.

dm.roomedSella: T10-set3: Frederick put Sella into a real dead-man room on the Saltwidow register (the late 'Corliss'). She is now inside the network as a dead name — the escape she EARNED at T7, executed for real, not held in reserve.

dm.successorAtWork: T10-set3: The dusk rescue RAN — the struck row moved sideways into the dead-man rooms under flood-cover (network hands + Strap boats + Ospra on routes), Sella counting the uncounted up out of the water. Batgal (a Sunn) among the dry-saved. Maddan watched his successor at her work; the bond settled ('you're his, he's yours, the drowned are both of yours'). Sella keeps his traitor-secret buried, still UNSPENT. The Circle will strike a row at dawn and find it empty, no name to blame.

dm.emptyLeash: T10-set3: By morning Corran finds an empty leash and, on the Saltwidow book, 'Sella Voss, drowned in the flood, name off the ledger.' She struck herself cleaner than his chalk could — took the only door off a patient man's list (a grave in the book). He'll do the sum: 'a dead woman who keeps turning up alive is a sum he'll one day work again. The Maw is small.' Residual, patient threat — NOT resolved, deferred. He does NOT know she engineered it (yet).

dm.rowSaved: T10-set3: Susannah's whole struck row carried up out of the flood into the dead-man rooms under dusk cover — the Circle's flood-erasure defeated for this row/night by turning the uncounted's own hiding-machinery to rescue-work. The Circle will strike a row at dawn and find it empty, no name to blame (all 'dead men already, on the books').

dmlog.dmNotes: T10 set3 CLOSER. Resolution beat, no roll — Sella executes the disappearance she ASSEMBLED across the set (network earned T7, Iron-Strap allied T8), cost already paid (her identity). Reframes the T9 climax-FAIL as the thing that taught her the only real exit: strike herself off the book cleaner than Corran's chalk. fact_canonized = her engineered legal death (resolves to real text, legit XP). Ties every thread: erasure theme (her weapon now), flood (cover), network (earned), Maddan/successor (her new place), the boy (saved), Corran (outleft, not outfought — residual patient threat deferred). Ace stays unspent. Bittersweet, not triumphal. Advance to dusk = Day 3 closes.

dmlog.text: The rescue's clean while it's just carrying — but the river doesn't keep to a plan, and I can hear it under the boards outpacing us, coming up faster than Frederick's count allowed for. So I go where the work is worst instead of where it's safe: the lowest room on the row, the one the water reaches first, where whoever's slowest to move is going to be trapped when the black comes up through the floor. I take the lantern and go down into it — and if there's a soul in there too old or too frightened or too fast-drowning to climb into their dead man's grave on their own, I get my shoulder under them and I haul them up out of the rising water myself, coat and boots be damned. I've spent this whole town's worth of nights being careful. Tonight I spend my back.

I've spent this whole town's worth of nights being careful. Tonight I spend my back.

The lantern shows you the room the way a lantern shows you a grave: a little at a time, and none of it good. It is the last cell on the bottom of the row, boards sprung, and the flood is already in it — black and cold and climbing the walls in a slow tide-line you can watch move. On the cot, too far gone to climb, is an old man the quarter calls **Halder** who mended kettles for forty years and cannot feel his legs, and he is not frightened, which is worse; he has the flat calm of a man who has decided the water is a fair way to go and is only sorry to make you wet. "Leave it, girl," he says. "I'm already off the book. Save one that's got a walk left in 'em." The dead man's room he's meant for — Corliss's neighbor, a lodger nine years gone — is up a short ladder to the mezzanine that stays above the line, and it is nothing, three rungs, except that it is everything when the thing you're carrying is a hundred-odd pounds of man who cannot help you and the current is already at your knees and pulling for the door with the patience of the whole rising Maw behind it. You set the lantern on the highest shelf where it might live a minute longer, and you get your shoulder into Halder's ribs, and you take his weight, and the black water takes yours.
dmlog.dmNotes: First real physical/danger beat of Sella's campaign — telegraphed lethal hazard (visible rising water), Athletics haul. Fail lands honestly (first blood + flood front ticks + lantern lost) and the saved NPC survives via the established network, not by softening her roll.

dmlog.text: (I roll Athletics: 4)

You get your shoulder in and you lift, and for one heartbeat you think strength will be enough — and it is exactly the wrong heartbeat to think it, because that is when the current finds the open door behind you and the whole room becomes a throat and swallows. Your boots go out. Halder's weight, that you were carrying, is carrying you now, down into the black and along the wall — and your reaching hand closes on the ladder frame and the ladder frame, sprung already, tears loose in your fist, so there is nothing to stop you and the cold takes you all the way under with a crack of your shoulder against the sunk cot that you will feel for a week. The lantern goes off its shelf into the water and the last of your light drowns. You are under, in the dark, in a dead man's flooding room, with a paralytic's collar still fisted in one hand because you will not — it turns out, at the very bottom of yourself — let go. And it is not your strength that saves it. Two more pairs of hands come down the flooding row looking for exactly this: Frederick, and a Strap boatman with arms like moorings, hauling you both up by main force onto the mezzanine's dry boards while the river takes the room entire behind you. You lie there gutted, half-drowned, one shoulder screaming, having failed the single thing you went down there to do alone — and alive, and Halder alive beside you, only because you spent this whole town building the hands that just caught you. "Told you," the old man coughs, "to leave me." Below, in the dark you can no longer light, the water is winning faster than any count of Frederick's allowed for. The Maw is filling, and you have just learned the exact weight of a thing you cannot carry alone.

payload.note: Hooded Lantern lost to the floodwater

dm.floodRescueLowRoom: T-set05: NAT-1 fumble — Sella's solo haul of Halder failed catastrophically; the current took her under, the ladder frame tore loose, her shoulder cracked on the sunk cot, the lantern drowned. Saved only because Frederick + a Strap boatman came looking. The flood took the low room and is now outpacing the rescue's count (external front 2/6 -> 3/6).

dmlog.dmNotes: Live crit-magnitude resolution of the nat-1 fumble (total 4 vs DC 14, magnitude 11). Full-failure spike: -5 HP (first blood of her whole campaign), lantern lost, flood front ticks 2->3, saved via the established network not by softening the roll. The lesson lands: the one thing she can't do is the thing she does alone.

dmlog.text: Lesson learned, and paid for in the only currency I've got left tonight — blood and a shoulder that won't lift a kettle, let alone a man. So I stop trying to be the strongest thing in the room, because I never was, and I go back to being the smartest. I let Frederick's boatman have Halder and I don't touch another dying body with these arms. I climb instead — up to the driest, highest span I can find that still overlooks the whole flooding row, and I do two quick things. First I strap my own shoulder tight with a strip off my ruined coat and a splint of broken lath, gritting through it, because a woman running a rescue can't be a body being rescued. Then I do the thing I'm actually good at: I read the water and the dark the way I read a mark, looking for the one failure point that sinks all of this at once — the span that's about to give, the choke where the boats will jam, or worse, the good coat that's noticed a whole quarter of dead men suddenly getting out of bed. Find the thing that ends us, and I'll spend the rest of the night making sure it's the thing that doesn't happen.

You bind the shoulder the way you've bound worse — teeth set, a strip of ruined coat, a splint of broken lath cinched cruelly tight — and it does not stop hurting, it only stops moving, which is all you asked of it. It buys you nothing back but the ability to keep going, and you take that trade the way you take every bad trade tonight: because the alternative is worse. Then you climb, and from the high dry span the whole flooding row lays itself out below you like a cheat's-eye view of a card table, and because reading a room is the one thing in this world you have never once had to roll for, you read it clean. You see the two failures the water is going to give you: the **north footspan**, the old rope-and-plank crossing the whole east half of the row depends on, already knee-deep and groaning, one good surge from parting — and the **resin-gate choke** below it, where three lanes of dead-man rooms funnel to a single boat-slip and the Strap's little craft are already stacking up, a jam that will strand a dozen people on the wrong side of a rising river. Those you can plan around. Those are just water, and water is honest. What you cannot yet place is the third thing — the itch at the back of your professional neck that says the water is not the only patient thing working this quarter tonight. Somewhere down in the moving dark and the bobbing lantern-light, in all that chaos of the dead getting out of bed, your gut insists there is a shape that does not belong to the rescue and is not panicking the way drowning people panic. You go still on the high span and you spend one breath doing the thing you actually do — reading the crowd for the predator in it.

dm.floodFailPoints: T-set05 T2: Sella read the flooding row from the high span — two physical failure points: the NORTH FOOTSPAN (rope-plank crossing the east half depends on, near parting) and the RESIN-GATE CHOKE (three lanes funnel to one boat-slip, jamming). Both plannable. She also senses a third, human threat working the flood — unplaced.

dmlog.dmNotes: Granted the physical board-read as rogue competence (free, no roll) — the two water-failures are planted as plannable hooks. The roll is only the hard part: catching the human predator (the Circle clerk building a came-back-from-the-dead list) before it acts. Insight because she's reading intent in a crowd. No HP from the shoulder-bind (no healing skill/kit — she stays 4/9). Threat referred to by role, not minted, to avoid roster collision.

dmlog.text: There. You find it because it is the one wrong thing in a field of right ones: everyone down there moves like water — toward high ground, away from the cold, the honest animal scramble of the nearly-drowned. Everyone but one. A man in a good dry coat is moving *across* the current of the panic, unhurried, going room to room along the struck row — and he is not helping and he is not looting. He has a board and a stub of something pale, and at each dead-man door he stops and he *makes a mark*, and moves on. It is the dawn's clerk, or its twin, and he has understood exactly what you understood — that the struck row is climbing into the graves the Circle already dug — and he is standing in the middle of your rescue writing down which corpses have suddenly, impossibly, started breathing. He is building the Circle a list of every dead name that came back to life tonight, and yours, freshly inked as drowned-in-the-flood, will be on it by the time he reaches the Saltwidow register. He has not seen you on the high span. He has all the patience in the world, and he thinks he has all the time. You know exactly where he is, exactly what he's doing, and — for perhaps a hundred count — exactly how blind he is to you.

dm.floodClerk: T-set05 T2: Sella spotted the human threat — a Circle CLERK (the dawn-count's twin) moving room to room along the struck row in the flood, marking down which dead-man rooms have new occupants, i.e. building a list of every struck name that came back to life tonight. He has NOT seen Sella (on the high span). Sella's own new 'drowned' entry will be exposed when he reaches the Saltwidow register. He is unhurried, thinks he has all the time.

dmlog.text: A hundred count of a blind patient man, and a blade in the dark is the one argument I can still win with a bad shoulder. That board is a death-list with my new name coming up on it, and I'll not let it reach the Saltwidow register with breath behind it. So I go down off the high span the way water goes down — quiet, cold, and where nobody's looking — using the flood's own noise and every bobbing lantern for cover, coming around and behind him along the struck row until I'm close enough to smell the dry wool of that good coat. And then I take him. Left hand over his mouth, right hand bringing the dagger up under the coat to rest against his kidney where he can feel exactly what it is, and I put my lips to his ear: "The board. Slow. And every mark you made tonight, you're going to tell me who else has read it — because a clerk who can be replaced is worth more to me talking than the mess you'll be if you shout." I'd rather walk him into the dark and take the list breathing than leave a body for Corran to count. But if he opens his mouth to bring the Circle down on a quarter full of people I just dragged out of the river, the dagger finishes the sentence for him.

But if he opens his mouth to bring the Circle down on a quarter full of people I just dragged out of the river, the dagger finishes the sentence for him.

You go down off the span into the flood-dark and you become weather. The rescue is a hundred small noises and a hundred bobbing lights and you move through all of it the way a lie moves through a true story — belonging, unremarkable, there and then not. The clerk works with his back to the water and his front to the doors, which is a countinghouse habit and a fatal one, because it means the whole drowned world behind him is yours. You come up the struck row at his spine. Close enough to hear his stub of chalk tick against the board. Close enough to smell the dry wool that marks him as a man who has never once had to run. Your bad shoulder is a live coal and the boards under you are wet and sprung and every one of them is a decision. One creak and a patient man's arithmetic gets a very loud new number in it. You reach the last board between you and the small of his back, and you set your weight to cross it.
dmlog.dmNotes: Surprise ambush of a lone soft target — the uncertain part is closing unseen (Stealth, no prof, DC 13). Success hands off the kill/keep decision to the player (agency) after the NPC's terror-honest answer; she gains the tally-board (real loot/plot item). Fail opens genuine combat vs an enforcer at 4 HP — the honest, telegraphed (set-03 enforcer+clerk pairing) cost of a blown ambush, leaning into the fight per the set brief. No dmOnly leak; threat referred to by role/first-name, not codex-minted.

dmlog.text: The board holds its tongue.
