You cross it like it isn't there, and then the good coat's world ends without a sound: your left hand seals his mouth before his lungs know to use it and your right brings the dagger up under the wool to lie cold against the kidney, and you feel the exact instant a man who has never run understands, all at once, what running was for. He does not shout. His whole soft body goes to water in your hands. Against your palm his answer comes out in a wet terrified rush, muffled and honest the way only the truly frightened are honest — "nobody, nobody's read it, it goes to Vale at dawn, I'm the only one that's — I only count, I only count what I'm told—" and the board hangs slack in his grip, a plank scratched with a dozen fresh marks, every one a dead-man room the Circle now knows is occupied, the Saltwidow register not yet among them because he works the low row up. It is, for this one held breath, entirely yours: the list, the man, and the choice of what a dead woman does with a Circle clerk in the dark. He waits, shaking, for you to tell him whether he lives.

add.name: The Circle's flood-tally board
add.note: A plank scratched with a dozen fresh marks — every dead-man room the struck row reoccupied tonight. The Circle's list of who came back from the dead. Saltwidow register not yet on it.

dm.clerkTaken: T-set05 T3: Sella took the Circle flood-clerk from surprise (silent, unseen). Seized his tally-board (the came-back-from-dead list). He confessed: nobody else has read tonight's marks yet; the list goes to Corran Vale at dawn; he hadn't reached the Saltwidow register. He's a soft functionary, terrified, now Sella's prisoner-or-corpse (her open choice). The Circle will notice a clerk who vanished before dawn.

res.note: Sella Voss can't carry that much — over the 360 lb hard cap.

dmlog.text: "I only count what I'm told" — that's not a confession, friend, that's a job opening. I ease the blade off his kidney just enough that he can breathe and think in the same minute, but not enough that he forgets it's there. "Listen to me, because I'm about to be the only person in this town who ever offered you a door instead of a chalk-line. You said it yourself: you only count. Which means the day the Circle decides your count's gone soft, they strike YOUR name and hand your board to the next frightened man, and nobody down here weeps for a clerk. You're already on the list. You just haven't been told your number yet." I turn him, slow, so he can see the dark rows full of the people I dragged out of the river tonight — the whole drowned quarter of the erased. "But there's another way to be uncounted, and it's warmer than the Circle's. Here's the trade, and it's the only one you'll get: you go to Vale at dawn and you give him a true-looking board that says this row drowned clean — no dead men walking, no names come back, just water doing what water does. You write the lie that keeps a hundred people breathing, and in exchange the uncounted keep YOU breathing when the Circle finally comes to strike the clerk who's seen too much. Cross me and I'll know, because I'll be reading your count same as you read ours. So. Do you want to be the Circle's pen — or your own man, on our book, for the first time in your life?"

The clerk breathes where you let him, and you can feel the exact machinery of a small frightened man working behind the wool — a lifetime of being the hand that holds someone else's pen, and no one, not once, offering him the pen for himself. He does not answer fast. A man who counts does not do anything fast. His eyes go where you turn them, out over the dark drowned rows and the shapes of the people you hauled up into dead men's graves tonight, and something moves in his throat that might be the first honest arithmetic of his life: what the Circle is worth to him, measured against what it would do to him the day his count went soft. "You'd — " he starts, and stops, and the board trembles in his hands. "They don't let clerks leave. You know that. Nobody leaves the Circle, they just get — reassigned." He is not saying no. He is saying he is afraid, which is a different thing, and you have spent your whole life on the exact distance between the two. He waits, the pen of his whole life hanging between the fist that's held it and the door you've just shown him.
dmlog.dmNotes: Genuine social flip: leverage (blade + proven-lethal) + a TRUE offer (he's expendable; the uncounted's door) → Persuasion adv DC 13. Success mints Wend Ossle (explicit unique id, roster-clean) as a deep inside asset + exercises the FIXED attitude_shift path (target/int). NearMiss = fear-compliance (bought the night not the dawn). Fail = the Circle is the deeper fear (Frederick-echo), returns the kill/keep binary honestly. Fail carries NO social_check (refusal). No dmOnly leak.

dmlog.text: The door you showed him is not big enough for the fear you're up against. You see it lose to the older thing right in front of you — his face closing, not toward you but away, into the flat resignation of a man choosing the devil he's counted for over the stranger with the knife. "No," he whispers, and it's Frederick's word from the wash-yard all over again, the whole town's word: no, cousin, I'll not be the one they catch. "You can open me here in the dark and it's a kinder count than what they'd do to a clerk who wrote them false. I've seen what they do. You haven't. Not yet." And he means it — he would rather your blade than the Circle's patience, and that is the truest thing anyone's told you tonight. He will not write your lie. Which leaves you, at four points of blood on a flooding span, exactly where you were before you got clever: a Circle clerk who has seen the dead walking, who goes to Vale at dawn, and only one crude way left to stop him — the one you'd hoped not to use.

dm.clerkWontTurn: T-set05 T4: Sella's flip of the clerk FAILED — his terror of the Circle is deeper than the knife (Frederick-echo: 'a kinder count than what they'd do'). He won't write a false count. Sella is back to the hard binary at 4 HP: kill him, or let him carry the truth to Vale at dawn. UNRESOLVED.

dmlog.text: "I've seen what they do. You haven't." He thinks that's a wall between us. It's the only thing we have in common. I stand there one breath too long — long enough to feel the whole weight of it, because I've conned and cut and lied my way across three towns and a grave of my own tonight, but I have never once done this, and I want to be sure I know that I'm doing it. He won't turn. He won't be trusted. And his tidy little dawn-count puts a hundred people I just pulled out of the river back under it by noon. There's no clever left. There's just the arithmetic he taught me — one frightened clerk against a whole drowned quarter — and for once the count is simple. "You're right," I tell him, quiet, and I mean it as the kindest thing I've got. "I haven't. And I'd have spared you if you'd let me." Then I don't use the knife — a knife leaves a mark, and this town's already given me a mark that hides everything. I take him by that good dry collar and I put him into the black water off the span, and I hold him there with my whole ruined shoulder screaming, and I let the flood do to him the one honest thing it's done all night, until the struggling stops and the Maw has one more body it can blame on the weather. Then I let go, and I let the current take him down toward the glass with all the other drowned, and I climb back up onto the span a thing I wasn't an hour ago, and I go finish getting my people to their graves. The dead can't testify. That's rather the point of them.

He hears the change in your voice before he understands it — the particular gentleness that isn't mercy — and he starts to say something, your name maybe, or God's, but you have already decided and deciding was the hard part; the rest is only weight and water. You do not use the knife. A knife is a signature and you have spent all night learning that the flood signs nothing. You take him by that good dry collar, the one that marked him as a man who never had to run, and you put him over the edge into the black, and you hold him there while your ruined shoulder tears white fire down your arm and his hands find your wrists and grip, not fighting so much as holding on to the last warm thing in the world, and you make yourself keep your eyes open because a person who does this owes it that much. It does not take as long as you feared. It takes exactly as long as it takes. Then his grip is only weight, and you let the current have him, and Wend Ossle who counted what he was told goes down toward the glass with all the other things the Maw drowned tonight, one more number the weather can be blamed for. You climb back onto the span. Your hands are shaking and you let them; you'll not insult it by pretending they aren't. Somewhere below, the rescue is still moving people into the graves the Circle dug, and it needs you, and you go — a woman who was a liar and a thief and a great many things at dawn, and is one thing more than that now, and will carry the exact weight of it the way she carries everything, quietly, and forever. The dead can't testify. That was the point of them. It is a colder point from this side of it.

payload.what: The Circle's flood-clerk, Wend Ossle, drowned in the night — his dawn-count of the reoccupied dead-man rooms never reached Corran Vale. The Maw blamed the flood. The list of who came back from the dead died with the man who kept it.

dm.clerkDrowned: T-set05 T5: Sella could not turn the clerk (T4 fail) and would not trust him, so she drowned him in the flood off the span — no knife, no wound, the water as alibi. Her FIRST on-camera kill; it marked her (carried as quiet, permanent weight, not a mechanic). The Circle loses its counter + board with no evidence of foul play (clean flood-death) — the exposure of the reoccupied rooms is closed. Corran gets no list at dawn.

dmlog.dmNotes: Resolution beat, no roll — she had a subdued soft man dead to rights; forcing a check on a settled killing would cheapen it. Full weight given (her first kill; a real character cost, not a clean win). fact_canonized for the durable world-fact (the dawn-count never reaches Vale) → legit +1 XP as it resolves to text (not the BUG-15 blank case). NO Circle front tick — undiscovered clean flood-death, so no evidence for them to respond to; the threat closes in her favor at a moral price. No dmOnly leak.

dmlog.text: Back to the work, and the work has gotten worse while I was busy becoming a murderer: the north footspan — the rope-and-plank the whole east half of the row crosses on — is going, knee-deep and groaning, and there are still people on the wrong side of it with the water climbing. An hour ago I'd have thrown my own body at it and drowned three of us. I know better now. I don't have the back for it; I have the head, and I have a coil of good rope, and I have more hands than the Circle ever counted. So I rig it instead of carry it. I run my rope as a second line above the failing span — belayed hard to the ironwood pilings that'll hold when the planks won't — and I set the network's strongest at the anchors, not me, and I turn the crossing into a hand-over-hand ferry where a body that slips catches the line instead of the river. My job's the part I'm actually built for: reading the pilings for the one that's rotten before it takes the whole rig, calling the timing so we're not loading the span when the next surge hits, and being the calm voice on a dark bridge full of scared people that makes them move in order instead of all at once. Tools and timing and other people's arms. That's how you carry a thing too heavy to lift.

You rig it the way you'd rig a con — the load-bearing part invisible, the thing everyone trusts not actually the thing holding them up. Your rope goes up as a second line, belayed hard to the ironwood pilings that have stood since before the village hung, and you put Frederick's biggest at the anchors and keep your own torn shoulder out of it entirely, because you have finally learned the price of the other thing. Then it's a ferry: hand over hand, one scared body at a time, the failing planks underfoot but the true line overhead, so that a foot that goes through a rotten board drops a person onto rope instead of into the river. It works because it's built to work. And now the whole thing lives or dies on the part that is actually yours — the calm dark-bridge voice keeping them moving in order, and your eye on the pilings, because rope is only as good as the wood it's tied to, and one of these old posts is lying about how much of it the water's already eaten. The next surge is coming up the crater from the low end; you can hear it building. You have until it arrives to find the piling that's going to betray you.
dmlog.dmNotes: Clever tool+teamwork rig — the T1 lesson applied. Uncertain crux is the read she named (rotten piling before the surge): Investigation adv DC 14. Advantage for the genuinely smart approach + her real toolkit (rope, thieves'-eye). Fail costs the RESCUE (flood front + a cut-off dozen) not primarily her HP — a die shouldn't anticlimactically kill her at 4 HP; the rope-rig saves lives even on a fail (her competence isn't wholly negated). No dmOnly leak.

dmlog.text: The wood lies better than you read. You brace for the surge on the pilings you trust and the one you should not have trusted is one of them — it looks sound and it is a shell, and when the surge comes up the crater and slams the span it takes that post and half your rig with it, and the failing planks go into the black in a splintering rush with two people still on them. Your rope earns its keep even in failure: the second line catches them both, and the network hauls them up the bank soaked and screaming and alive, so your rig was not for nothing — but the crossing is gone, torn out by the river, and the dozen still on the far side are cut off now with the water rising and no bridge, and you'll have to move them the long slow dangerous way around by boat while the flood gains a whole reach of the low quarter. You saved the people on the span. You lost the span, and the river took the hour you needed.

dm.footspanLost: T-set05 T6: Sella misread the rotten piling — the surge took the footspan; her rope-line still saved the two people on it (network hauled them up), but the crossing is destroyed, a dozen cut off on the far side needing the slow boat-route, and the flood gained a reach (external front 3/6->4/6). The rescue slowed and got more dangerous.

dmlog.text: The span's gone and a dozen souls are stranded on the far side with the water still climbing, and here's the thing I finally understand at the bottom of this ruinous night: it is not my job to save them. It's my job to make sure the machine that saves them doesn't jam. So I don't get in a boat and play hero with four points of blood and one arm. I stand at the choke where the routes knot and I do the one thing I'm better at than anyone in this quarter — I run the traffic. I put Maddan's quiet Strap boats on the long black leats where the Circle doesn't watch, I set Ospra and Frederick's people as relays at every turning so nobody's ever alone in the dark with a full boat, and I keep the count myself, out loud, calm, a name for every soul that goes and a name for every soul that lands, because a rescue drowns the same way people do — in the gap where nobody's sure who's already across. Twelve to move, by boat, in the dark, past a guild that would very much like to know why its dead keep needing ferrying. I keep my eyes up and my voice level and I watch the water and the shadows both, because a night this loud is exactly the kind of cover a patient man's people use too.

The machine runs because you built it to, and for a while you are simply the best version of the thing you've always been — not a hero, a fixer, the calm voice at the center of other people's fear making the pieces move in an order that keeps them alive. Boats slide the black leats. Frederick's relays call the turnings. Your count holds: eight across, then nine, a name landing safe for every name that leaves, the gap where people drown kept closed by nothing but your voice and your refusal to lose track of a single soul. Nine. Ten. And on the count of ten is when the shadow you've been watching for all night finally decides it's watched enough. He comes up the choke against the flow of your traffic the way the clerk did — unhurried, wrong-way, a man with all the time your rescue doesn't have — but this one is not soft. Broad through the shoulders, Circle wool gone black with rain, a cudgel of raw ironwood hanging easy from one fist, and a face that has asked hard questions of frightened people for a living and expects tonight to be no exception. **Vesk.** He stops a few feet into your light, and his eyes go over your little operation — the boats, the ferried dead, the count on your lips — and then to you, and something in them settles, because a missing clerk has just been explained. "You'd be the reason Ossle didn't come back," he says. Not a question. He rolls the cudgel once in his grip. Behind you, mid-river, boat eleven is still on the water with two souls in it and nowhere to land but here, and you are a woman with four points of blood, a bad arm, a dagger, and a thousand ball bearings, standing between a Circle enforcer and the last of the people you swore across. He takes a step. The choke is narrow. He has decided how this goes. He is waiting, the way his whole guild waits, for you to catch up.

dm.boatRun: T-set05 T7: Sella ran the boat-extraction of the cut-off dozen as pure coordination (delegated, ran traffic + the count — her arc's lesson mastered). Ten of twelve across safe when Vesk (Circle enforcer, T3's named muscle) arrived at the choke hunting his missing clerk-partner Ossle. Boat eleven (2 souls) still on the water needing to land AT the choke Vesk now holds. Vesk has ID'd Sella as the reason Ossle vanished. Combat imminent — Sella at 4/9 HP, narrow choke, her kit (dagger, 1000 ball bearings, the dark, the water). Telegraphed; handed off.

dmlog.dmNotes: Granted the coordination as competence (her mastered lesson — no roll, rewards the arc). The enforcer Vesk (callback to T3's unfired fail-branch mint) arrives as motivated forward pressure (hunting his missing clerk-partner). Ends at the threshold and HANDS OFF — I do NOT pick her combat tactics; the fight resolves next turn from whatever verb she invents. Danger telegraphed (she declared she was watching the shadows; he's described in full before he acts). At 4 HP this is genuinely lethal. No dmOnly leak; Vesk referred by name only, not yet codex-minted.

dmlog.text: He's decided how this goes, which means he's already lost, because a man who's sure is a man who's not watching his feet. I don't square up — squaring up is how a four-blood woman with one arm dies fast. I give him the fight he wants to see for exactly one second: I flinch back like prey, all the way to the choke's narrowest tongue where the wet plank runs between two ironwood pilings over open black water, and I let him follow me onto it, big and certain and closing. And on the back-step my good hand's already at my belt, and I don't throw the dagger — I throw the bag. A thousand ball bearings across a rain-slick plank right under a heavy man's next confident stride. Then I do the only honest thing this town's taught me all night: I let the flood have him. As his boots hit the bearings and the certainty goes out of his face, I get low and inside the cudgel's arc where a big man can't bring it to bear, and I use every pound of him that's already going the wrong way — a shove, a hooked ankle, my whole weight where his balance used to be — and I put Vesk into the same black water that took his clerk, and I stay on my feet on the piling side, because I have spent this entire night learning exactly where the edge of the drowning is and how to be on the right side of it.

You give him prey and he takes it, because a man who has decided how a thing ends stops reading it — he follows your flinch onto the narrow tongue of wet plank between the pilings, big and sure and closing, the black water on both sides of him now and no more certain than he knows. Your hand is already at your belt on the back-step. Not the dagger. The bag. A thousand ball bearings go out across the rain-slick plank in a hissing silver spray right under the place his next confident stride is going to land, and you get low, and inside, and the whole night comes down to whether a con artist who has spent every hour since dusk learning the exact edge of the drowning can put a Circle enforcer over it.
dmlog.dmNotes: The fight at 4 HP, resolved in one decisive Acrobatics gambit (harness-safe — no combat_start round-tracker, which wouldn't persist). Advantage for a genuinely clever environmental setup (bearings + wet plank + chosen ground + his overconfidence). Success = rogue environmental kill, no blow traded, sheds the ball bearings (also clears her carry cap). Fail = nonlethal capture (motivated: Vesk wants Ossle answers) — TESTS BUG-04 (does the nonlethal flag land her 0-stable vs dying?). Genuinely lethal stakes honored. No dmOnly leak; Vesk by name only.

dmlog.text: He does not buy the flinch all the way — or the bearings scatter a half-second late, or a Circle enforcer's boots are simply better on bad ground than a bag of steel promised — and inside the arc, which is exactly where you meant to be, turns out to be exactly where he meant you to be too. The cudgel doesn't windmill. It comes down, short and hard and expert, across your skull, and the flood and the choke and the count and the whole ruinous night go out like a snuffed candle. You do not go into the water. That is not mercy; it is arithmetic. The last thing you feel is a fist closing in your collar — the same grip you used on Ossle, turned around on you — and Vesk's voice a long way off and unhurried: "No, you don't drown yet. You've got a great deal to tell me about a clerk first." Then nothing. You have four points of blood and he has all the time his guild ever has, and the black that takes you is not the river's.

payload.note: 1000 ball bearings scattered on the plank, lost

dm.sellaTaken: T-set05 T8: Sella's ball-bearing gambit FAILED — Vesk landed the cudgel, dropped her, and took her ALIVE (nonlethal capture — he wants answers about the missing Ossle before she drowns). She is captured, unconscious, 0 HP stable. The rescue's coordinator is gone; boat eleven+twelve and the count now hang on the network alone. CLIFFHANGER into T9.

dmlog.text: I come back the way I went out — all at once, and without letting my body tell anyone. Cold water somewhere, a rope at my wrists, the taste of my own blood and the ache where the cudgel found my skull. I keep my eyes closed one breath longer than he thinks and I inventory it all: how many of them breathing in the room, how good the knots, whether that's dawn I feel getting grey against my eyelids, and above all the shape of the man who took me — because Vesk didn't drag me up the chain to Corran while I was out cold, did he. He kept me. For himself. Which means he's a Circle enforcer working a private errand off the books, hunting a partner who's never coming back, and that is not a strong man's position. That's a frightened one wearing a strong man's coat. So when I open my eyes I don't beg and I don't lie clumsy — I give him the one thing worth more than his cudgel: a way to not be the man who lost Ossle AND grabbed a stranger nobody sanctioned. "Ossle's dead," I tell him, flat, true, because true is the only currency he'll trust from a woman he's already hit. "The flood took him same as it's taking half this quarter — I watched it. You can drag me up to Vale at dawn and explain how you know that, explain why you were down here freelancing a snatch on a night the Circle wanted spent counting, explain the woman you've got trussed that isn't on anybody's warrant — or you can cut these ropes, let me walk back into a flood that's about to swallow the evidence of all of it, and be a man who was simply never here tonight. One of those two mornings ends with you still holding a coat. Your count, enforcer. You're better at it than Ossle was."

You have been out for hours — you can feel it in the stiff cold of your own body and the particular grey pressing at your eyelids that is the Maw's dawn leaking up through the boards, Day Four now, the flood's long night finally spending itself. Somewhere far off the rescue is a memory of noise winding down; your machine ran without you, because you built it to, and the not-knowing whether the last boats made it is its own specific torture. Nearer, there is Vesk. He has you in a lockup that smells of rope and old fish, wrists bound, and he has not brought you up the chain — that fact alone, once you have it, is worth more than the dagger he took off you. He's been sitting with a problem all night, and the problem is that a missing clerk and a trussed stranger and a freelance snatch nobody sanctioned add up, in the cold light coming, to a very bad morning for an enforcer who's supposed to be a strong sure man. When your eyes open he doesn't startle. He just looks at you the way a man looks at a sum he can't make come out. "Ossle," he says. That's all. He wants it to be a lie so he can hit you until it's a better one. You give him the truth instead, and the door out you've built him in the same breath, and then you do the last thing you have the strength for: you hold his eye in the grey light and you let him do his own arithmetic, and you wait to see whether a frightened man wearing a strong man's coat picks the morning where he still gets to keep the coat.
dmlog.dmNotes: She's finally on her home turf (talk out of a capture) after four cold physical/social rolls — strong TRUE leverage (Vesk's off-books grab is his liability) → Persuasion adv DC 14. Advantage for the genuine, well-read leverage. Fail = the Frederick/town 'fear-of-Corran-beats-cleverness' motif one more time (delivered to Corran, her ace becomes her last card). No hp event needed — the overnight hold already roused her to 1/9. No dmOnly leak; Vesk by name only.

dmlog.text: The arithmetic you handed him loses to the older fear, the same one that beat you at the wash-yard and on the span all night: it is easier to be afraid of Corran Vale than to outthink him. "You talk like Ossle counted," Vesk says, and there's something almost sorrowful in it, "clever, and sure the cleverness is worth something. It isn't. Vale decides what a thing's worth, not me, and I'll not be the enforcer who let a live problem walk on her own say-so." He hauls you up, rope and all, and turns you toward the chains and the grey and the long climb up to a patient man's morning, and every step is a step back toward the one clean item left on Corran Vale's list — delivered to him now not by cleverness but by the plain arithmetic of a bigger man's hands. You have one point of blood, no dagger, bound wrists, and a card still up your sleeve that a patient man is about to give you every reason to play.

dm.sellaDelivered: T-set05 T9: Sella's out-talk FAILED — Vesk's fear of Corran beat her leverage; he's dragging her bound up the chains to deliver her to Corran Vale at dawn. Worst outcome: captured + delivered to the one man hunting her, at 1 HP. Her unspent ace (Maddan's traitor-secret) is now her last card. CLIFFHANGER into T10.

dmlog.text: The chains, the grey, the long climb up to the ironwood door I spent three days trying to get off the list of, and here I am delivered to it trussed like a Sunn's-day goose. No dagger, no clever left, one point of blood and one card, and I will not play the card, because the card is Maddan's throat and I did not spend my name and my night saving a hundred people to spend an old man's life saving my own. So I do the last true thing I've got. When they stand me in front of Corran Vale in the dawn light I don't struggle and I don't beg — I read the room the way I've read every room since I was nine, and I hand the patient man his own arithmetic, out loud, in front of his people: "Morning, Corran. Your enforcer's brought you a drowned woman off the books, on a night you wanted spent counting, and he's short one clerk he can't account for, and he did it all on his own say-so because he was scared of what the flood took. That's your leak, right there in the good coat — not me. I'm the thing you asked for in the first hour: a woman who looks, and who's useful by dawn instead of a loose end by dark. You said grow me slow or prune me. So grow me. Put me on your string where you can see me, and I'll be worth more to you than any ten men who only count what they're told — because I'm the one who noticed your Vesk was the hole while your Vesk was busy handing me to you as the fix." I look him dead in his mild eyes and I give him the only truth that keeps us both in profit: "You wanted a leash on me since the Tree. Here's my wrist. I'd rather be the patient man's item than the dead man's regret." And I let Corran Vale do the sum, because it's the one game in this town I've finally learned I can't win — so I'll settle for being on the winning side of it, and keep my ace, and my allies, and my life, and go on.

Corran Vale takes you in the way he took you in on the first morning — completely, unhurried, a man reading a card he already suspected was in the deck. He lets your whole speech land in the dawn quiet, and the pale sliver of ironwood turns once between his fingers, and when he finally moves it is not toward you. It is a slow, mild look, sideways, at Vesk — and you watch a patient man rebuild an entire night in the space of one breath, watch him arrive exactly where you led him, because you told him nothing that wasn't true and the true things all point one way. "Vesk," he says, gently, the way he says everything, "you were counting the low quarter with Ossle. And now you're holding a woman off the book, and Ossle isn't holding anything at all." He does not raise his voice. He never will. But Vesk, who is a strong sure man, goes the specific grey of a man who has just felt the ground he stood on all night turn to ball bearings under his boot, and he does not say a word, because there is no word, and the two Circle folk by the door are already looking at him the way people look at a thing about to be pruned. You did that. Bound and bloodied and out of every trick, you did the one thing you never stopped being able to do: you read the room and told the truth that repriced everyone in it.

Corran turns back to you. "You are," he says, and there's something almost like pleasure in it, the appreciation one professional gives another, "a great deal of trouble. And you're right, which is worse." The wood stills in his hand. "I told you at the Tree: we don't buy clean starts, we grow them, and we prune what won't take. You've spent three days proving you'll take. So." He nods, once, and someone cuts the rope from your wrists, and the blood comes back into your hands like a debt repaid at bad interest. "You're mine now, Voss. On the string, in the light, where I can watch a woman who looks. You'll do small useful things and you'll do them quietly and you'll live, one day at a time, as long as the looking stays useful. That's not freedom. It was never going to be freedom. It's arithmetic." He is already turning away, the morning's business resumed, the flood receding under the boards, the Maw hanging on its chains for one more day. "Go get warm, dead woman. You'll want your strength. I've a great many things that need noticing."

And so it ends where it began, on a patient man's terms, with a leash on your wrist you talked your own way into wearing — because the alternative was a corpse, or a burned ally, or a hundred people un-saved, and you would not pay any of those. Sella Voss, drowned in the flood, walks out of the Ironwood door into the Day-Four dawn as the Circle's own quiet creature, one point of blood and a whole night's worth of the dead behind her, breathing. You lost the war with the patient man; you were always going to. But Maddan's throat is still your secret and not his rope. The network still runs and thinks you drowned a hero. And folded small and warm in your sleeve, unspent, unsuspected, is a card that says the man who just leashed you has taken a knife into his own house and called it an asset. The Maw is small, Corran. You said so yourself. You'll have all the time in the world to work the sum of me. So will I.

payload.what: Sella Voss — the woman the town book records as drowned in the flood — became the Ironwood Circle's leashed asset at dawn on Day 4, taken onto Corran Vale's own string as 'a woman who looks,' after her captor Vesk was exposed as the Circle's real leak. Delivered as a prisoner, she talked her way into being kept as a tool: not free, but breathing.

dm.leashedSella: T-set05 T10 CLOSE: Corran took Sella onto his own string as a live asset ('a woman who looks') after she — bound, 1 HP, out of tricks — read the room and exposed Vesk as his real leak (the missing Ossle + the off-books freelance snatch). Corran's hour-one deal ('useful by dusk or a loose end') paid in full: she's his creature now, in the light, doing small useful things to stay alive. He respects her ('right, which is worse'). VESK is now the one being pruned. Corran does NOT know: (1) Sella killed Ossle + drowned Vesk's partner-hunt; (2) she is secretly the Refugee-Quarter network's, the uncounted's; (3) she still holds Maddan Strole's traitor-secret UNSPENT. He has taken a mole into his house and called it an asset.

dm.setCloseState: T-set05 close (Day 4 dawn): flood receding, rescue completed overnight by the network without Sella (her arc's proof). Two Circle men dead in the flood undiscovered (Ossle T5, Vesk-hunt T8). Sella now the Circle's leashed asset on Corran's string — a mole inside the dominant faction, ace (Maddan's secret) unspent. She kept: her life, her allies, the network's secret, the ace. She lost: her freedom, her dagger, her blood, and her innocence (first kill, T5).

dmlog.dmNotes: CLOSE — resolution beat, no roll (this is Corran's own hour-one deal paid in full, not a fresh gamble; a sixth cold die would be absurd and the finale rightly turns on her agency/choice). Corran takes the arithmetic she hands him — keeps her useful, prunes Vesk (the real leak). fact_canonized (her new status as the Circle's leashed asset) → legit +1 XP. Circle front ticks 4->5 (their APPARENT consolidation — they think they gained an asset; really they took a mole; the hidden reversal is noted, huge continuing tension: Circle one tick from doom, Sella inside it). She did NOT play the ace (won't burn Maddan — her one line). Bittersweet bookend to the Tree: the unbeaten patient man wins the sum, the dead woman goes on, leashed, ace hidden. No dmOnly leak.

dmlog.text: I walk out of the ironwood door slow and easy, a woman with all the time in the world — because I'm one of theirs now, and the first thing a leash buys me is the right to not look hunted. But I don't go to my own people; a drowned woman who walks out of the Circle's own door alive is a woman the network will read as turned, and I'll not undo three days of trust in one dawn. So I find the warmest, quietest, most nowhere corner of the Maw a Circle creature is allowed — a boarded tea-stall, a chain-anchor nook out of the wind — and I get warm, and I bind what's left of me, and for the first hour of my new life I do nothing at all but breathe and take the exact measure of what I've become. One point of blood is not a body that can afford another mistake today. I rest, and I let the Maw believe its dead woman is simply obeying the man who owns her.

The nook you find is a boarded tea-stall wedged against a chain-anchor, canvas gone stiff with old smoke, and it is the first place in three days no one is looking for you — because the one man who owns the looking has told them all, without a word, that you are his now. That is the strange arithmetic of a leash: it is also a wall. You get the little brazier's coals breathing, and you strip the ruined coat, and you bind the shoulder properly this time with clean strips instead of lath and desperation, and the warmth comes into you slow and mean, the way warmth comes back to a body that spent a night at the bottom of its own strength. The blood settles. The shaking stops. You are not whole — a night like that does not wash out in an hour — but you are no longer a woman one hard cough could finish. Through a gap in the canvas the Maw resumes itself: the flood is going down under the boards, sucking back into the glass it came from, and along the low chains the rescue is a memory of noise winding down to nothing. Your machine ran without you. You built it to. And once, while the coals tick, a small barefoot child you have never seen stops at the mouth of the stall, looks at you with the flat incurious accounting of someone who has been told to, and then moves on — not a threat, not a question. Just the string, letting you feel its weight. The morning is yours, dead woman, and it is the first morning in a long while that nothing in it is trying to kill you. What you do with a thing like that is its own kind of test.

dm.leashStart: T1-set4: Sella walked out the Ironwood door as Corran's leashed asset ('a woman who looks'), took a short rest in a nowhere tea-stall to claw back from 1 HP. Corran has NOT yet tasked her; he expects her to recover and then 'notice things.' A Circle child was set to lightly watch/mark her (the string made visible, non-hostile). Corran does NOT know: she killed his clerk Ossle, she is the Refugee-Quarter network's, she holds Maddan's Iron-Strap secret unspent.

dmlog.dmNotes: T1 = recovery + status-reset beat. No check (resting in an uncontested nowhere corner). Rest event owns the HP number; narration stays honest about partial recovery without stating a figure. Slow drip: the leash-as-wall, the flood receding, the network running without her, the child-as-string. Hand off open.

dmlog.text: An hour by a stale brazier bought me warmth and not much blood, and a woman at one point of life is no use to Corran, to my people, or to myself. I need real sleep — the eight-hour kind that knits a body back together — and for the first time I understand the price of it here. So I do the thing I've watched this whole town do and never once risked myself: I find a dead-man's cot in a flood-emptied upper room, and I lie down facing east like all the drowned and all the living of the Maw, deliberate, exact, the way Maddan taught me without meaning to — not because I fear the dream, but because I finally know what the east-facing buys: it's the Sunns' old bargain, don't let the crater see you take. And I have taken so much. A clerk's breath. A dead man's name. A patient man's trust and a whole quarter's. If the glass is going to look at anyone tonight, let it look at a woman lying the right way, giving nothing back it can name. I sleep, and I heal, and I let whatever the Shared Sleep shows a taker come.

The upper room still holds a hand's-breadth of flood-stink in its corners, but the cot is dry and the boards above the waterline, and there are three others already laid out in it when you climb up — an old woman, a boatman, a child — all of them on their sides, all facing the same way, east, toward the lightening gap in the chain-wall. No one told them to. No one has to. You lie down among the drowned-who-aren't and turn your face east with the rest, and the strangeness of it is how little strangeness there is: a whole town lying one way, like iron filings snapped into their field, and you the newest filing. You are so tired that sleep does not come like a tide; it comes like a dropped stone. And because you lay the right way, the Maw does not punish the taking — it starts to show you something instead, the way it shows the ones who keep the old courtesy. You dream of the glass from underneath. Faces in the color, a whole house of them, not screaming, only waiting the way ironwood waits, the way a patient man waits — a father and a son and eight more behind, all turned east even down there under the poured centuries, all looking at the same gap of light from the wrong side of it. The twice-struck one opens his mouth in the glass and no sound comes, but you read the unsaid the way you always have: not a scream. A count. He is counting, still, down there. They all are. — And that is exactly as far as the Maw lets you go, because the dream doesn't end, it is *ended*: a boot splinters the door below and the whole room comes awake at once. Not the Circle's unhurried courtesy — the other thing a flood leaves behind. Wreckers. Scavengers working the emptied upper rooms for what the water drove the valuables up to, three or four of them by the sound, already on the stair, and they do not know or care that the rooms aren't empty. The old woman beside you is scrambling back against the wall; the child has gone the perfect silent still of a child who has learned that silence is the only lock a poor door has. The grey gap of light has become a hard afternoon glare; the day slipped past you in the broken dozing of the badly hurt, and now, at the very end of it, the Maw collects the debt for letting you lie down at all. Your body has not knit back into anything — the raid robs the rest of its whole benefit, the count in the glass follows you up out of the dream, and you come to still exactly, mockingly, a woman with one point of blood in her: no sword's-length of recovery bought, a wet heavy tread three steps down and closing, and the wrong end of a day that would not let you have it.

dm.sharedSleepObserved: T2-set4: Sella took her first LONG rest in the Maw, deliberately observing the Shared Sleep taboo (lay facing east with the town), understanding it now via Maddan's account as the Sunns' old bargain ('don't let the crater see you take'). Because she lay the RIGHT way, the taboo functioned as its intended small-oracle rather than a punishment: a Strange-band true-dream of the drowned Sunn house UNDER the glass — a father, a son (the twice-struck Wemric), and eight more, all turned east even down there, all silently COUNTING. Drips the 'Sunns went into the glass' thread + connects the twice-struck Wemric to something unfinished (still counting = the debt/claim not settled). No hard canon minted; a dream-impression Sella now carries.

dmlog.dmNotes: T2 = long rest to restore HP + the taboo hook finally paid off, obeyed knowingly. No check (she observes the taboo correctly, so no 'dream goes wrong' failure). Rest event owns the HP restore; narration describes deep healing sleep and lets the engine set the number. The dream drips the Sunn-well thread (already established via Maddan) without leaking any dmOnly noun — 'counting' echoes the census/dawn-count motif honestly. Hand off open (she wakes whole, morning gone to afternoon).

dmlog.text: One point of blood can't win a fight and I don't intend to have one — a knife is the argument you make when you've run out of better ones, and I have exactly one better one left, freshly bought and still bleeding on my wrist. So I don't reach for the dagger. I get up off the cot slow and unbothered, the way a body with all the time in the world gets up, and I step my one useless body between the stair and the old woman and the silent child, and I let the first wrecker up into the room find me already looking at him, bored, like he's late. "You picked the wrong upper room, friend," I tell them, easy and cold, and I hold up my bandaged wrist where the rope-burn still shows like a brand. "This row's counted. I'm the one that counts it now — Corran Vale's newest set of eyes, and he is very, particular, about spoilage in his inventory. You can go back down those stairs having seen nothing and taken nothing, and I'll have forgotten your faces by supper. Or you can make me remember them, and explain to a patient man why his count came up short in a room his own woman was sleeping in." I don't raise my voice. I learned that from the best man in this town. I just let them do the arithmetic of who the Maw is actually dangerous to.

The first wrecker comes up into the room the way the flood came up into it — sure it will find nothing that can stop it. He is a big-shouldered man with a pry-bar and a sack, river-muck to the knees, and behind him on the stair are the wet heavy treads of at least two more. He finds you already on your feet and already looking at him, and for one beat the sheer wrongness of that — a woman who isn't running, isn't begging, is bored — makes him stop. You hold up the wrist. The rope-burn shows in the hard afternoon light, raw and unmistakable, the brand of a night spent in hands harder than his. You name the patient man in the flat quiet voice you learned across a card-table from the best in the Maw. And you watch it work on him, the arithmetic — the Circle is the one thing in this drowned town that everyone, wrecker and widow alike, has watched make an example. His eyes go to the wrist, to the door behind you, to his own two men on the stair who've gone quiet listening. But greed is also arithmetic, and the room behind you is full of the dry upstairs valuables a flood drives up and a wrecker lives on, and you are, whatever your mouth says, one hurt woman between him and a season's take. The pry-bar shifts a half-inch in his grip. He has not decided. He is deciding — and everything you have left tonight rides on whether a desperate man believes a bandaged stranger is worth more trouble than a wet sack is worth. If he decides wrong, there is no second bluff and no blood left in you to spend on the fight it becomes.
dmlog.dmNotes: T3 = the leash weaponized. She refuses a fight she'd lose at 1 HP and instead bluffs with her TRUE new status (Deception, her proficiency; adv for the strong real lever — universal Circle fear + visible brand + Corran named). Fail branch is genuinely lethal (combat at 1 HP, noncombatants at her back) and TELEGRAPHED (armed desperate men, no blood left, no second bluff). Setup ends at the threshold; her full action was declared, so the check only adjudicates whether it lands. No coaching.

dmlog.text: The arithmetic comes out your way. The big man's pry-bar lowers first, and that is permission for the other two — you watch the exact moment a season's take stops being worth a patient man's attention, watch three desperate men choose the wet sack they already have over the one the Circle would collect for. "Didn't see nothing," the big one says, to the room, to himself, and it is not surrender so much as accounting, and then the treads go back down the stair heavier and faster than they came up, and the flood-emptied room is yours and the old woman's and the child's again. The old woman lets out a breath she has held since the door broke. And you have learned the second thing a leash is: not just a wall, but a weapon — the patient man's fear, worn on your own wrist, turned to your own use in a room he will never know you saved. It cost you nothing but the truth, told to men who couldn't check it.

dm.leashAsWeapon: T3-set4: at 1 HP, Sella turned flood-WRECKERS off a rich upper-room take with a Deception play weaponizing her NEW Circle-asset status (held up the rope-burn as a brand, named Corran, flat menace) — NOT a fight (she can't survive one at 1 HP). Success: they backed off empty-handed, protected the vulnerable sleepers (old woman, boatman, child) in a room Corran will never know she saved. She has learned the leash is a WEAPON as well as a wall — the Circle's fear worn on her wrist, wielded without his knowledge. First on-camera use of the asset-status as leverage.

dmlog.text: The stair goes quiet and I let out the breath I didn't show them I was holding. Then I turn to the two who watched me do it — the old woman with flood-survivor eyes and the child gone silent-still — and I look at them properly for the first time, reading what I just became in their faces. Because I saved them with the Circle's name, and there's no crueller thing to be rescued by in this town, and they'll have to decide what I am now. The old woman's the one I want. A body that's outlasted this many floods in a refugee quarter is a body that knows how to mend one, and I am past the point where pride outweighs one point of blood. So I go to her low and honest, no card and no angle, and I show her the shoulder and the rest of it. "I'm no more the Circle's than you are, mother," I tell her quiet, "but the Circle's a good coat to wear when wolves come up the stairs. You saw what I did with it. Now I'm asking the other way: I've got a wound that'll kill me slower than those men would've, and I think you know the herb for it. Help me mend, and I'll owe the debt to whoever you say — that's a better kind of counting than the one the good coats do." And while she decides, I keep my eyes gentle and my read sharp, learning whether this room is just frightened refugees or a knot of my own network I haven't met yet.

The old woman looks at you for a long time, and it is not fear she's weighing — you'd know fear, you deal in it — it's arithmetic of her own, the slow careful kind the uncounted learn because they cannot afford a wrong sum. You read her right back, because that is the one thing a night at the bottom of your strength did not take: she is not a frightened refugee. She is one of the erased, network to her bones, a fen-wife who has mended flood-hurt in this quarter since before the chains you came in on were hung — and she knows exactly what room she is in and who lets it. "The Circle's woman," she says at last, tasting it the way the wrecker did but arriving somewhere else entirely. "There's a story going round the low chains since the flood. About a drowned woman who pulled half the struck row out of the black and went under doing it. A hero, they're saying. And here's the Circle's newest coat, wearing her face, saving my life with the good coat's own name." She wets a rag from a clay pot that smells of tannin and something greener. "Two stories about one woman, and they can't both live in a small town." But her hands are already moving — because whatever you are, you stood between her grandchild and three pry-bars, and a fen-wife pays what she owes. She works the herb into the shoulder and binds it right, and makes you drink something bitter, and lets you lie in the safe quiet of a room you bought for two whole hours — the mend you've been chasing since dawn, finally, from the last hands in the Maw you'd have dared ask. It is not all your blood back. But it is enough to stand, enough to think, enough to be a woman again instead of a wound. When she finishes she holds your eye. "You'll want to decide which of those two women you are," she says, "before the quarter decides for you. Small town, girl. It's already talking."

dm.twoLegends: T4-set4: the fen-wife Sella saved (an uncounted network herb-healer, referred by role, NOT minted) gave her earned care (+4 HP, mundane herb-tending + 2h safe rest → 5/9). KEY THREAD: Sella's network cover-legend ('the drowned HERO who pulled the struck row out of the flood', now spreading along the low chains) is COLLIDING with her public status ('the Circle's newest coat'). The fen-wife named it: 'Two stories about one woman, and they can't both live in a small town.' The quarter is ALREADY talking. Sella's double identity (network's secret mole vs Corran's visible asset) is on a collision course in the town's mouth — a live, self-advancing social danger. She must manage which face the quarter settles on.

dmlog.dmNotes: T4 = the mend, finally, earned. Insight read = free competence (she's proficient; reading people is her craft) → the old woman is network, not a stranger. The care-grant needs no roll: Sella just saved this woman's grandchild and offered an honest, motivated deal — refusing would be unmotivated. HP +4 is fiction-grounded mundane care (fen-herb + 2h uninterrupted safe rest), NOT a fabricated die — the engine models no HD-on-rest heal, so this is the honest care path. The turn ALSO plants the session's spine problem: her two legends (network hero / Circle coat) can't coexist in a small town, and the town is already talking. Hand off open (mended, standing, a new social danger named).

dmlog.text: The fen-wife's right: two stories can't both live in a small town, and the deadliest one isn't the quarter's — it's the version where Corran Vale hears his newest set of eyes is also the drowned hero who dragged his struck row out of the flood, and does the one sum I can't afford him doing. A patient man given a loose thread pulls it slow until the whole coat comes apart. So I don't wait for the story to reach him raw. I go find Fenn on the spans — my own handler, the Circle's ear, the man who takes everything at exact change — and I surface to him plain and unhurried, a woman reporting for work like she was told to. "Word for Corran, and it's the good kind," I tell Fenn. "The quarter's grown a story since the flood — a drowned woman, a hero who saved the low row. They half-think it's me. I didn't plant it and I won't kill it, because a woman the uncounted trust is a woman who can walk into rooms your good coats never will and come back with what's said in them. Tell him his string just got longer. Tell him I'm not asking to be off the leash — I'm asking to be aimed." I give Fenn the truth folded once, the way you fold a marked card so the mark handles it himself: let Corran hear I'm building the quarter's trust FOR him, and never once hear that I already have it because it's mine.

Fenn takes the report the way he takes everything, at exact change, no interest paid and none charged. You watch him receive the folded card — the hero-story offered up as an asset, the truth of it tucked inside the fold where a relay's hands will never feel it — and something moves behind the flat courteous eyes that in a warmer man might have been respect and in Fenn is just filing. "I'll carry it," he says. That's all. He does not tell you it's good. He does not tell you anything. He simply folds himself back into the dusk toward the ironwood door, and you are left on the swaying span to learn the first real rule of being on a patient man's string: you do not get to know when he's decided. You only get to feel the line go taut.

It goes taut faster than you'd have liked. Fenn is back before full dark — a patient man moves at exactly the moment he chooses, and he has chosen to move quickly, which is its own message. "He heard you," Fenn says. "He says: aimed, then. He says a woman who can walk where his coats can't should walk there and bring him back the thing he's been missing since the flood-count came up crooked." Fenn's flat eyes hold yours, and for once the message underneath is not hidden, because it is not meant to be. "Somebody's been hiding the struck. Rooms that flood and stay empty on the book but aren't. Names off the roll that keep breathing. His count came up short by a whole quarter's worth and he wants to know whose hand's been doing the subtracting." A pause, exact. "Find him the hand, Voss. That's the first thing his string pulls. He says you'll understand why it's the right test." And then Fenn is gone, and you are standing in the dusk holding your very first task from the man who owns you — which is to hunt, through the trust of the uncounted, the exact machinery of the uncounted: the dead-man rooms, the keepers, Frederick, Susannah, the whole quiet network that is not the Circle's and is very much yours. He has aimed his new knife at the only wound that would prove which way it cuts.

dm.firstTask: T5-set4: Sella pre-empted the two-legends danger by reporting to Corran via Fenn — folding the spreading 'drowned hero' story into her cover ('a woman the uncounted trust can spy their rooms FOR you'; hiding that she IS that hero and IS network). Corran did NOT buy or reject it — the PATIENT-MAN move: he TESTS it. First task (via Fenn, fast = a message in itself): 'find the hand that's been hiding the struck' — the network keeper-machinery (dead-man rooms, Frederick, Susannah) that subtracted a quarter's worth of names from his flood-count (the machinery Ossle's destroyed list was tracking). Corran explicitly framed it as 'the right test' — a loyalty trap: aim the mole at her own people. Sella must either betray the network, or feed Corran a convincing false hand while protecting the real one. The double-agent seam, live. Corran STILL does not know she's the network's / the hero / Ossle's killer.

dm.networkHunted: T5-set4: the Circle now actively hunts the dead-man-room KEEPER MACHINERY (Corran's task to Sella) — the flood-count came up 'a quarter's worth' short, and Corran wants the hand behind the hidden/struck-but-breathing. Frederick, Susannah, and the whole network are the target. Sella (secretly network) is the assigned hunter. Live existential danger to the network + Sella's cover, driven by Corran.

dmlog.dmNotes: T5 = the trap sprung, patient-man style. Sella's framing is neither bought nor rejected (no gifted win) — Corran TESTS it, which is his established character (grows useful things, prunes what won't take). His first task aims the mole at her own network — the perfect loyalty-test that also drives the back half of the session. No roll: delivering a pitch + reading Fenn is competence; Corran's counter is NPC forward-pressure (agency via NPC, not fiat over the PC). Fenn referred by role (not minted). Hand off: she holds a task that points at Frederick/Susannah — her move next.

dmlog.text: He wants a hand. Fine — I'll give him a hand, but not one that's still attached to anyone I mean to keep. The trick with a patient man isn't lying to him; he'll pull a lie apart at his leisure. The trick is handing him a truth that closes the question so completely he never wants to open it again. And I have the perfect corpse for it, because the town book already killed her: the drowned hero. So I don't go near Frederick or Susannah — a mole who visits the hive she's been sent to burn is a fool, and the string might be watching. I work it alone, at a remove, the way I work everything. I spend the dusk quietly gathering the true, checkable bones of a story: which struck names came back breathing, which flood-empty rooms were used, and the shape of the woman the low chains are already mythologizing — and I build them all into one airtight account with one dead culprit at the center. The hand that hid the struck was the drowned woman herself. She ran the dead-man rooms out of some refugee saint's foolishness, she subtracted the names, and then the flood took her doing the last of it, and she's in the glass now where no one can ask her a thing. It even explains the hero-story — a hider of the struck IS a saver of the struck, seen from the other side. Then I fold it and hand it up the string through Fenn: here's your subtracting hand, Corran. She's dead. The count's closed. You're welcome. And I pray the best reader in the Maw wants a solved problem more than he wants to keep pulling.

You build it the way you build everything that has to survive a professional: out of true bricks. You do not invent a woman; you assemble the one the town has already half-built, and you make sure every part of her that Corran could check comes back solid. The struck names that came back breathing — real, and you can list them. The flood-empty rooms with warm ash in them — real, and you know which. The hero the low chains are singing about — real, and dead, her drowning on the town book in Corran's own hand. You lay the bricks so the wall only stands one way: the hand that subtracted the count was the drowned saint herself, foolish and kind and gone into the glass, and the count is closed because the counter is dead. You even leave him the loose end that makes it true — a hider of the struck is a saver of the struck; his leak and the quarter's hero are one drowned woman, and neither can be questioned, because the Maw already has her. Then you fold it small and you hand it up the string through Fenn in the last of the dusk, and there is nothing left to do but wait to feel the line, because you have just told the best reader in the Maw a story whose central corpse is your own faked death, and if he pulls the one thread you cannot afford — *and where is this drowned woman's body, then* — the whole wall comes down on the living. You set it up as clean as it will go. Now it is his to read, and yours to have said, and there is no taking it back.
dmlog.dmNotes: T6 = the fold within the fold. Real high-stakes Deception (DC 16, her hardest audience) with advantage for anchoring on true bricks + a dead culprit. She smartly does NOT contact the real network (no trail). The stakes are genuine both ways: success protects everyone but plants a latent hero=asset unraveling risk; fail turns the patient man's interest onto her own faked death (the one thread she can't afford). Fail ticks the internal front (Circle tightening) — proportionate, not a campaign-ender. Setup ends at the threshold; full action declared → check only adjudicates the landing. No coaching.

dmlog.text: The line goes taut, and this time it pulls. Fenn is at your shoulder before you've left the span, and his voice is exactly as courteous as ever, which is how you know. "He read it," Fenn says, "and he says it's the best-built thing anyone's handed him in a year, and he means it as the compliment and the accusation both." A pause, exact and terrible. "A dead culprit, delivered by his newest eyes, the same night he set them looking? He says: nobody hands a patient man a closed book that fast unless they're afraid of what he'd find open. He's not angry, Voss. He's interested. And a patient man's interest is the thing you spend three days trying to get off the list of." The hunt has not closed. It has doubled, and turned, and the knife he aimed at the network he now half-suspects points the wrong way — back at the hand that threw the corpse too quick. He will pull the one thread now: where is the drowned woman's body. And every day the count stays open, the Circle's grip closes another finger on the quarter it's hunting.

dm.smelledTheFold: T6-set4 (Deception FAIL): Corran smelled the fold — a too-fast, too-perfect dead-culprit decoy from his newest eyes the same night he set them looking. Not angry; INTERESTED ('nobody hands a patient man a closed book that fast unless they're afraid of what he'd find open'). He now half-suspects his knife points the wrong way (back at Sella) and will pull the thread she can't afford: WHERE IS THE DROWNED WOMAN'S BODY. Cover fraying; the network-hunt has doubled and turned toward her. Live existential danger to Sella's mole cover.

dm.huntDoubled: T6-set4 (fail): Sella's decoy backfired — Corran's network-hunt doubled and turned partly toward HER. The Circle tightens its grip further (internal front +1) as the hunt goes hostile. Network + Sella's cover both at rising risk.

dmlog.text: A patient man is going to pull one thread — where is the drowned woman's body — so I'd best have an answer waiting where his hand falls, and the only answer that survives him is a real one. There's a whole flood's worth of dead in the Maw tonight, and the low glass takes them the way it takes everything: down into the color where no one digs them out. That's my cover if I can dress it right — a hero with no grave isn't suspicious in a town whose crater eats its drowned. But I need to KNOW it before I lean on it, and if there's an unclaimed woman among the flood-dead near enough my age and build, well — I've made a corpse do an alibi's work before, and I'm not too proud to let a stranger be a saint. So I wait for the deepest part of the night and I go down to the Drowned Port, quiet as I've ever moved, because a Circle asset has no honest reason to be counting corpses at the glass-edge and Corran's eyes are curious about me now in particular. I keep to the dark water and the dead spans, I read where the flood laid its dead and whether the glass has already started taking them, and I look for the one unclaimed drowned woman who can be the hero's missing body — all without a single soul, least of all the string, ever seeing the patient man's newest creature down among the counting dead.

You wait for the hour the Maw belongs to no one — the dead middle of the night when even the patient keep watch in shifts and the shift is thin — and you go down through the sleeping village toward the Drowned Port like water finding its level, low and dark and unremarkable. The flood has left the port a graveyard it has not finished burying. The dead lie where the receding water set them down along the glass-edge, and the glass, catching the low green light of its own depths, is doing the thing you came to confirm: it is taking them. Not fast. The way ironwood takes a carving. A drowned man half-sunk already into color that was solid rock an hour of years ago, going down into the Maw's poured centuries to lie with everything else the crater has ever swallowed. The low chains have no graves because the low chains have the glass, and the glass keeps what it takes. That is your answer, and it is a true one: a hero drowned in this flood would have no body, would never have a body, because the Maw ate her the way it eats all its drowned — and now the missing grave you feared is not a hole in your story but the plainest fact in the quarter. You do not need to plant a corpse. The crater is the corpse's keeper. But you are a reader of the unsaid, and standing among the taken you cannot help but read the one thing the glass shows only to someone who came down here in the counting-dark: the drowned do not go down screaming. They go down turned. Every last one of them, however the flood left them, has settled facing the same way — east, toward the same gap of light the living lie toward — as if the glass itself observes the Shared Sleep, as if the house in the color is still adding names to a count that has never once stopped. You have your alibi. You also have the cold specific sense that you learned something down here you were not looking for, and that the counting Sunn in your dream was not a dream so much as a door left open.
dmlog.dmNotes: T7 = sever the thread + a texture shift to physical infiltration (Stealth = DEX +3, no prof per her sheet, consistent w/ prior sets). Success gives her a TRUER solution than planting a corpse (the glass eats its dead → no grave expected) — smarter, unfalsifiable — plus a Sunn-thread drip (east-turned drowned, the never-stopping count, tying the T2 dream + taboo + Sunns-in-glass). Fail feeds Corran's EXACT T6 suspicion (asset with a personal reason to know how the Maw keeps its dead) and ticks the internal front. Setup ends at the threshold; no coaching. All three branches keep the alibi (she gets her answer) — the variable is whether she's SEEN, which is the real risk given his new interest.

dmlog.text: No one sees you. The counting-dark keeps you the way it keeps the dead, and you move back up out of the Drowned Port with your alibi intact and unwitnessed — the glass eats its drowned, a hero has no grave because no one in the Maw ever does, and the thread Corran means to pull comes up, when he pulls it, holding nothing but the plainest truth in the quarter. You spent nothing and no one saw you spend it. And folded in with the alibi, unlooked-for and colder, is the thing the glass showed you: the drowned turned east, the count that never stops, the door your dream left open onto the Sunns in the color. You came down here to bury a question and you carried a different one back up.

dm.glassKeepsItsDead: T7-set4 (Stealth success): Sella slipped to the Drowned Port in the deep-night unseen and CONFIRMED the setting-truth that solves Corran's body-thread — the fused-glass crater slowly TAKES its flood-dead down into itself; the low chains have no graves because the glass keeps what it takes. So a drowned hero would have no body ever — the missing grave is not a hole in her decoy but the plainest fact in the quarter (she does NOT need to plant a corpse). ALSO (Sunn thread drip): the drowned all settle facing EAST as they sink, as if the glass observes the Shared Sleep and the drowned Sunn house in the color is still adding to a count that never stops — connecting the T2 true-dream, the east-facing taboo, and the Sunns-in-the-glass into a single unresolved mystery ('a door left open'). No hard canon minted beyond the observation.

dm.bodyThreadDefused: T7-set4: Sella pre-solved the 'where is the drowned woman's body' thread Corran means to pull — the glass eats the Maw's flood-dead, so a hero having no grave is normal, not suspicious. Her cover has a true answer waiting where his hand falls. Does NOT undo his T6 INTEREST in her (the too-fast decoy still hangs), but removes the specific killing detail he'd have pulled.

dmlog.text: The glass showed me a house still counting, and I can't un-see it. A patient man leashed me because I'm a woman who looks — well, I've looked, and what I saw is the crack under his whole floor: the Circle's power is the Throat's oil, and the Throat's oil was the Sunns', and the Sunns aren't gone, they're down in the color still keeping their count. If I'm going to work the sum of Corran Vale, I need what's under him, not what's beside him. And there's one place in the Maw that watched it all happen — the tree Batgal pointed me to on the first morning and I've never once dared visit: the Traitor's Tree, where a house got betrayed into the glass and a patient man likes to sit and wait. So I go there now, in the dead of the night when he won't be waiting, alone. I put my hands on the black bark that grew up out of the ruin, and I read the place the way I read a room — the old marks, the worn spots where bargains got struck, whatever the betrayal left behind that a careful eye can still find a hundred years on. I want to know exactly what door got opened, who opened it, and whether the house that went into the glass left anyone above it — because a house not all the way buried is a hand I could put on Corran's throat the day I need one.

The Traitor's Tree is worse up close, and better. It grows straight up out of the fused ruin the way a nail grows out of a coffin lid, black-barked and leafless, its roots gone down into the poured color where the drowned keep their count, and even in the dead of night no dew sits on it and no bird will. This is where Batgal pointed you the first morning — where a patient man likes to sit and let you come to him — and it is empty now, which is the only reason you dare put your professional hands on a hundred years of other people's worst moment. You read it the way you read a mark's hands: not the story it tells, the wear it can't help. There is a notch worn smooth at sitting-height, polished by generations of palms laid flat to swear on — a bargaining-spot, the Maw's own courthouse, where a deal too ugly for any roof got struck under open sky. And there are cuts. Old ones, deliberate, a tally scored into the ironwood and then scored THROUGH, the way you strike a name off a list — the way Corran's clerk struck the Sunns, the way the twice-struck Wemric was cut so deep it split the grain. You have seen this hand before. Whoever founded the Circle's claim learned his counting HERE, at this tree, from whatever he did to the house that kept the well.
dmlog.dmNotes: T8 = the deepest thread pays off — the Sunns-in-the-glass / taboo / well converge into the CIRCLE'S FOUNDING CRIME, read at the long-unvisited Traitor's Tree (open since Day 1). Investigation (INT +2, not proficient) DC 15, adv for the genuine prior knowledge she brings. Success canonizes the founding-betrayal as world-fact (fact_canonized → legit +1 XP if it resolves to text) and hands her a SECOND leverage card (the founding crime + surviving-heir LEAD, kept as inference not an over-minted NPC — grounds on Maddan's established 'house not all the way buried'). nearMiss splits it (crime yes, heir unknown). fail keeps it buried + raises exposure (her at his tree). Setup ends at the threshold; no coaching. Careful NOT to hard-mint a surviving-Sunn NPC — left as a lead for future sets.

dmlog.text: A hundred years is a long time to keep a secret, and the tree has kept better ones than you. You read wear and you read cuts and you read a bargaining-notch, but the story won't close — too many hands, too many years, the founding crime scored over and over until it's just scarring. And a professional knows when a read has gone cold and staying longer only spends what a read never earned: you are a woman with a Circle coat and a suspicious mind, at the patient man's own waiting-tree, in the dead of a night your owner is already curious about. Every heartbeat you spend here with your hands on his throne is a heartbeat that could climb the string. You leave the way you came, empty, carrying nothing off the tree but the certainty that there's something in it worth a hundred years of keeping — and the cold arithmetic that you were the one seen reaching for it.

dm.treeReadColdRisky: T8-set4 (Investigation FAIL): Sella could not read the Traitor's Tree's betrayal (a century of over-scoring; the read went cold) — she leaves empty. She confirmed only that SOMETHING in the Circle's founding is worth a hundred years of keeping. Risk: she spent time at Corran's own waiting-tree, in the deep night, hands on his ground, while he's already curious about her — a suspicious behavior that could climb the string. No lever gained; exposure risk raised.

dmlog.text: Two cold reaches in one night, and a smart woman knows when the dice have turned and the only winning move is to stop reaching and start covering. I was seen at his tree, maybe — and a suspected asset caught with her hands on the patient man's throne is a dead asset by dawn unless she gives the night an innocent shape first. So I do the thing a good creature does, and I make it true, because true survives him: I go find Fenn before the light and I report like the diligent set of eyes I'm pretending to be. "Been out all night looking, like I'm for," I tell him, easy, giving my own dark wandering its alibi in the same breath I make it useful. "Here's what the looking got you: there's a wrecker crew working the flood-empty upper rooms — four of them, organized, hitting the dead-man rows while everyone's counting their drowned. They ran when I put the Circle's name on them, but they'll be back, because a flood only fills a good coat's rooms once a decade and they know it. Corran wants his count clean? That's a hole in it, and it's got nothing to do with dead women — it's got to do with live thieves eating his quarter while he watches me." I give him the true thing that costs my people nothing and buys my cover everything: a diligent asset, out all night, catching real leaks — and if the tree comes up the string, well, of course I was near it, I was walking the whole quarter for him, wasn't I.

Fenn is where the Circle's ear is always somehow already waiting, in the grey before the grey, and he takes your report at exact change like he takes everything. You watch him weigh it — and the weighing goes your way, because the thing about a true report is that it weighs true. A wrecker crew, organized, eating the good coat's quarter while the good coat watches his newest creature: that is a real hole in a real count, the kind a patient man actually wants filled, and it has the great virtue of being exactly the shape of a night spent walking the whole quarter for him. You feel your alibi set like wax cooling — of course you were near the tree; you were near everything; you were out all night being what he made you. "I'll carry it," Fenn says, same as ever. And then, because Fenn gives exact change and never a coin more, he tells you the one thing his flat courtesy can't help telling you, which is nothing at all: he does not say Corran's pleased, he does not say the tree came up the string, he does not say you're clear. He just folds back toward the ironwood door with your true report and your innocent frame, and leaves you to understand the real shape of your new life in the greying dark — that you can hand a patient man a hundred true useful things and never once buy the one thing you want, which is for him to stop being interested. You bought the dawn. You did not buy the man. The interest is still there under the exact change, patient as the tree, waiting the way he waits for everything: for you to catch up.

dm.coverRebuilt: T9-set4: after two cold reaches (T6 decoy fail, T8 tree fail) Sella did DAMAGE CONTROL — reported a REAL wrecker crew (the T3 flood-wreckers, organized, hitting the dead-man rows) to Fenn, converting her suspicious night-wandering into a diligent-asset alibi that ALSO frames the tree-visit innocently ('out all night looking, for you'). The true intel is genuinely useful (a real hole in Corran's count, harmless to her people). Result (non-generous): surface cover rebuilt + tree-exposure contained by the true frame, BUT Corran's T6 INTEREST is UNDISSOLVED — a patient man banks a useful report without dropping his watch; a too-useful suspect is still a suspect. She bought the dawn, not the trust. The interest simmers on into future sets.

dm.wreckersReported: T9-set4: the organized flood-wrecker crew (working the flood-empty upper rooms / dead-man rows) is now on the Circle's radar via Sella's report — a live quarter-threat the Circle may move to manage. Harmless to the network (they prey on empty rooms, not the keepers). A true deliverable Sella spent to rebuild cover.

dmlog.dmNotes: T9 = damage control, honestly non-generous. No roll: a TRUE, verifiable deliverable isn't a d20 gamble, and after two failed gambits I do NOT gift her a clean absolution — a patient man banks useful intel and keeps his interest. She buys survival-to-dawn + an innocent frame for the tree-visit (which works because it's genuinely true), but Corran's T6 suspicion persists into future sets. Insight read of Fenn = free competence (his exact-change nothing IS the tell). Fenn referred by role. Hand off toward the close — she understands the real shape of her new life (endless useful service never buys off the patient man's interest).

dmlog.text: Dawn's coming up grey over the chains again — a whole day and night since I walked out that ironwood door, and I'm still breathing, which is the only score that ever mattered. So I take the ledger of it, honest, the way I'd tally a night's work: I healed a little and bled a little; I turned the leash into a weapon and saved a room; I kept my people off his hook and lost the read that would've put my hand on his throat; and I learned the one true rule of the string — you can serve a patient man a hundred years and never once buy his patience back. Fine. He said it himself at the Tree: he's got all the time in the world to work the sum of me. So do I. I'm not going to win this in a night, and a woman who tries to is a woman who ends up in the glass. I'm going to win it the way he'd win it — slow. So I find a safe dry cot at last, the night's wolves all spent, and I lie down east with the counting dead and the sleeping living, and I let myself have the rest I've been chasing since yesterday's dawn. Not hiding. Banking. A knife doesn't have to be drawn to be a knife.
